questions.stem: After storage, the strength of cement:
questions.solution:
**Decreases.**

> The source gives the schedule of loss: **3 months — 20%; 6 months — 30%; 12 months — 40%; 24 months — 50%.** Hence after storage the strength of cement decreases.

**Why cement loses strength in the bag:**

> **Cement is HYGROSCOPIC — it absorbs moisture from the air.**

> **That moisture begins hydrating the cement prematurely, while it is still in the bag.** The compounds that should have reacted with the mixing water have already partly reacted with atmospheric humidity, so less remains to develop strength in the concrete.

> **The reaction also forms lumps**, which is the visible symptom: **a bag containing hard lumps that cannot be crushed between the fingers has aerated and should be rejected.**

**The rate of loss:**

| Storage period | Strength lost |
|---|---|
| **3 months** | **20%** |
| **6 months** | **30%** |
| **12 months** | **40%** |
| **24 months** | **50%** |

> **Note that the loss is FASTEST EARLY ON** — 20% in the first three months, then only another 10% over the next three. The exposed surface reacts first, and the partly hydrated skin then slows further ingress.

> **Which is why the practical rule is a short shelf life rather than a long one with a large discount**: cement older than about **three months should be retested** before structural use.

**Correct storage practice:**

| Requirement | Reason |
|---|---|
| **Raised timber platform, ~150–200 mm above the floor** | Keeps damp out from below |
| **300–450 mm clear of external walls** | Walls carry moisture |
| **Stack height limited to 10 bags** | Prevents **warehouse pack** — consolidation under its own weight |
| **Covered, dry, well-ventilated store** | — |
| **FIRST IN, FIRST OUT** | The oldest cement is used first |

> **"Warehouse pack" is the second, quite separate deterioration mechanism**: cement stacked too high consolidates under pressure into a mass that must be broken up. **It is a handling problem rather than a chemical one, and it does not itself destroy strength**, which is why it is distinguished from aeration.

**Why option (d) is the tempting wrong answer:**

> **"May increase or decrease" would be right for a material whose behaviour depends on conditions.** Cement's does not: **there is no storage condition under which it gains strength.** Even perfect storage merely slows the loss.

> **The direction is one-way**, and that is what makes (a) unambiguous.

**The soundness link:** aerated cement also tends to **fail the soundness test**, because the partly hydrated free lime expands later. **Le Chatelier (free lime) and autoclave (magnesia) tests** are the checks, and a doubtful bag should be tested rather than used on judgement.

examTip.trick: **Cement is HYGROSCOPIC** — it absorbs atmospheric moisture and hydrates prematurely in the bag, so less is left to react with the mixing water. The direction is one-way.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) is tempting but wrong**: there is no storage condition under which cement gains strength. Good storage only slows the loss.
examTip.mnemonic: **20 / 30 / 40 / 50% lost at 3 / 6 / 12 / 24 months** — fastest early, because the reacted skin then slows further ingress. Retest anything over three months old.

questions.stem: What kind of slope do closely spaced equal contour lines indicate?
questions.solution:
**A steep slope.**

> The source states it among the characteristics of contour lines: **if the contour lines are very close to each other, this indicates a STEEP slope; if the contour lines are at a very large distance to each other, this indicates a GENTLE slope.**

**Why — the reasoning is one line:**

> **The contour INTERVAL is the same everywhere on a map — it is the fixed vertical rise between successive lines.**

> **So the horizontal distance between two lines is the ground distance needed to climb that fixed height.**

> **A short horizontal distance for the same rise means a steep gradient. A long one means a gentle gradient.**

> **Slope = contour interval ÷ horizontal spacing**, which makes the relationship exact rather than impressionistic.

**The full properties of contours** — worth having complete, since they are asked directly:

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **Close together** | **STEEP slope** ← |
| **Widely spaced** | **GENTLE slope** |
| **Equally spaced** | **UNIFORM slope** |
| **Never CROSS** | Except at an **OVERHANGING CLIFF or a cave** |
| **Never SPLIT or merge** | — |
| **Close on themselves** | Within the map or beyond its edge |
| **Higher elevation in the centre of closed lines** | A **HILL** |
| **Increasing elevation moving away from closed lines** | A **POND or DEPRESSION** |
| **Steepest slope is the SHORTEST distance between contours** | Perpendicular to the lines |

> **The hill-versus-depression pair is the one most often confused**, and the test is simply which way the values run: **rising toward the centre is a hill, falling toward the centre is a hollow.**

> **A vertical cliff makes contours COINCIDE; only an OVERHANG makes them actually cross**, because only then is one elevation genuinely above another at the same plan position.

**And what fixes the contour interval:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Scale of the map** | **Small scale → LARGE interval**, to avoid overcrowding |
| **Purpose** | Detailed design → small interval |
| **Nature of ground** | **Flat → small interval; steep → large** |
| **Time and funds** | Less available → larger interval |

> **The terrain and scale pull the same way for a reason**: on steep ground the contours already crowd together, so a small interval would merge them into an unreadable band. **The interval is chosen to keep the SPACING on the paper legible** — a drafting constraint as much as a surveying one.

> **The rule of thumb: CI (m) = 25 ÷ (centimetres representing 1 km on the map).**

**Why option (d) is not a slope at all:** **"V-sloped" describes the SHAPE a contour makes in plan, not a gradient.** A V pointing **upstream** indicates a valley; a rounded U pointing **downhill** indicates a ridge. **That is a different property from steepness**, and the question asks about spacing.

examTip.trick: **The contour interval is fixed, so spacing measures gradient directly.** Slope = interval ÷ horizontal spacing — a short distance for the same rise means steep.
examTip.trap: **"V-sloped" is a contour SHAPE, not a gradient.** A V pointing upstream is a valley; a rounded U pointing downhill is a ridge. Different property from steepness.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rising toward the centre of closed contours = HILL; falling = DEPRESSION.** And contours coincide at a vertical cliff but only **cross at an overhang**.

questions.stem: This joint is mostly used at such places where pipes contract or expand due to change in atmospheric temperature:
questions.solution:
**The expansion joint.**

> The source describes it: **this joint is adopted at places where pipes expand or contract due to variation in atmospheric temperature. Here the socket end is cast flanged and the spigot end is plain. A flanged ring and a rubber gasket are arranged in place on the spigot end. Then the spigot end is entered into the socket end and nuts and bolts are secured.**

**Why the joint is needed at all — the magnitude is the point:**

> **Free thermal movement is δ = α L ΔT.**

> **For a 100 m cast iron main (α ≈ 11 × 10⁻⁶/°C) through a 30 °C annual swing:**
>
> **δ = 11 × 10⁻⁶ × 100,000 mm × 30 = 33 mm**

> **Thirty-three millimetres of movement in a buried pipeline is far more than a rigid joint can absorb**, and if it is prevented the pipe develops an axial stress instead:

> **σ = E α ΔT** — and note the **LENGTH CANCELS**. For cast iron at 30 °C that is around **30–40 N/mm²**, regardless of how long the pipe is.

> **So restraint does not become less severe on a short pipe.** A 5 m length fully restrained carries the same stress as a 500 m one.

**How the expansion joint accommodates it:**

> **The spigot is left PLAIN and enters the socket without being fixed against it**, so it can slide axially. **The rubber gasket, compressed by the flanged ring, maintains watertightness while permitting that slide.**

> **Watertight but not rigid** — which is exactly the combination the problem requires, and the reason a bolted flange joint will not do.

**The pipe joint family, as the source sets it out:**

| Joint | Used for |
|---|---|
| **SOCKET and SPIGOT** | **Cast iron of all sizes**; concrete below 60 cm. Filled with **lead, bitumen or sulphur–sand** |
| **EXPANSION joint** | **Thermal movement** ← |
| **FLANGE joint** | **Bolted, RIGID** — where a joint must transmit thrust or be dismantled |
| **SCREW (socket) joint** | Small-diameter GI pipes, threaded |
| **COLLAR joint** | Pipes under pressure |
| **BANDAGE joint** | Concrete pipes, mortar-butted |

> **The FLANGE joint is the instructive contrast: it is rigid by design.** Two flanges bolted face to face transmit axial force, which is what you want at a pump or valve and precisely what you do not want where the pipe must move.

**Where the movement is dealt with in other systems:**

| System | Provision |
|---|---|
| **Buildings** | **Expansion joints every 30–45 m** |
| **Bridges** | **One FIXED bearing, the rest sliding** |
| **Long pipelines** | Expansion joints, bellows, or a deliberate loop |
| **Rails** | Expansion gaps, or stress-relieved continuous welded rail |

> **A buried pipeline is partly restrained by soil friction anyway**, which is why expansion joints are placed at intervals rather than continuously — and why **thrust blocks are needed at bends**, where the unbalanced force has nothing else to react against.

examTip.trick: **The spigot is left PLAIN so it can slide, with a compressed rubber gasket keeping it watertight.** Watertight but not rigid — exactly what thermal movement requires.
examTip.trap: **A FLANGE joint is rigid by design** — two flanges bolted face to face transmit axial force. Right for a pump connection, wrong wherever the pipe must move.
examTip.mnemonic: **σ = EαΔT and the LENGTH CANCELS** — a 5 m restrained pipe carries the same stress as a 500 m one (~30–40 N/mm² for cast iron at 30 °C). Restraint never gets safer by being short.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is INCORRECT regarding a plasticizer?
options: Used for flowing mortar in a heavy dam
Increases strength with reduction in water and increasing cement
Acts as both water reducer and retarder
questions.solution:
**Option (b) is the incorrect statement** — a plasticizer **REDUCES** the cement content, it does not increase it.

> The source's own list of what plasticizers do includes, in its own words: **"Reduce the cement content and water requirement."** Option (b) asserts the opposite.

**Checking each statement against that list:**

| Option | Verdict |
|---|---|
| **(a) Flowing mortar in a heavy dam** | **TRUE** — the source lists "enable the construction of **mass concrete**, pile foundations and pumping concrete" |
| **(b) Reduction in water AND INCREASING cement** | **FALSE — cement is REDUCED, not increased** |
| **(c) Water reducer and retarder** | **TRUE** — many plasticizers are retarding, and the source notes "slow the setting rate while retaining flowing properties" |
| **(d) Workability without affecting strength** | **TRUE** — this is the defining claim of a plasticizer |

**Why (b) is not a small slip but the reverse of the mechanism:**

> **A plasticizer works by DISPERSING flocculated cement particles.** Cement grains carry surface charges and clump together, trapping water inside the flocs where it does no lubricating work.

> **The admixture neutralises those charges, the flocs break up, and the trapped water is released to lubricate the mix.**

> **So the SAME workability is achieved with LESS water** — and since strength depends on the **water–cement ratio**, less water at the same cement content means **higher strength.**

> **Equivalently, the same strength can be had with less cement AND less water**, which is the economy the source refers to. **Either way the cement goes down or stays the same. It never goes up.**

**The three ways a plasticizer can be used, which is what makes (d) true:**

| Objective | How the mix is adjusted |
|---|---|
| **More workability, same strength** | Add the admixture, change nothing else |
| **More strength, same workability** | **Reduce WATER, keep cement** — w/c falls |
| **Same both, lower cost** | **Reduce water AND cement together** — w/c held constant |

> **Option (d) describes the first case exactly**, which is why it is a correct statement rather than the answer.

**Typical water reduction:**

| Admixture | Water reduction |
|---|---|
| **Plasticizer** | **5 – 15%** |
| **SUPERPLASTICIZER** | **15 – 30%** |

> **Superplasticizers are what make modern high-strength and self-compacting concrete possible**, since a w/c ratio low enough for 60 MPa concrete would otherwise be unplaceable.

**And the practical warning:** **adding water on site to improve workability is the malpractice a plasticizer exists to prevent.** Water improves the slump and ruins the strength, invisibly, until the 28-day cubes fail. **A plasticizer buys the same workability without touching the water–cement ratio.**

verification.notes: The source keys option (a), but its own explanation contradicts that on both counts: it lists "enable the construction of mass concrete, pile foundations and pumping concrete" (making (a) a TRUE statement about dam work) and separately states that plasticizers "reduce the cement content and water requirement" (making (b), which claims increasing cement, the FALSE statement). Since the question asks which statement is incorrect, the answer is (b). Corrected to (b) on the source's own reasoning.

examTip.trick: **A plasticizer DEFLOCCULATES cement grains**, releasing water trapped inside the clumps. Same workability with less water — so cement goes down or stays level, never up.
examTip.trap: **The source's key contradicts its own explanation here.** It lists mass-concrete use (making (a) true) and cement reduction (making (b) false). Read the explanation against the letter.
examTip.mnemonic: **Three uses: more workability at the same strength; more strength by cutting WATER; or lower cost by cutting both.** Option (d) is the first of these — a true statement, not the answer.

questions.stem: The expected out-turn of cement concrete 1:2:4 per mason per day will be:
questions.solution:
**5.0 m³.**

> The source defines the term and gives the figure: **the capacity of doing work by an artisan or skilled labour in the form of quantity of work per day is known as the OUT-TURN of the labour.** Its table gives **cement concrete (1:2:4) — 5.0 m³.**

**The out-turn table, as the source sets it out:**

| Item of work | **Out-turn per mason per day** |
|---|---|
| **Cement concrete (1:2:4)** | **5.0 m³** |
| **Lime concrete in foundation** | **8.50 m³** |
| **R.C.C. work** | **3.0 m³** |
| **Brickwork in lime or cement mortar, foundation and plinth** | **1.25 m³** |
| **Reinforced brick work** | **1.0 m³** |

**The ordering is the part worth understanding rather than memorising:**

> **Out-turn falls as the work becomes more INTRICATE, not as it becomes heavier.**

| Work | Why its rate is what it is |
|---|---|
| **Lime concrete, 8.5 m³ — HIGHEST** | Bulk placement, no reinforcement, no precision |
| **Cement concrete, 5.0 m³** | Bulk, but requires proper mixing and compaction |
| **RCC, 3.0 m³** | **Reinforcement must be placed and concrete worked around it** |
| **Brickwork, 1.25 m³** | **Unit-by-unit laying — inherently slow** |
| **Reinforced brickwork, 1.0 m³ — LOWEST** | Unit laying **plus** reinforcement |

> **RCC is only 60% of plain concrete's rate** for exactly one reason: the reinforcement obstructs placing and compaction, and the concrete must be worked into congested cages without displacing the steel.

> **Brickwork is slowest because it is assembled from individual units.** No amount of effort makes laying a thousand bricks as quick as pouring a cubic metre.

**Why out-turn matters:**

> **It converts a QUANTITY of work into a LABOUR COST, which is the labour half of every rate analysis.**

> **Labour required = Quantity ÷ Out-turn**

> **For 40 m³ of 1:2:4 concrete: 40/5.0 = 8 mason-days.**

> **It also drives the CONSTRUCTION PROGRAMME.** The same division gives the duration: **8 mason-days is 8 days with one mason, or 2 days with four** — which is how a bar chart or CPM duration is actually estimated for a labour-driven activity.

**Where it sits in the rate:**

| Component of a rate | Note |
|---|---|
| **Materials** | Quantities per unit, at market rates, **including wastage** |
| **LABOUR** | **From out-turn / task-work figures** ← |
| Plant and machinery | Hire or depreciation |
| **Overheads and contractor's profit** | **10 – 15%** |
| **Water charges** | **1 – 2%** |
| Contingencies | 3 – 5% |

**And the caution about applying published figures:**

> **Out-turn is not a constant of nature.** It varies with the **degree of mechanisation, site access, weather, supervision, worker skill and the size of the pour.**

> **A published table is a starting point for an estimate, not a measurement.** On a constrained urban site with hand mixing it will be optimistic; with a batching plant and pump it will be pessimistic.

> **Which is why a detailed estimate is expected to be accurate to about ±5% and a preliminary one only to ±15–20%** — the labour rates are among the softest numbers in it.

examTip.trick: **Out-turn falls with INTRICACY, not weight.** Lime concrete 8.5 → cement concrete 5.0 → RCC 3.0 → brickwork 1.25 → reinforced brickwork 1.0 m³.
examTip.trap: **RCC is only 60% of plain concrete's rate** — the reinforcement obstructs placing and compaction. That gap is the whole reason the two have separate figures.
examTip.mnemonic: **Labour = Quantity ÷ Out-turn**, which gives both the cost and the DURATION: 40 m³ ÷ 5.0 = 8 mason-days, so 2 days with four masons.

questions.stem: The type of stone used for the construction of a retaining wall is:
questions.solution:
**Heavy.**

> The source's answer is brief and to the point: **stone must be heavy.**

**Why WEIGHT rather than strength is the property that matters:**

> **A gravity retaining wall resists earth pressure by its own DEAD WEIGHT and nothing else.** There is no reinforcement and no anchorage — the wall stands because it is heavy enough not to be pushed over or slid along its base.

> **So the design checks are all weight-driven:**

| Check | Requirement | Role of weight |
|---|---|---|
| **Overturning** | FOS ≥ 1.5 (or 2) | **W provides the restoring moment** |
| **Sliding** | FOS ≥ 1.5 | **F = μW** — friction is proportional to weight |
| **No tension at the base** | Resultant in the **middle third** | Weight pulls the resultant back toward the centre |
| Bearing pressure | Within the safe value | Weight is the load, so this one limits it |

> **Three of the four checks improve with a heavier stone and only the last is worsened by it** — and bearing capacity is usually the easiest to satisfy, since a retaining wall spreads its load over a wide base.

> **That asymmetry is why "heavy" is the answer.** A light stone of excellent crushing strength would make a wall that overturns.

**Why the other options are not the governing property:**

| Option | Comment |
|---|---|
| **Soft** | Wrong outright — soft stone weathers and crushes |
| **Hard** | **Desirable but not the point.** Retaining wall stones carry modest compressive stress; the failure modes are overturning and sliding, not crushing |
| **Light** | **Exactly the wrong direction** |

> **Option (b), "hard", is the trap for anyone who reasons about material strength in the abstract.** Hardness matters for a road aggregate under traffic abrasion, or for a stone carrying a concentrated load. **For a gravity wall, mass is the resource being bought.**

**Typical unit weights, for scale:**

| Stone | Unit weight |
|---|---|
| **Basalt / trap** | **28 – 30 kN/m³** |
| **Granite** | **26 – 28 kN/m³** |
| Limestone | 24 – 26 kN/m³ |
| **Sandstone** | **22 – 24 kN/m³** |

> **Basalt against sandstone is about a 25% difference in restoring moment for the same wall geometry** — which in practice is the difference between a wall that needs a wider base and one that does not.

**And the other requirements of a good building stone**, since they are commonly asked alongside:

| Property | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Crushing strength** | **> 100 N/mm²** for heavy work |
| **Water absorption** | **< 5%**, preferably under 0.6% |
| **Specific gravity** | **> 2.7** for heavy engineering work |
| Hardness (Mohs) | > 17 by Dorry's test for road stone |
| Toughness index | > 19 |
| **Appearance and durability** | Resistant to weathering and frost |

> **Note that a HIGH specific gravity and LOW water absorption tend to go together**, because both follow from a dense, non-porous structure — so a heavy stone is usually a durable one as well. **The requirements are less independent than the list suggests.**

**The drainage point, which matters more than the stone:** **a retaining wall must have WEEP HOLES and a granular backfill drain.** Water accumulating behind it adds a hydrostatic thrust that no reasonable increase in stone weight can offset — **saturated backfill can nearly double the pressure**, and it is the commonest cause of retaining wall failure.

examTip.trick: **A gravity wall stands by its own DEAD WEIGHT.** Overturning, sliding and the middle-third rule all improve with a heavier stone — three checks out of four.
examTip.trap: **"Hard" is the trap.** Hardness matters for road aggregate under abrasion; a retaining wall fails by overturning or sliding, not crushing. Mass is the resource being bought.
examTip.mnemonic: **The stone matters less than the DRAINAGE.** Weep holes and a granular drain are essential — saturated backfill nearly doubles the pressure and is the commonest cause of failure.

questions.stem: The coefficient of passive earth pressure is:
questions.solution:
**K_p = (1 + sinφ)/(1 − sinφ).**

> The source states both coefficients together: **K_p = (1 + sinφ)/(1 − sinφ) and K_a = (1 − sinφ)/(1 + sinφ), where φ is the angle of internal friction.**

**The two are RECIPROCALS, which is the fastest way to keep them straight:**

> **K_p = 1/K_a**

> **Option (b) is K_a**, offered as the obvious distractor — and the discrimination is simply which way up the fraction sits.

**How to be certain which is which, without recall:**

> **PASSIVE resistance is LARGE; ACTIVE pressure is SMALL.** The soil resists far more than it pushes.

> **So K_p must be GREATER THAN 1 and K_a LESS THAN 1.**

> **Since sinφ is positive, (1 + sinφ)/(1 − sinφ) has the larger numerator — it exceeds 1, so it must be the passive one.** Option (b) has the smaller numerator and is therefore active.

> **That check takes two seconds and needs no memory at all.**

**The values at φ = 30°, which are worth carrying:**

| Coefficient | Value at φ = 30° |
|---|---|
| **K_a** | **(1 − 0.5)/(1 + 0.5) = 1/3** |
| **K₀ (at rest)** | **1 − sinφ = 0.5** |
| **K_p** | **(1 + 0.5)/(1 − 0.5) = 3** |

> **A NINEFOLD ratio between passive and active** — and note **K_a < K₀ < K_p always**, with the at-rest value sitting between, since it corresponds to no movement in either direction.

**The tangent forms are equivalent:**

> **K_a = tan²(45° − φ/2)** and **K_p = tan²(45° + φ/2)**

> **Both express the same thing**, and the ± φ/2 tells you which: **subtracting shrinks the angle and gives the small coefficient.**

**The movement required — and why it decides which one is used in design:**

| State | Wall movement needed |
|---|---|
| **ACTIVE** | **Very small — about 0.001 H, AWAY from the soil** |
| **PASSIVE** | **Large — 0.02 to 0.05 H, INTO the soil** |

> **A 5 m wall reaches the active state after moving 5 mm**, which happens during backfilling. **It would need 100–250 mm to mobilise full passive resistance** — far more than any structure can tolerate.

> **Which is why passive resistance is routinely DISCOUNTED or ignored**: it exists, but the movement needed to develop it would render the structure unserviceable first.

**And a caution about Rankine's assumptions**, since this is Rankine's coefficient:

> **Rankine assumes a vertical, SMOOTH wall with NO WALL FRICTION**, a planar rupture surface, and a cohesionless, homogeneous, semi-infinite soil in plastic equilibrium.

> **Neglecting wall friction OVERESTIMATES active pressure — which is SAFE — but for PASSIVE pressure the position reverses.** Coulomb's theory, which includes wall friction, badly **overestimates** passive resistance at high φ because the real failure surface is **curved, not plane**.

> **So the conservatism runs opposite ways for the two states**, and that is the single most important practical point about earth pressure theory.

examTip.trick: **Passive resistance is LARGE, so K_p > 1.** Only (1 + sinφ)/(1 − sinφ) has the bigger numerator. Two seconds, no memory needed.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) is K_a** — the same fraction inverted. K_p = 1/K_a, so the only question is which way up it sits.
examTip.mnemonic: **At φ = 30°: K_a = 1/3, K₀ = 0.5, K_p = 3** — a ninefold ratio. And passive needs **0.02–0.05 H** of movement, which is why it is usually discounted in design.

questions.stem: Sands of zone I are:
questions.solution:
**Coarse sand.**

> The source states the two ends of the scale: **sand zone I represents COARSE sand whereas zone IV represents FINE sand.**

**The four grading zones of fine aggregate (IS 383):**

| Zone | Grading | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **I** | **COARSEST** | Coarse sand ← |
| **II** | Medium | **The general-purpose zone; most natural sands** |
| **III** | Fine | Finer sand |
| **IV** | **FINEST** | **Very fine — restricted use** |

> **The numbering runs COARSE to FINE, which is worth fixing because intuition often runs the other way** — one might expect zone I to be the finest, as with sieve numbering where a higher number means a finer mesh.

> **Here the zone number and the fineness increase together: I is coarsest, IV is finest.**

**How the zones are defined:**

> **By the percentage passing the 600 micron sieve** — the single most discriminating sieve for sand:

| Zone | Passing 600 µm |
|---|---|
| **I** | **15 – 34%** |
| **II** | **35 – 59%** |
| **III** | **60 – 79%** |
| **IV** | **80 – 100%** |

> **A sand with only 15–34% passing 600 µm has most of its material coarser than that**, which is what makes zone I coarse. **Zone IV, with 80–100% passing, is almost entirely finer.**

**Which zone to use, and why it matters:**

| Zone | Suitability |
|---|---|
| **I and II** | **Preferred for structural concrete** |
| **III** | Usable, with mix adjustment |
| **IV** | **NOT recommended for RCC unless tested; restricted to mortar and plaster** |

> **Zone IV is restricted for a definite reason: very fine sand has a large SPECIFIC SURFACE AREA**, so it demands much more water to wet all its particles for the same workability.

> **More water means a higher water–cement ratio, and by Abrams' law that means lower strength.** The fineness is not itself a defect; the water demand it creates is.

> **Conversely a very coarse sand gives a harsh, unworkable mix that segregates and finishes badly** — which is why zone I is acceptable but zone II is preferred.

**The FINENESS MODULUS, which measures the same thing on one number:**

> **FM = (sum of cumulative percentages retained) ÷ 100**

| Aggregate | Fineness modulus |
|---|---|
| **Fine sand** | **2.2 – 2.6** |
| **Medium sand** | **2.6 – 2.9** |
| **Coarse sand** | **2.9 – 3.2** |
| Coarse aggregate | 5.5 – 8.0 |

> **A higher FM means a coarser aggregate**, so FM and zone number run in **opposite** directions — zone I has the highest FM. **That inversion is a genuine trap when the two systems appear in the same question.**

**And the practical consequence for mix design:** the **coarse aggregate to fine aggregate ratio must be adjusted for the zone.** IS 10262 gives the volume of coarse aggregate for zone II, and it is **increased for zone I and decreased for zones III and IV** — because a finer sand already supplies more of the fine fraction the mix needs.

examTip.trick: **Zone number and fineness increase together: I is COARSEST, IV is FINEST.** Defined by the percentage passing the 600 µm sieve — 15–34% for zone I, 80–100% for zone IV.
examTip.trap: **FINENESS MODULUS runs the OPPOSITE way** — zone I has the highest FM (2.9–3.2). When both systems appear in one question, that inversion is the trap.
examTip.mnemonic: **Zone IV is restricted because fine sand has a huge SPECIFIC SURFACE AREA** — it demands more water, raising w/c and cutting strength. The fineness isn't the defect; the water demand is.

questions.stem: The gradual decrease in volume of soil on application of load due to expulsion of air is called:
questions.solution:
**Compaction.**

> The source gives the pair in one line: **consolidation — expulsion of pore WATER; compaction — expulsion of pore AIR.**

**The stem contains the discriminator, and it is a single word:**

> **"Expulsion of AIR" identifies compaction. "Expulsion of WATER" would identify consolidation.**

> **Nothing else in the question needs to be read** — and that is exactly how this pair is examined, in almost every paper.

**The two processes in full:**

| | **COMPACTION** | **CONSOLIDATION** |
|---|---|---|
| **Expels** | **AIR** | **WATER** |
| Soil state | **Partially saturated** | **Fully SATURATED** |
| Cause | **MECHANICAL energy** — rolling, ramming, vibration | **Sustained LOAD** |
| **Time** | **MINUTES** | **YEARS** |
| Nature | **ARTIFICIAL — an engineering operation** | **NATURAL — a response to loading** |
| Test | **PROCTOR** | **OEDOMETER** |

> **Compaction expels AIR in minutes by machine; consolidation expels WATER over years under load.** Those two sentences separate them completely.

**Why options (a) and (c) are the more interesting distractors:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **COLLAPSE** | **A sudden loss of volume when a partly saturated soil is WETTED** — collapsible soils such as loess. Caused by **adding water**, not by expelling air |
| **SHRINKAGE** | **Volume reduction on DRYING**, from capillary tension as water leaves. Caused by **removing water**, and needs **no applied load at all** |

> **Both are genuine volume-change phenomena, which is what makes them plausible** — but each is driven by a change in water content rather than by an applied load expelling air.

> **The stem specifies "on application of LOAD", which rules out shrinkage immediately**, since a soil shrinks on drying whether it is loaded or not.

> **COLLAPSE is worth knowing properly** because it is genuinely dangerous: a loess or lightly cemented silt can carry a structure for years and then lose volume abruptly when a leaking drain wets it. **The trigger is water arriving, not load.**

**The Proctor test, which defines compaction in practice:**

| | **Standard Proctor** | **Modified Proctor** |
|---|---|---|
| Blows per layer | **25** | **25** |
| Layers | **3** | **5** |
| Hammer | **2.6 kg, 310 mm drop** | **4.89 kg, 450 mm drop** |
| **Compactive energy** | **≈ 592 kJ/m³** | **≈ 2674 kJ/m³ — about 4.5×** |

> **More energy gives a HIGHER maximum dry density at a LOWER optimum moisture content** — the whole compaction curve shifts up and to the left.

> **That is the single most useful fact about the test**, and it explains why a modified Proctor specification cannot be met at the standard test's optimum moisture.

**And the field control:** **relative compaction = (field dry density ÷ laboratory maximum dry density) × 100**, typically specified at **95% for embankments and 98% for subgrades**, with the moisture held within about **±2% of optimum** — because compacting dry of optimum leaves air behind and wet of optimum makes the soil unstable under the roller.

examTip.trick: **One word decides it: AIR means compaction, WATER means consolidation.** Nothing else in the stem needs reading.
examTip.trap: **COLLAPSE and SHRINKAGE are real volume changes**, but each is driven by a change in water content — collapse by wetting, shrinkage by drying. The stem says "on application of load".
examTip.mnemonic: **Modified Proctor has 4.5× the energy of standard**, which shifts the curve UP and LEFT — higher max dry density at LOWER optimum moisture. That is why the two specifications are not interchangeable.

questions.stem: As per IS code, what is the maximum permissible settlement for an isolated foundation on sand?
questions.solution:
**40 mm.**

> The source quotes IS 1904: **for isolated foundations the maximum permissible settlement is 40 mm on sandy soil and 65 mm in clayey soils. For a raft foundation, 65 mm on sandy soil and 65–100 mm on clay. Differential settlement: 25 mm for a foundation on sand and 40 mm on clay.**

**The permissible settlements, as a set:**

| Foundation | **On SAND** | **On CLAY** |
|---|---|---|
| **Isolated footing** | **40 mm** | **65 mm** |
| **RAFT** | **65 mm** | **65 – 100 mm** |
| **DIFFERENTIAL** | **25 mm** | **40 mm** |

**Two patterns run through that table, and both have reasons:**

> **1. CLAY is allowed MORE than sand.**
>
> **Settlement on sand is IMMEDIATE — it occurs as the load is applied, during construction.** Settlement on clay is **CONSOLIDATION settlement, spread over years.**
>
> **Slow settlement is far less damaging**, because the structure and its finishes can accommodate gradual movement by creep and minor cracking. **The same total settlement arriving suddenly would crack it.**

> **2. A RAFT is allowed MORE than an isolated footing.**
>
> **A raft is a single stiff element, so it tends to settle as a unit** — and uniform settlement does little harm.
>
> **Isolated footings settle independently of one another**, so their total settlement translates much more directly into DIFFERENTIAL settlement between columns.

**Which is the point that matters most:**

> **DIFFERENTIAL settlement causes the damage, not total settlement.**

> **A building that settles 100 mm uniformly is undamaged — the door frames still fit and nothing is distorted.** One that settles 25 mm at one corner and nothing at another is cracked.

> **Hence the differential limits (25 mm on sand, 40 mm on clay) are the tighter and more meaningful numbers**, and the ANGULAR DISTORTION limit is tighter still:

| Distortion (δ/L) | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **1/500** | **Safe limit for framed buildings** |
| 1/300 | Cracking in panel walls likely |
| **1/150** | **Structural damage** |

> **And note that a rigid load-bearing masonry structure is far more sensitive than a framed one**, because it has no ductility — a frame redistributes, a brick wall cracks.

**The design consequence:**

> **SAFE BEARING CAPACITY is the LESSER of two values** — the shear-failure capacity divided by a factor of safety of 2.5–3, and the pressure that produces the permissible settlement.

> **On sand, SETTLEMENT usually governs rather than shear failure**, because sand is generally strong in shear but compressible. **On soft clay, shear failure is more often critical.**

> **Which is why footings under one structure are often proportioned for EQUAL PRESSURE rather than equal factor of safety** — equal pressure gives more nearly equal settlement, and it is differential settlement that must be controlled.

**A note on the option set:** **10 mm and 20 mm are both below even the DIFFERENTIAL limit of 25 mm**, so they can be discarded as implausibly tight for a total settlement. **60 mm is close to the clay figure of 65 mm** — right table, wrong soil.

examTip.trick: **Clay is allowed MORE than sand** because clay settlement is slow consolidation while sand settles immediately — gradual movement is far less damaging than sudden.
examTip.trap: **60 mm is close to the CLAY figure (65 mm)** — right table, wrong soil. And 10/20 mm are below even the 25 mm differential limit, so they cannot be total-settlement values.
examTip.mnemonic: **DIFFERENTIAL settlement does the damage: 25 mm sand, 40 mm clay, angular distortion 1/500.** A building settling 100 mm uniformly is undamaged; 25 mm at one corner cracks it.

questions.stem: Which type of roller should be selected to have effective compaction of coarse grained soil?
questions.solution:
**A vibratory roller.**

> The source's table matches equipment to soil: **rammers or tampers — all soils; smooth wheel rollers — crushed rocks, gravels, sand; pneumatic tyre roller — sand, gravel, silt, clayey soil; sheep foot roller — clayey soil; VIBRATORY roller — SAND.**

**Why vibration is the right mechanism for a coarse soil:**

> **A coarse-grained soil is compacted by REARRANGING its particles into a denser packing.** The grains must slide and roll past one another into the gaps.

> **Vibration is what breaks the inter-particle friction that holds them in a loose arrangement.** Under vibration the grains momentarily lose contact, and gravity settles them into a tighter configuration.

> **Static pressure alone cannot do this** — it presses the existing arrangement down without letting the grains find better positions.

> **And a cohesionless soil has no cohesion to resist the rearranging**, which is precisely why the method works so well on sand and not on clay.

**The equipment-to-soil match, and the reason behind each:**

| Roller | Suits | Mechanism |
|---|---|---|
| **VIBRATORY** | **Sand, gravel — cohesionless** | **Vibration rearranges particles** |
| **SHEEP FOOT (sheepsfoot)** | **CLAY — cohesive** | **KNEADING action; the feet penetrate and remould the clay** |
| **SMOOTH WHEELED** | Crushed rock, gravel, sand; **finishing surfaces** | **Static pressure** |
| **PNEUMATIC TYRE** | **Wide range — sand, gravel, silt, clay** | Kneading plus static pressure |
| Rammers / tampers | **All soils; confined spaces and trenches** | Impact |

> **The sheepsfoot roller is the exact counterpart of this question**, and it is the classic paired distractor: **it is the CLAY roller.** Its protruding feet penetrate the layer and knead the cohesive soil, which is what a clay needs and what vibration cannot supply.

> **Asking "cohesive or cohesionless?" answers most compaction-equipment questions on its own.**

**Why a PNEUMATIC roller is the reasonable second answer:**

> **It genuinely does suit sand** — the source's own table lists sand first among its soils. **But it suits everything**, which makes it a general-purpose machine rather than the *effective* choice the question asks for.

> **Where a question asks for the MOST effective rather than a workable option, the specialist machine wins.**

**The Proctor curve, which is what any roller is trying to reach:**

> **Dry density plotted against moisture content peaks at the OPTIMUM MOISTURE CONTENT and the MAXIMUM DRY DENSITY.**

| Compacting | Result |
|---|---|
| **Dry of optimum** | Air remains; density below maximum |
| **At optimum** | **Maximum dry density** |
| **Wet of optimum** | **Water occupies volume the solids could have; the soil becomes unstable under the roller** |

> **Note that a cohesionless soil's curve is FLAT** compared with a clay's — its density is far less sensitive to moisture, which is why sand can be compacted over a wide moisture range and why **saturating it ("flooding and vibrating") is sometimes used deliberately.**

> **A clay's curve is sharply peaked**, so its moisture must be controlled within about **±2% of optimum** or the specified density is unreachable at any number of passes.

**And the field controls that go with it:** **layer thickness 200–300 mm loose, 4 to 8 passes**, with **relative compaction 95% for embankments and 98% for subgrades.** Exceeding the layer thickness is the commonest site failure — the roller's influence does not reach the bottom of a thick lift, whatever the pass count.

examTip.trick: **Ask cohesive or cohesionless.** Vibration rearranges the grains of a cohesionless soil; a clay needs the KNEADING of a sheepsfoot roller. That one question answers most equipment problems.
examTip.trap: **The pneumatic roller genuinely suits sand too** — but it suits everything, so it is the general-purpose machine, not the *effective* one. When a question asks for the most effective, the specialist wins.
examTip.mnemonic: **A sand's Proctor curve is FLAT; a clay's is sharply PEAKED.** So sand compacts over a wide moisture range, while clay must be held within ±2% of optimum.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a correct formula for dry density?
questions.solution:
**All of the above** — the three expressions are the same quantity written for different given data.

> The source confirms it: **Gγ_w/(1+e), γ_b/(1+w) and (1−n_a)Gγ_w/(1+wG) — these all are correct formulas for dry density.**

**Why there are three, and when each is used:**

| Expression | Use it when you know | Derivation |
|---|---|---|
| **G γ_w/(1 + e)** | **Void ratio e** | Weight of solids per total volume |
| **γ_b/(1 + w)** | **Bulk unit weight and water content** | Strips the water out of the bulk weight |
| **(1 − n_a) G γ_w/(1 + wG)** | **Air content n_a** | The general form, valid at any saturation |

> **They are not competing formulae — they are the same relationship expressed in whichever variables happen to be measured.**

**The middle one is the one used most, and it is worth being able to derive:**

> **γ_d = W_solids/V** and **γ_b = (W_solids + W_water)/V = W_solids(1 + w)/V**
>
> **Therefore γ_b = γ_d(1 + w), so γ_d = γ_b/(1 + w)** ✓

> **That is the everyday field calculation**: a core cutter or sand replacement test gives the bulk density, an oven gives the water content, and this converts one to the other.

**The third is the general case, and the other two are its special cases:**

> **At full saturation n_a = 0, and the expression reduces to γ_d = Gγ_w/(1 + wG)** — the saturated form.

> **Substituting the fundamental relation Se = wG** (with S = 1 at saturation, so e = wG) **turns that into Gγ_w/(1 + e)**, which is the first expression.

> **So all three collapse into one another through Se = wG** — the single most useful identity in soil phase relationships, and the reason the question's answer is "all".

**Why DRY density rather than bulk density is the quantity specified:**

> **Bulk density depends on how wet the soil happens to be, so it is not a measure of how well compacted it is.**

> **Dry density measures the mass of SOLIDS packed into a unit volume**, which is exactly what compaction is trying to maximise.

> **Two samples of identical bulk density can have quite different dry densities** if their moisture contents differ — and only the dry density tells you which is the better fill.

> **Hence every compaction specification is written in terms of dry density**, and relative compaction is **field dry density ÷ laboratory maximum dry density.**

**The related phase relationships:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **Void ratio** | **e = n/(1 − n)** |
| **Porosity** | **n = e/(1 + e)** |
| **Degree of saturation** | **Se = wG** |
| **Saturated unit weight** | **(G + e)γ_w/(1 + e)** |
| **Submerged unit weight** | **(G − 1)γ_w/(1 + e)** |
| **Bulk unit weight** | **(G + Se)γ_w/(1 + e)** |

> **Notice that every one of them has (1 + e) in the denominator.** That is because **e is defined against the volume of SOLIDS**, so a total volume is always (1 + e) units when the solids are taken as 1.

> **Recognising that turns six formulae into one pattern**, and it is the fastest way to reconstruct any of them under examination conditions.

examTip.trick: **All three are the same quantity in different variables** — chosen by whether you know e, or γ_b and w, or the air content. They collapse into one another through **Se = wG**.
examTip.trap: **Derive the everyday one rather than memorising it**: γ_b = γ_d(1 + w), so γ_d = γ_b/(1 + w). That is the field calculation from a core cutter plus an oven.
examTip.mnemonic: **Every phase formula has (1 + e) beneath it**, because e is defined against the volume of SOLIDS — so the total volume is (1 + e) when solids are 1. Six formulae, one pattern.

questions.stem: Which of the following factors does NOT affect soil compaction?
questions.solution:
**Bed stability.**

> The source's answer is direct: **bed stability.**

**The factors that genuinely govern compaction:**

| Factor | Effect |
|---|---|
| **MOISTURE CONTENT** | **The most important — there is an OPTIMUM, not a maximum** |
| **COMPACTIVE EFFORT** | More energy → higher max dry density at **lower** optimum moisture |
| **TYPE of compaction** | **Impact, kneading, static pressure or vibration — each suits a different soil** |
| **SOIL TYPE and grading** | **Well graded compacts denser than uniform** |
| **Number of blows / passes** | Part of the compactive effort |
| Admixtures, layer thickness | Secondary but real |

> **Options (a), (b) and (c) are three of the four principal factors**, which is what makes this a clean discrimination rather than a guess.

**Why "bed stability" is not among them:**

> **It is not a recognised parameter of compaction at all.** The term belongs to river hydraulics — the stability of a channel bed against scour — not to soil mechanics.

> **Compaction is governed by what is done to the soil (energy, method, number of passes) and by what the soil is (type, grading, moisture).** "Bed stability" describes neither.

> **Where a plausible-sounding term appears among three genuine technical factors, checking whether it belongs to the subject at all is the fastest route to the answer.**

**The most important factor, since the question invites the comparison:**

> **MOISTURE CONTENT, and the key insight is that more is not better.**

| Compacting | Result |
|---|---|
| **Dry of optimum** | Insufficient lubrication; air remains trapped |
| **AT OPTIMUM** | **Maximum dry density** |
| **Wet of optimum** | **Water occupies volume the solids could have taken** |

> **Water lubricates the particles so they slide into a denser packing — but past a point it starts occupying space itself**, and since dry density counts only solids, the density falls.

> **That is why the compaction curve has a PEAK rather than rising indefinitely**, and it is the single most examined idea in the topic.

**And the effect of compactive effort:**

> **Increasing the energy shifts the whole curve UP and to the LEFT** — a higher maximum dry density at a **lower** optimum moisture content.

> **Modified Proctor has about 4.5 times the energy of standard Proctor** (2674 against 592 kJ/m³), which is exactly why a modified specification cannot be achieved at the standard test's optimum moisture.

**The line of optimums and the zero air voids line:**

> **No compaction curve can cross the ZERO AIR VOIDS line**, which is the theoretical density at 100% saturation. **The curves approach it but never reach it**, because some air is always trapped.

> **The peaks of curves at different energies fall along the LINE OF OPTIMUMS**, roughly parallel to the zero air voids line at about **80–90% saturation.**

> **A field result plotting above the zero air voids line is impossible and indicates a test error** — usually a wrong specific gravity — which makes it a useful check on laboratory data.

examTip.trick: **"Bed stability" belongs to river hydraulics, not soil mechanics.** When one plausible-sounding term sits among three genuine factors, ask whether it belongs to the subject at all.
examTip.trap: **Moisture content has an OPTIMUM, not a maximum.** Water lubricates the grains, then starts occupying space itself — which is why the curve peaks instead of rising.
examTip.mnemonic: **More energy shifts the curve UP and LEFT.** And no curve can cross the **ZERO AIR VOIDS line** — a result above it means a test error, usually a wrong specific gravity.

questions.stem: Which of the following does NOT contribute to the stability of a slope?
questions.solution:
**An increased slope angle** — it reduces stability rather than contributing to it.

> The source explains: **as the slope angle increases, the driving forces (gravity) acting downslope become greater. This can lead to instability, especially if the resisting forces (shear strength of the soil) are insufficient.**

**The factor of safety, which frames the whole question:**

> **FOS = Resisting forces ÷ Driving forces = Shear strength available ÷ Shear stress mobilised**

> **Every stabilising measure works by RAISING the numerator or LOWERING the denominator.** Steepening the slope does the opposite — it raises the driving force.

**How each option acts:**

| Measure | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Surface drainage** | **Prevents infiltration**, so pore pressure does not rise |
| **Sub-surface drainage** | **LOWERS pore pressure directly — raises effective stress and hence strength** |
| **Retaining wall** | **Adds an external resisting force** |
| **Increased slope angle** | **RAISES the driving force — destabilising** ✗ |

**Why the two drainage measures are the most effective of the three:**

> **Shear strength depends on EFFECTIVE stress: τ = c′ + σ′ tanφ′, with σ′ = σ − u.**

> **Raising the pore pressure u directly reduces σ′ and therefore the strength available** — without any change to the soil itself or to the load on it.

> **This is why the overwhelming majority of slope failures occur during or just after heavy rainfall**, and it is why drainage is almost always the cheapest and most effective remedial measure.

> **In Nepal's monsoon that is not a refinement but the central design consideration** — a slope that stands for eleven months can fail in the twelfth for no reason other than pore pressure.

**And RAPID DRAWDOWN is the mirror-image case worth knowing:**

> **When water in front of a slope falls quickly, the external support disappears while the pore pressure inside has not yet dissipated.**

> **Effective stress falls and the slope fails.** Earth dam **upstream** slopes are checked specifically for this, and it is often more critical than the reservoir being full.

**The methods of analysis:**

| Method | Applies to |
|---|---|
| **Infinite slope** | Long uniform slopes; **failure parallel to the surface** |
| **Swedish circle / method of slices** | **Finite slopes, circular arc — the general workhorse** |
| **Taylor's stability number** | Rapid check: **S_n = c/(F γ H)** |
| **Bishop's simplified method** | Slices, with inter-slice forces — more accurate |
| Friction circle | φ-c soils |

> **For a purely cohesive slope (φ = 0), Taylor's chart gives S_n = 0.261 for a vertical cut**, hence **H_c = 3.83 c/γ** — very close to the **4c/γ** obtained from Rankine's plane-wedge analysis, the small difference arising because Taylor assumes a **circular** failure surface.

**The three failure modes:**

| Mode | Occurs |
|---|---|
| **Face failure** | Weak soil in the upper part |
| **TOE failure** | **The usual case for steeper slopes** |
| **BASE failure** | **Flat slopes over a soft deep layer — the arc passes BELOW the toe** |

> **Base failure is the one most often missed**, because the failure surface lies outside the slope itself and an analysis that only considers arcs through the toe will not find it.

examTip.trick: **FOS = resisting ÷ driving.** Every stabilising measure raises the numerator or lowers the denominator; steepening the slope raises the driving force instead.
examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. The other three are all genuine stabilising measures — and the two drainage ones are the most effective of them.
examTip.mnemonic: **τ = c′ + σ′tanφ′ with σ′ = σ − u**, so rising pore pressure destroys strength without touching the soil or the load. That is why slopes fail in the monsoon — and why **rapid drawdown** is the mirror case.

questions.stem: The coefficient of curvature for well graded soil lies between:
questions.solution:
**1 to 3.**

> The source states it: **coefficient of curvature — for well graded soil, 1 < C_c < 3; for gap graded soil, C_c < 1 or C_c > 3.**

**The two grading coefficients:**

> **Coefficient of UNIFORMITY: C_u = D₆₀/D₁₀**
>
> **Coefficient of CURVATURE: C_c = D₃₀²/(D₆₀ × D₁₀)**

| Particle size | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **D₁₀** | Size at 10% finer — the **EFFECTIVE SIZE** |
| **D₃₀** | Size at 30% finer |
| **D₆₀** | Size at 60% finer |

**What each coefficient tells you — and they are not interchangeable:**

| Coefficient | Measures | Well graded requires |
|---|---|---|
| **C_u** | **The RANGE of sizes present** | **> 6 for sand, > 4 for gravel** |
| **C_c** | **Whether the distribution is SMOOTH or has a GAP** | **Between 1 and 3** |

> **C_u alone is not enough, and that is the whole reason C_c exists.**

> **A soil can have a wide range of sizes (large C_u) and still be badly graded** if the middle sizes are missing — coarse gravel mixed with fine sand and nothing in between.

> **C_u would report that soil as well graded; C_c catches the gap**, because D₃₀ then sits far from where a smooth curve would put it and the ratio falls outside 1–3.

> **So the two conditions must BOTH be satisfied**, and a question asking for "well graded" without both is incomplete.

**Why well graded soil is wanted:**

> **The smaller particles fill the voids between the larger ones**, so a well graded soil reaches a **higher maximum dry density** and a **lower void ratio** than a uniform one.

| Property | Well graded | Uniform (poorly graded) |
|---|---|---|
| **Max dry density** | **HIGHER** | Lower |
| **Void ratio** | **LOWER** | Higher |
| **Shear strength / φ** | **HIGHER** | Lower |
| **Permeability** | **LOWER** | Higher |
| Compactibility | Good | Poorer |

> **That is why a well graded material is specified for a fill, a sub-base or a concrete aggregate** — it packs densely with less binder and less compactive effort.

> **And why a UNIFORM material is chosen where PERMEABILITY is the object** — a filter or drainage layer needs the voids left open, so a single-size aggregate is used deliberately.

**The USCS symbols that follow:**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **GW / SW** | **Well graded** gravel / sand |
| **GP / SP** | **Poorly graded** gravel / sand |
| GM / SM | Silty gravel / sand |
| GC / SC | Clayey gravel / sand |

> **Note that "poorly graded" in USCS covers BOTH uniform and gap-graded soils** — the classification does not distinguish them, though their behaviour differs. **A gap-graded soil is also liable to internal erosion**, because the fine fraction can wash through the voids of the coarse.

> **Which is why filter design uses explicit criteria (Terzaghi's D₁₅/D₈₅ rules) rather than relying on a grading label.**

examTip.trick: **C_c = D₃₀²/(D₆₀ × D₁₀) between 1 and 3**, AND C_u > 6 (sand) or > 4 (gravel). Both conditions are required — either alone is insufficient.
examTip.trap: **C_u can report a GAP-GRADED soil as well graded**, because it only measures the range of sizes. C_c exists precisely to catch the missing middle sizes.
examTip.mnemonic: **Well graded packs densely — higher density, lower voids, higher φ, LOWER permeability.** Which is why filters use UNIFORM material deliberately: the voids must stay open.

questions.stem: The difference between the total energy line and the hydraulic grade line represents the:
questions.solution:
**The velocity head.**

> The source states it: **HGL = TEL − velocity head, so velocity head = TEL − HGL. The difference between the total head line and the hydraulic gradient line is always constant for a particular pipe flow and it is equal to the velocity head.**

**What each line plots:**

| Line | Plots |
|---|---|
| **TEL (total energy line)** | **z + p/γ + V²/2g** — all three heads |
| **HGL (hydraulic grade line)** | **z + p/γ** — the **PIEZOMETRIC** head only |
| **Difference** | **V²/2g — the VELOCITY head** ✓ |

> **Subtracting one from the other leaves exactly the term the HGL omits.** No recall is needed — it falls straight out of the definitions.

**Why option (a) is the interesting distractor:**

> **"Piezometric head" is what the HGL ITSELF represents (z + p/γ), not the difference.** It is the right term attached to the wrong line, which is a more convincing error than simply naming a wrong quantity.

**The behaviour of the two lines:**

| Property | TEL | HGL |
|---|---|---|
| **Direction** | **ALWAYS falls** in the flow direction (unless a pump adds energy) | **May rise or fall** |
| Position | Upper | **ALWAYS below the TEL** |
| In a uniform-diameter pipe | — | **PARALLEL to the TEL** |

> **The TEL can only fall because energy is only lost, never gained, without external input** — that is the second law applied to a pipe.

> **The HGL can RISE, and the case where it does is worth knowing: in an EXPANDING pipe** the velocity falls, so velocity head converts back into pressure head and the HGL climbs even as the TEL continues to drop.

> **In a uniform pipe the velocity is constant, so the gap between them is constant and the two run parallel** — which is exactly what makes the difference a well-defined single value in this question.

**Two practical readings of the diagram:**

> **1. Where the HGL falls BELOW the pipe, the pressure is NEGATIVE.** The pipe is under suction, air can be drawn in through joints, and if the pressure approaches the vapour pressure the water will **cavitate**.

> **2. The HGL is the level to which water would rise in a piezometer** inserted at that point — which is what makes it directly measurable rather than merely notional.

> **A siphon works entirely in the region where the HGL is below the pipe**, and the limit on its height is set by exactly this: the pressure cannot fall below the vapour pressure, which caps the practical suction lift at about **7 m** against the theoretical 10.3 m.

**And the source's own closing observation, which is a good check on understanding:**

> **The TEL and HGL can never intersect in a pipe flow**, because at the intersection the velocity head would be zero — meaning the flow has stopped, which is impossible in a flowing pipe.

**Bernoulli's equation with losses**, for completeness:

> **z₁ + p₁/γ + V₁²/2g = z₂ + p₂/γ + V₂²/2g + h_L**

> **h_L is the vertical drop of the TEL between the two sections**, which is the most useful way to read the diagram: **the slope of the TEL is the rate of energy loss.**

examTip.trick: **TEL = z + p/γ + V²/2g; HGL = z + p/γ.** Subtracting leaves exactly the term the HGL omits — the velocity head. It falls out of the definitions.
examTip.trap: **"Piezometric head" is what the HGL ITSELF is**, not the difference — the right term on the wrong line, which makes it the convincing distractor.
examTip.mnemonic: **The TEL can only FALL; the HGL may RISE** (in an expanding pipe, velocity head converts back to pressure). And where the HGL drops below the pipe, the pressure is **negative**.

questions.stem: The rise of a liquid in a capillary tube is due to:
questions.solution:
**Surface tension.**

> The source states it: **capillary rise is mainly caused due to cohesive forces in the liquid and adhesive forces acting between the liquid and the tube material. Surface tension is the property by which liquid surfaces act like a stretched elastic membrane. The rise of a liquid in a capillary tube is due to surface tension.**

**The mechanism:**

> **ADHESION between the liquid and the tube wall pulls the liquid up; COHESION within the liquid holds the column together so it rises as one body.**

> **Surface tension is the manifestation of that cohesion at the surface**, and it is what supports the weight of the raised column.

> **The equilibrium is a simple force balance: the vertical component of the surface tension around the perimeter carries the weight of the water lifted.**

**The formula follows directly from that balance:**

> **Surface tension force = σ × (πd) × cosθ**
>
> **Weight lifted = γ × (πd²/4) × h**
>
> **Equating: h = 4σcosθ/(γd)**

> **The key result is h ∝ 1/d — the NARROWER the tube, the HIGHER the rise.**

> **The reason is a ratio of geometry: the supporting force grows with the PERIMETER (d) while the weight grows with the AREA (d²).** Halving the diameter halves the force but quarters the weight, so the rise doubles.

**Contact angle decides the direction:**

| Liquid on glass | θ | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **Water** | **≈ 0° — WETTING** | **RISES; concave meniscus** |
| **Mercury** | **≈ 130° — NON-WETTING** | **DEPRESSES; convex meniscus** |

> **cos130° is negative, so the formula returns a negative rise — a depression.** Mercury's cohesion exceeds its adhesion to glass, so the liquid pulls away from the wall rather than climbing it.

> **The same formula covers both cases**, which is why the contact angle rather than a separate rule handles the difference.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Viscosity** | Resistance to **SHEAR** — it governs how FAST the liquid rises, not how high |
| **Osmosis** | Solvent movement across a **semi-permeable membrane** — there is none here |
| **Diffusion** | Mixing by molecular motion down a concentration gradient |

> **Viscosity is the instructive distractor**, because it genuinely acts during the rise: **a viscous liquid climbs slowly.** But the **equilibrium height** is set entirely by surface tension, and viscosity has dropped out of the force balance because there is no motion at equilibrium.

> **"How fast" and "how high" are different questions**, and only one of them is asked.

**Where capillarity matters in civil engineering:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Capillary rise in soils** | **Clay 10–30 m, silt 1–10 m, sand 0.1–1 m** |
| **FROST HEAVE** | Capillary feeding of growing ice lenses |
| **Apparent cohesion in moist sand** | Menisci bind the grains — the sandcastle effect |
| **Rising damp in masonry** | Hence the damp proof course |
| Manometer correction | Tubes specified at **≥ 6 mm bore** |

> **SILT is the most frost-susceptible soil** because it has **both** a substantial capillary rise **and** enough permeability to feed a growing ice lens quickly. **Clay has the rise but is too impermeable; sand is permeable but has too little rise.**

> **And apparent cohesion is the practically dangerous one: moist sand stands in a vertical cut because of its menisci — and that cohesion VANISHES on saturation or on complete drying**, which is why trench faces collapse after rain.

examTip.trick: **h = 4σcosθ/(γd), so h ∝ 1/d.** The supporting force grows with the PERIMETER while the weight grows with the AREA — halve the diameter and the rise doubles.
examTip.trap: **Viscosity genuinely acts during the rise** — a viscous liquid climbs slowly. But the equilibrium HEIGHT is set by surface tension alone. "How fast" and "how high" are different questions.
examTip.mnemonic: **cos130° is negative, so mercury DEPRESSES** — one formula covers both by way of the contact angle. And **SILT heaves worst**: enough rise AND enough permeability to feed an ice lens.

questions.stem: For liquid fluids, the capillary rise (or fall) will ______ with a rise in temperature.
questions.solution:
**Decrease.**

**Why — and the reasoning matters here, because the source's own explanation gets it wrong:**

> **h = 4σcosθ/(γd)**

> **Capillary rise is directly proportional to SURFACE TENSION σ.**

> **Surface tension DECREASES as temperature rises.** Molecular thermal motion increases, which weakens the cohesive attraction between molecules at the surface — the very attraction that surface tension measures.

> **So σ falls, and with it h falls.** ✓

**The source's stated reason is not correct, and it is worth being clear about:**

> The compilation argues that **"surface tension on a liquid's surface is directly proportional to its density. Therefore, if we increase the temperature, the density of the liquid decreases and consequently there is a decrease in the capillary rise."**

> **Surface tension is not proportional to density.** Mercury is **13.6 times denser** than water yet its surface tension is only about **7 times** water's; and many oils are less dense than water with far lower surface tension. **There is no such proportionality.**

> **The keyed ANSWER is right and the reasoning is wrong.** The real mechanism is the direct temperature dependence of σ.

> **Note also that falling density works AGAINST the conclusion**, not for it: γ sits in the DENOMINATOR of h = 4σcosθ/(γd), so a lower unit weight would **raise** the capillary rise. The source's own argument, followed through, predicts the opposite of its answer.

**The magnitude of the two competing effects:**

| Property of water, 20 °C → 80 °C | Change |
|---|---|
| **Surface tension σ** | **0.0728 → 0.0626 N/m — falls about 14%** |
| **Density ρ** | **998 → 972 kg/m³ — falls only 2.6%** |

> **The surface tension effect is roughly five times the larger**, so it dominates and the rise decreases. **Both effects are real; they simply do not have comparable size.**

**Surface tension of water at a few temperatures:**

| Temperature | **σ (N/m)** |
|---|---|
| **0 °C** | **0.0756** |
| **20 °C** | **0.0728** |
| **50 °C** | **0.0679** |
| **100 °C** | **0.0589** |

> **σ falls monotonically and reaches ZERO at the critical temperature**, where the distinction between liquid and vapour disappears and there is no surface left to have tension.

> **That limiting behaviour confirms the direction: heating always reduces surface tension, never increases it**, which is why option (d) — "first decrease then increase" — has no physical basis.

**The practical consequences:**

| Effect of warming | Note |
|---|---|
| **Capillary rise falls** | This question |
| **Detergency improves** | Hot water wets and penetrates better |
| **Bubbles and droplets less stable** | Less tension to hold them |
| **Frost heave** | Occurs in cold conditions, where σ is at its highest |

> **The frost heave connection is worth noting**: capillary action is strongest when cold, which is precisely when ice lenses are growing and drawing water up through silt. **The two effects reinforce each other.**

**And for the other fluid property that changes with temperature, note the contrast:** **liquid VISCOSITY falls with temperature while GAS viscosity rises** — a genuinely opposite behaviour, and a separate examination point from this one.

examTip.trick: **h ∝ σ, and σ falls with temperature** — thermal motion weakens the cohesive attraction between surface molecules. Water: 0.0728 N/m at 20 °C down to 0.0589 at 100 °C.
examTip.trap: **The source's reasoning is wrong** — it claims σ ∝ density, which is false (mercury is 13.6× denser but only ~7× the surface tension). Worse, falling density would *raise* h, since γ is in the denominator.
examTip.mnemonic: **σ reaches ZERO at the critical temperature**, where liquid and vapour become indistinguishable. Heating always lowers surface tension — which rules out any "decrease then increase".

questions.stem: Supercritical flow occurs in a:
questions.solution:
**A channel with a steep slope.**

> The source explains: **supercritical flow occurs when the flow velocity in a channel exceeds the critical velocity. Steeper slopes allow the water to accelerate due to gravity, leading to a higher flow velocity. This higher velocity can surpass the critical velocity, resulting in supercritical flow characteristics: rapid and turbulent flow, Froude number greater than 1, and water depth less than the critical depth.**

**Why slope determines the regime:**

> **On a steep slope the downslope component of gravity exceeds what boundary friction can balance at a tranquil depth**, so the flow accelerates until it is shallow and fast.

> **Fr = V/√(gy)** rises as V rises and y falls — both of which happen on a steep slope, so the two effects compound.

**But the classification is HYDRAULIC, not geometric — and this is the substance of the question:**

> **"Mild" and "steep" are defined by comparing the NORMAL depth with the CRITICAL depth, not by the physical gradient.**

| Comparison | Slope is called | Normal flow |
|---|---|---|
| **y_n > y_c** | **MILD** | **Subcritical** |
| **y_n = y_c** | **Critical** | Critical |
| **y_n < y_c** | **STEEP** | **SUPERCRITICAL** |

> **So the SAME physical channel can be mild at one discharge and steep at another**, because y_c depends on the discharge while y_n depends on slope and roughness.

> **A gradient of 1 in 500 is not inherently mild or steep** — it depends on what is flowing down it. That is genuinely counter-intuitive and a favourite examination trap.

**Why option (c), a horizontal channel, cannot give supercritical flow:**

> **A horizontal bed (S₀ = 0) has NO downslope gravity component to drive acceleration.** It is classified as an **H (horizontal) slope**, on which no uniform flow exists at all — the normal depth is infinite.

> **An ADVERSE slope (rising in the flow direction) is likewise incapable of it.**

> **Supercritical flow can pass THROUGH a horizontal reach** if it arrives already supercritical from upstream — but it decelerates, and a hydraulic jump forms. **The horizontal reach cannot generate the condition.**

**The two regimes compared:**

| | **SUBCRITICAL** | **SUPERCRITICAL** |
|---|---|---|
| **Froude number** | **< 1** | **> 1** |
| Depth / velocity | Deep, slow | **Shallow, fast** |
| Also called | Tranquil, streaming | **Shooting, rapid, torrential** |
| **Disturbance travels upstream?** | **YES** | **NO** |
| **Control from** | **DOWNSTREAM** | **UPSTREAM** |

> **In supercritical flow the water outruns its own waves**, so nothing downstream can influence what happens above — which is why the control section sits upstream.

**Where supercritical flow is deliberately created, and what must follow:**

> **On spillways, chutes and steep drops.** It is then killed in a **STILLING BASIN** by forcing a **HYDRAULIC JUMP**, which converts the excess kinetic energy into turbulence.

> **If the jump is not forced to occur where it is wanted, it forms wherever the tailwater dictates — possibly beyond the apron on unprotected bed** — and the resulting scour undermines the structure.

> **Design targets Fr₁ between 4.5 and 9.0**, where the jump is stable and dissipates 45–70% of the energy, and **avoids Fr₁ of 2.5–4.5**, whose oscillating jump throws waves far downstream and erodes the banks.

**And the caution about designing at critical:** **never proportion an ordinary channel at critical depth.** The specific energy curve is flat there, so a small change in energy produces a large and unpredictable change in depth, and the surface becomes wavy and unstable. **Canals run comfortably subcritical.**

examTip.trick: **Steep slope → gravity outruns friction → shallow, fast flow.** Fr = V/√(gy) rises as V rises and y falls, so both effects compound.
examTip.trap: **"Mild" and "steep" are HYDRAULIC, not geometric** — defined by y_n vs y_c. The same channel can be mild at one discharge and steep at another, because y_c depends on the flow.
examTip.mnemonic: **A horizontal bed has no driving component**, so it cannot generate supercritical flow — only pass it through, with a jump. And never design a channel AT critical: the E–y curve is flat there.

questions.stem: The head loss at the entrance of a pipe is ______ that at its exit.
questions.solution:
**Half.**

> The source works it directly: **h_entrance = 0.5V²/2g and h_exit = V²/2g, so h_entrance = 0.5 h_exit, giving a ratio of 0.5.**

**Working:**

> **Entrance (sharp-edged) loss: h_in = 0.5 V²/2g**
>
> **Exit loss: h_out = 1.0 V²/2g**
>
> **Ratio = 0.5** ✓

**Why the exit loss is the full velocity head — and it is complete, not partial:**

> **At the exit the water discharges into a large reservoir or the atmosphere and its velocity is dissipated in turbulence.**

> **ALL of the kinetic energy is lost**, because the jet mixes into still water and none of it is recovered as pressure. **Hence exactly V²/2g.**

> **That is why the exit coefficient is 1.0 and cannot be improved by shaping the outlet** — a flared outlet reduces the velocity before discharge, but a plain exit always loses the whole velocity head at whatever velocity it has.

**Why the entrance loses only half:**

> **At a sharp-edged entrance the streamlines cannot turn the corner, so the flow SEPARATES and forms a vena contracta just inside the pipe**, then expands again to fill the section.

> **The loss occurs in that re-expansion, not in the contraction itself** — and it amounts to about half the velocity head.

> **This is why the entrance loss CAN be reduced by shaping**, unlike the exit loss:

| Entrance type | **K** |
|---|---|
| **Sharp-edged (flush)** | **0.5** |
| **Slightly rounded** | **0.25** |
| **BELL-MOUTHED / well rounded** | **0.04 – 0.05** |
| **Re-entrant (projecting pipe)** | **0.8 – 1.0** |

> **A bell mouth cuts the loss by more than ninety per cent**, because the streamlines are guided smoothly in and never separate. **That is why intakes, penstock entries and nozzles are shaped rather than cut square** — an enormous gain for a small amount of forming work.

**The minor loss coefficients, as a set:**

| Fitting | **K** (× V²/2g) |
|---|---|
| **Entrance, sharp** | **0.5** |
| **EXIT** | **1.0** |
| Sudden enlargement | **(1 − A₁/A₂)²** |
| Sudden contraction | ≈ 0.5 |
| **90° elbow** | **0.9** |
| Gate valve, fully open | 0.2 |
| **Globe valve, fully open** | **10** |

> **A fully open globe valve is worth about twenty sharp entrances** — which is why valve selection matters far more to a pumping head than pipe fittings do, and why gate or butterfly valves are used where throttling is not required.

**When do minor losses actually matter?**

> **h_f = fLV²/(2gD)** for friction, against **ΣK V²/2g** for the fittings.

> **The two are comparable when fL/D ≈ ΣK.** With f ≈ 0.02, that is **L/D ≈ 50 ΣK.**

| Pipe | Minor losses |
|---|---|
| **L/D > ~1000 (long pipeline)** | **Negligible — hence the name** |
| **L/D < ~100 (pump house, plant piping)** | **DOMINANT** |

> **In a treatment works or pump house the "minor" losses are usually the larger part of the total**, and calling them minor there is a misnomer inherited from long-pipeline practice.

examTip.trick: **Entrance K = 0.5, exit K = 1.0**, so the ratio is a half. The exit loses the FULL velocity head because the jet mixes into still water and nothing is recovered.
examTip.trap: **The exit loss cannot be reduced by shaping; the entrance loss can.** A bell mouth cuts K from 0.5 to about 0.04 — over ninety per cent — which is why intakes are shaped, not cut square.
examTip.mnemonic: **Minor losses matter when L/D < ~100** — in a pump house they dominate, and the name is a misnomer inherited from long pipelines. A globe valve (K = 10) is worth twenty sharp entrances.

questions.stem: The friction factor for laminar flow is given by:
questions.solution:
**f = 64/Re.**

> The source states it: **for a laminar fully developed flow through pipes, the friction factor f found from the exact solution of the Navier–Stokes equation is f = 64/Re. Thus the friction factor is inversely proportional to the Reynolds number, so on a log plot it is a straight line coming downwards — which is what you see for laminar flow on the Moody chart.**

**Where it comes from — it is derived, not measured:**

> **Hagen–Poiseuille gives the laminar head loss exactly: h_f = 32μVL/(ρgD²)**
>
> **Darcy–Weisbach defines the friction factor: h_f = fLV²/(2gD)**
>
> **Equating the two: f = 64μ/(ρVD) = 64/Re** ✓

> **This is the ONLY part of the Moody chart that is analytical.** Everything in the turbulent region is empirical — Colebrook–White, Nikuradse's experiments, the roughness curves.

> **The laminar line is exact because the Navier–Stokes equations can be solved in closed form for that case.** That distinction is worth knowing: it is why the laminar line is a clean straight line on the chart and the turbulent region is a family of fitted curves.

**The critical property of the laminar line:**

> **ROUGHNESS DOES NOT APPEAR.**

> **f depends on Reynolds number alone** — a rough pipe and a smooth pipe of the same diameter have the **same** friction factor in laminar flow.

> **The reason is physical: near the wall the fluid moves so slowly that the surface asperities are buried within the viscous layer and never disturb the flow.** Roughness only begins to matter once turbulent eddies reach down to the wall.

> **On the Moody chart this shows as a single line for all roughnesses below Re = 2000**, fanning out into separate curves only after transition.

**Why option (b), 16/Re, is the informative distractor:**

> **16/Re is the FANNING friction factor for laminar flow — a different but equally legitimate definition, exactly four times smaller.**

| Convention | Laminar value | Head loss equation |
|---|---|---|
| **DARCY (Moody)** | **f = 64/Re** | **h_f = fLV²/(2gD)** |
| **FANNING** | **f = 16/Re** | **h_f = 4fLV²/(2gD)** |

> **The factor of four sits in the head-loss equation, not in the physics** — both give the same h_f.

> **The tell is the 4: if the equation carries one, the friction factor is Fanning's.** Chemical engineering texts commonly use Fanning; civil and mechanical texts use Darcy. **A discrepancy of exactly four times between two sources is almost always this.**

**The flow regimes:**

| Reynolds number | Regime | f depends on |
|---|---|---|
| **Re < 2000** | **LAMINAR** | **Re only — f = 64/Re** |
| 2000 – 4000 | Transitional | Unpredictable |
| **Re > 4000** | **TURBULENT** | **Re and relative roughness k/D** |
| **Fully rough turbulent** | — | **ROUGHNESS ONLY — f independent of Re** |

> **Note the symmetry at the two extremes: laminar flow depends only on Re and not roughness; fully rough turbulent flow depends only on roughness and not Re.** The complicated middle is where both matter, and where the empirical curves are needed.

**Where laminar flow actually occurs in civil engineering:**

> **Almost never in water mains** — at ordinary velocities and diameters Re runs into the hundreds of thousands.

> **But it is exactly the regime of SEEPAGE THROUGH SOIL**, which is why **Darcy's law v = ki is LINEAR in the gradient** — the same laminar physics at pore scale.

> **And it is why Darcy's law breaks down in coarse gravel and rockfill**: the pore velocities there become high enough for turbulence, and the linear relation fails for precisely the reason f = 64/Re stops applying in a pipe.

examTip.trick: **Derive it: equate Hagen–Poiseuille with Darcy–Weisbach** and f = 64/Re falls out. It is the only analytical part of the Moody chart; everything turbulent is empirical.
examTip.trap: **16/Re is the FANNING friction factor** — legitimate but paired with h_f = 4fLV²/2gD. The tell is the 4 in the equation. A fourfold discrepancy between sources is almost always this.
examTip.mnemonic: **ROUGHNESS DOES NOT APPEAR in laminar flow** — the asperities are buried in the viscous layer. Note the symmetry: laminar depends on Re alone, fully rough turbulent on roughness alone.

questions.stem: What do you mean by cold frontal precipitation?
options: Small catchment area with heavy precipitation
Small catchment area with moderate precipitation
Large catchment area with heavy precipitation
Large catchment area with moderate precipitation
questions.solution:
**A small catchment area with heavy precipitation.**
