> **Waterlogging is a HIGH water table.** It occurs when the water table rises into the crop root zone, conventionally taken as within about **1.5 to 2 m** of the surface.

> **Pumping groundwater REMOVES water from the aquifer and DRAWS THE WATER TABLE DOWN.**

> **That is the exact reverse of the condition being asked about**, which is what makes option (d) unambiguously the answer.

**And it is not merely neutral — it is a recognised REMEDY:**

> **VERTICAL DRAINAGE by tube wells is a standard treatment for waterlogged land.**

> **It is particularly attractive because the pumped water is itself a resource**: one operation lowers the water table **and** supplies irrigation.

> **The one condition is that the groundwater must be of usable quality.** Pumping saline water onto the land accelerates the very salinisation the scheme is meant to prevent — so the remedy depends on water chemistry, not just on hydraulics.

**How the other three genuinely cause it:**

| Cause | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Seepage from unlined canals** | **Often the LARGEST single source** — 30–45% of diverted water is lost, much of it to the water table |
| **Inadequate drainage** | Water arrives and cannot leave |
| **Frequent flooding** | Direct submergence and recharge |

> **Canal seepage is the dominant cause in most irrigation systems**, which produces a genuine irony: **irrigation projects create the waterlogging they must then spend money to drain.**

> **Canal LINING attacks it at source and pays twice over** — more water reaches the field, and less enters the water table.

**Why waterlogging matters:**

| Effect | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **Roots deprived of AIR** | Saturated soil has no air-filled pores, and **roots must respire** |
| **SALT accumulation** | **Capillary rise brings dissolved salts up; evaporation leaves them at the surface** |
| Soil temperature falls | Wet soil warms slowly in spring |
| Nitrogen loss | Denitrification in anaerobic conditions |
| Poor trafficability | Machinery cannot enter the field |

> **SALINISATION is the lasting damage, and the distinction matters:**

> **Waterlogging can be drained away in a single season. The salt it deposits may take years to leach out, and in severe cases the land is abandoned.**

> **That is the mechanism which destroyed large areas of irrigated land in the Indus and Nile basins**, and it is why drainage is designed alongside irrigation rather than after it.

> **And leaching — applying water deliberately in excess of the crop requirement to wash salts below the root zone — is only possible IF DRAINAGE EXISTS to carry that water away.** Without drainage, leaching simply raises the water table again.

**The remedies, in order of attacking the cause:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **CANAL LINING** | **Cuts the largest source at source** |
| **Efficient irrigation** | Drip and sprinkler apply only what is needed |
| **Surface drains** | Remove excess surface water |
| **Subsurface (tile) drains** | **Lower the water table — spacing from HOOGHOUDT's equation** |
| **VERTICAL drainage (tube wells)** | **Pump and re-use** ← the mirror of this question |
| Phreatophytes | Deep-rooted trees that transpire groundwater |

> **A caution worth adding, since this question invites it: excessive abstraction has its OWN serious problems** — falling water tables, drying wells, saline intrusion in coastal aquifers, and **land SUBSIDENCE**, since lowering the water table raises the effective stress and consolidates the ground.

> **So the answer is that it does not cause waterlogging, not that it is harmless.** Those are different claims, and only the first is being asked.

examTip.trick: **Waterlogging is a HIGH water table; pumping LOWERS it.** Option (d) is the exact reverse of the condition — and vertical drainage by tube wells is a recognised remedy.
examTip.trap: Read the **NOT**. The other three are all genuine causes, and **canal seepage is usually the largest** — 30–45% of diverted water, which is why lining pays twice over.
examTip.mnemonic: **Waterlogging drains away in a season; the SALT it deposits may ruin the land for years.** And leaching only works **if drainage exists** — otherwise it just raises the table again.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT considered as a river-training structure?
questions.solution:
**A canal bund.**

> The source distinguishes them: **SPURS are wall-like structures that project from the riverbank into the stream, deflecting the flow and protecting the bank from erosion. A LAUNCHING APRON is a protective layer of stones placed at the riverbed where a structure meets the water, dissipating energy and preventing scour around the base. MARGINAL GUIDE BANKS are embankments built along the riverbanks to confine the flow within a desired channel. CANAL BUNDS, on the other hand, are embankments built alongside CANALS to contain the water and prevent it from overflowing onto surrounding land. They are NOT directly used for managing river flow and are primarily associated with irrigation canals or navigation channels.**

**The discriminator is simply WHICH WATER BODY the structure serves:**

| Structure | Acts on |
|---|---|
| **Spur / groyne** | **The RIVER** — deflects the current from a bank |
| **Launching apron** | **The RIVER** — armours against scour |
| **Marginal guide bank** | **The RIVER** — confines the flood |
| **CANAL BUND** | **A CANAL** — retains water within an artificial channel ✗ |

> **A canal bund is an irrigation structure, not a river structure.** It contains water the engineer has deliberately put into a channel; the other three manage water the river is moving of its own accord.

> **The similarity is that all four are earth or stone embankment works**, which is exactly what makes the distractor plausible — the confusion is one of purpose rather than of form.

**And note the near-miss in the option set:**

> **A MARGINAL BUND and a CANAL BUND are different things with confusingly similar names.**

> **A marginal bund runs along a RIVER to confine floodwater to the flood plain — it is a river training work.**
>
> **A canal bund runs along a CANAL to keep the supply in.**

> **The word "bund" appears in both, and only the qualifier distinguishes them** — which is the real trap here, not the word itself.

**What river training actually sets out to do:**

| Objective | Structure |
|---|---|
| **Protect a bank from erosion** | **Spurs, revetment / pitching** |
| **Confine the flood width** | **Guide banks, marginal bunds** |
| **Prevent OUTFLANKING of a structure** | **Guide banks** |
| **Guide the flow axially into a barrage or bridge** | Guide banks |
| **Prevent scour undermining a foundation** | **Launching apron** |
| Shorten a meander | Cut-off |

> **OUTFLANKING is the failure mode guide banks exist to prevent, and it is total**: the river simply goes **around** the structure and cuts a new channel beside it, leaving a barrage standing in a dry bed. **That has happened to real structures**, which is why guide banks are treated as essential rather than protective.

**The launching apron deserves its own note, since it is the most distinctive idea in the group:**

> **It is laid FLAT on the bed as a carpet of loose stone, and it is DESIGNED TO BE DESTROYED in a controlled way.**

> **As the river scours a hole beside it, the stone at the edge FALLS — launches — into the hole, armouring the newly exposed slope as fast as that slope forms.**

> **It works precisely BECAUSE the stone is loose.** A rigid grouted apron would be undermined and fail as a slab.

> **Its width is taken as 1.5 D** (D being the scour depth below bed level), derived from the launched slope of **2:1** and a launched thickness of **1.25 t.**

**And the scour depths the whole system is designed against:**

> **Lacey's normal scour depth R = 1.35(q²/f)^{1/3}**, multiplied by a location factor:

| Location | Multiplier |
|---|---|
| Straight reach | **1.25** |
| Moderate bend | 1.5 |
| **Bridge pier nose** | **2.0** |
| **GUIDE BANK HEAD** | **2.75 — the severest anywhere in the works** |

> **Which is why the guide bank head carries the heaviest stone and the largest apron of any part of a diversion headworks.**

examTip.trick: **Ask which water body the structure serves.** Spurs, aprons and guide banks act on the RIVER; a canal bund retains water in an artificial channel — an irrigation work, not a river work.
examTip.trap: **MARGINAL bund and CANAL bund share the word and differ entirely** — marginal confines a river's flood, canal keeps a supply in. Only the qualifier distinguishes them.
examTip.mnemonic: **The launching apron is DESIGNED TO BE DESTROYED** — loose stone falls into the scour hole as it forms. Width 1.5 D, from a 2:1 launched slope. A grouted apron would fail as a slab.

questions.stem: Lacey's regime velocity is proportional to:
questions.solution:
**R^{2/3} S^{1/3}.**

> The source gives the relation: **V = 10.8 R^{2/3} S^{1/3} for Lacey's regime theory**, and adds that **for non-regime flow V ∝ R^{3/4}.**

**The exponents are the whole question, and they are worth placing:**

> **Lacey's regime velocity: V = 10.8 R^{2/3} S^{1/3}**

> **Note how close this is to MANNING's equation: V = (1/n) R^{2/3} S^{1/2}.**

| | **Manning** | **LACEY (regime)** |
|---|---|---|
| **R exponent** | **2/3** | **2/3 — the SAME** |
| **S exponent** | **1/2** | **1/3 — DIFFERENT** |
| Coefficient | 1/n (roughness) | **10.8 (a constant)** |

> **The R exponent is identical; only the slope exponent differs.** Lacey's slope dependence is weaker, which reflects that in a regime channel the slope is not independent — the channel has adjusted its own slope to the discharge and the sediment.

> **That is the conceptual difference: Manning's equation describes flow in a channel of GIVEN geometry. Lacey's describes the geometry a channel will ADOPT.**

**Why option (c), R^{3/4} S^{1/3}, is the trap:**

> **The source itself notes that V ∝ R^{3/4} for NON-REGIME flow.**

> **So 3/4 is a real Lacey exponent — just for the wrong condition.** The question asks for the **regime** velocity, which takes 2/3.

> **A distractor drawn from the correct source but the wrong case is the hardest kind to reject**, and it is why the qualifier "regime" in the stem has to be read.

**Lacey's regime equations, as a complete set:**

| Quantity | Formula |
|---|---|
| **Wetted perimeter** | **P = 4.75 √Q** |
| **Hydraulic radius** | **R = 0.473 (Q/f)^{1/3}** |
| **Velocity** | **V = 10.8 R^{2/3} S^{1/3}**, or **V = [Q f²/140]^{1/6}** |
| **Bed slope** | **S = f^{5/3}/(3340 Q^{1/6})** |
| **Normal scour depth** | **R = 1.35 (q²/f)^{1/3}** |
| **Silt factor** | **f = 1.76 √d** (d in **mm**) |

> **Two forms of the velocity equation appear above and both are Lacey's** — one in terms of R and S, the other directly in terms of Q and f. They are consistent, and which is used depends on what is known.

**What "REGIME" means, since it is the operative word:**

> **A channel is in regime when it neither SILTS nor SCOURS over a year** — the sediment entering equals the sediment leaving, and the section is stable on average.

> **Lacey's equations then predict the width, depth and slope such a channel will settle at**, given only the discharge and one sediment parameter.

> **The three conditions Lacey required:** the discharge is **constant**, the channel flows through **incoherent alluvium** of the same character as it transports, and the **silt charge is constant.**

> **Real canals satisfy none of these exactly**, which is why regime theory gives a design starting point that is then checked and adjusted — not a final answer.

**LACEY against KENNEDY, which is the standard comparison:**

| | **KENNEDY (1895)** | **LACEY (1930)** |
|---|---|---|
| Predicts | **DEPTH only** | **Depth, WIDTH and SLOPE** |
| Silt term | **Critical velocity ratio m** | **Silt factor f** |
| Width | **Left to judgement** | **Determined (P = 4.75√Q)** |
| Slope | **Cannot predict it** | **Predicted** |

> **Kennedy's method left the width to the designer's judgement and could not give the slope at all** — that is Lacey's principal advance, and the reason Lacey's method superseded it.

**A caution about the constants:** **Lacey's equations are EMPIRICAL and DIMENSIONALLY INCONSISTENT.** The numbers 10.8, 4.75, 0.473, 3340 and 1.76 all carry hidden units, so **the formulae work only in the units they were calibrated in** — metres and cumecs, with the grain size in **millimetres**. **Converting units freely will give wrong answers**, which is the commonest error in the topic.

examTip.trick: **Compare with Manning: V = (1/n)R^{2/3}S^{1/2}.** Lacey shares the **2/3** on R and differs only on the slope exponent (1/3), because in a regime channel the slope is not independent.
examTip.trap: **R^{3/4} is a genuine Lacey exponent — for NON-REGIME flow**, as the source itself says. A distractor from the right source but the wrong case is the hardest to reject; read the word "regime".
examTip.mnemonic: **Lacey's constants carry hidden units** — 10.8, 4.75, 0.473, 3340, 1.76 — so the formulae work only in metres, cumecs and **millimetres** for grain size. Converting units freely is the classic error.

questions.stem: Irrigation interval is determined by:
options: Field capacity to maximum crop water requirement
questions.solution:
**The evapotranspiration rate.**

> The source's answer is direct: **evapotranspiration (ET).**

**Why ET sets the interval — the reasoning is a simple division:**

> **The soil holds a certain amount of water available to the crop, and evapotranspiration is the rate at which the crop uses it up.**

> **Irrigation interval = Available moisture depth ÷ Evapotranspiration rate**

> **The numerator is a fixed store; the denominator is the rate of withdrawal.** So the interval is simply how long the store lasts.

> **A worked illustration:** with **60 mm** of readily available moisture in the root zone and an ET of **5 mm/day**, the interval is **60/5 = 12 days.** In peak summer at 8 mm/day the same store lasts only **7.5 days** — which is why the interval shortens in hot weather even though the soil has not changed.

**Why option (a) is the closest and most instructive distractor:**

> **"Field capacity" is genuinely part of the calculation — but it defines the NUMERATOR, not the interval.**

> **The available moisture is the water held between FIELD CAPACITY and the PERMANENT WILTING POINT:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Saturation** | All voids water-filled |
| **FIELD CAPACITY** | **Water retained after free gravity drainage — the practical upper limit** |
| **Available moisture** | **Field capacity − wilting point** ← the store |
| **PERMANENT WILTING POINT** | **Water so tightly held the plant cannot extract it** |
| Hygroscopic water | Bound to particles, entirely unavailable |

> **So field capacity tells you HOW MUCH water is available; ET tells you HOW FAST it is used.** Only the second answers a question about timing.

> **In practice irrigation is applied before the store is exhausted — typically when 50% of the available moisture has been used** — because plants suffer stress well before the wilting point is reached.

**Why the other two are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually governs |
|---|---|
| **(b) Irrigation capacity / efficiency** | **A system PERFORMANCE ratio** — how much of the delivered water reaches the root zone. Affects the DEPTH applied, not the timing |
| **(d) Soil INFILTRATION rate** | **How FAST water can be applied** — it fixes the application rate and stream size, so the sprinkler or furrow must not exceed it, or runoff occurs |

> **Infiltration rate is the neatest to separate: it governs HOW FAST you may water, not HOW OFTEN.** Exceeding it causes ponding and runoff; it has nothing to do with the interval between waterings.

**What evapotranspiration is:**

> **ET = EVAPORATION from the soil surface + TRANSPIRATION through the plant.**

> **The two are combined because they cannot be separated in the field and both draw on the same soil moisture store.**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **PET (potential ET)** | The rate with **unlimited water available** |
| **AET (actual ET)** | The real rate, **limited by available moisture** |
| **Reference ET (ET₀)** | For a standard grass surface |
| **Crop ET** | **ET_c = K_c × ET₀** |

> **The CROP COEFFICIENT K_c is what converts a climate figure into a crop requirement**, and it changes through the growing season — low at emergence, peaking at full canopy, falling at maturity. **A single K_c for a whole season is a common oversimplification.**

**How ET is estimated:**

| Method | Note |
|---|---|
| **Penman / Penman–Monteith** | **The standard — combines energy balance and aerodynamic terms** |
| Blaney–Criddle | Temperature-based, simpler |
| Hargreaves | Temperature and radiation |
| **Lysimeter** | **Direct measurement — the reference against which formulae are checked** |
| Pan evaporation | ET₀ = K_pan × E_pan |

> **Penman–Monteith is the FAO standard** because it accounts for radiation, temperature, humidity and wind — the four drivers of evaporative demand — rather than temperature alone.

**And the related quantities:** **DELTA** is the total depth a crop needs over its whole base period, and **Δ = 8.64 B/D** links it to duty. **ET determines the interval; delta determines the total; duty determines the area a discharge can serve.**

examTip.trick: **Interval = available moisture ÷ ET rate.** A fixed store divided by the rate of withdrawal — 60 mm at 5 mm/day gives 12 days, but only 7.5 days at 8 mm/day.
examTip.trap: **Field capacity defines the NUMERATOR, not the interval.** It says how much water is available; ET says how fast it is used. Only the second answers a timing question.
examTip.mnemonic: **Infiltration rate governs how FAST you may water, not how OFTEN** — exceed it and you get ponding and runoff. Different question entirely.

questions.stem: The most commonly used vertical lift gate in modern days is:
questions.solution:
**The fixed wheel gate.**

> The source states it: **the FIXED WHEEL TYPE is the most commonly used vertical lift gate in modern days. The fixed-wheel type of gate, which derives its name from sets of wheels mounted on axles fixed to the gate, rolls upon and transmits the hydraulic load of the gate to guide tracks bearing on the hydraulic headwall structure.**

**Why wheels rather than sliding faces — the reason is friction:**

> **A gate holding back water carries an enormous hydrostatic thrust pressing it against its guides.**

> **For a 5 m × 5 m gate under 5 m of head, the total thrust is roughly γ·h̄·A = 9.81 × 2.5 × 25 ≈ 613 kN — over 60 tonnes.**

> **A SLIDING gate must overcome SLIDING friction against that entire force every time it moves.** With a coefficient of friction of perhaps 0.3, the hoist must supply about 180 kN merely to break it free.

> **A FIXED WHEEL gate converts that sliding friction into ROLLING friction**, where the coefficient is of the order of 0.01–0.03.

> **The hoisting force falls by roughly an order of magnitude**, which means a smaller hoist, a smaller motor, less power and — critically — **the gate can still be raised in an emergency when the head is at its maximum.**

> **That last point is the operational one: a gate that cannot be opened under full head is not a safety device.**

**The types compared:**

| Gate | Load transfer | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED WHEEL** | **Wheels on axles fixed to the GATE, rolling on fixed tracks** | **Modern standard** ← |
| **Sliding** | **Sliding faces** | **High friction; small gates and low heads only** |
| **Free roller (Stoney)** | **A separate train of rollers, not attached to the gate** | Lowest friction, but the roller train is a complication |
| Slotted | — | Not a standard vertical lift classification |

> **The FREE ROLLER (Stoney) gate is the interesting near-miss.** Its rollers are carried in an independent train that moves at half the gate's speed, so there is no axle friction at all — **the lowest friction of any arrangement.**

> **But the roller train must be maintained, aligned and retrieved**, and for most installations the fixed wheel gate's simplicity outweighs the marginal friction advantage. **The best-performing option is not always the most used one**, and this is a good example of engineering practice choosing robustness over optimality.

**The gate families, from the source's own classification:**

| Family | Types |
|---|---|
| **Vertical lift** | **Fixed wheel, vertical lift (sliding), free roller** |
| **RADIAL (Tainter)** | **Spillway crest, orifice spillway** |

> **A RADIAL or TAINTER gate is worth contrasting**, because it solves the same problem differently: **it is a curved skin plate pivoting on trunnions**, so the water thrust passes through the pivot and the gate is raised by rotating rather than lifting.

> **It needs no vertical slots and no lifting the full weight against friction**, which makes it the usual choice for **large barrage and spillway bays.** Vertical lift gates dominate at **under-sluices, intakes and outlets**, where a slot is acceptable and the span is smaller.

**And the design considerations for any gate:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Hydrostatic thrust** | The governing load — γ h̄ A |
| **Watertightness** | Rubber seals on the sill and sides |
| **Hoisting arrangement** | **Must work at MAXIMUM head, not just normal** |
| **Corrosion protection** | Permanently wet and dry cycling |
| **Trash and debris** | Trash racks upstream |
| Vibration | Partial openings can excite the gate |

> **Vibration at partial gate openings is a real and sometimes overlooked problem**: the jet issuing beneath a partly raised gate can excite it dynamically, and gates have been damaged by prolonged operation at an unfavourable opening.

examTip.trick: **Wheels convert SLIDING friction into ROLLING friction** — µ falls from ~0.3 to ~0.02, cutting the hoisting force by an order of magnitude. A 5 m × 5 m gate under 5 m head carries over 60 tonnes of thrust.
examTip.trap: **The FREE ROLLER (Stoney) gate has even lower friction** — but its separate roller train must be maintained and aligned. The best-performing option is not always the most used.
examTip.mnemonic: **A gate that cannot be opened at MAXIMUM head is not a safety device.** That operational requirement, not efficiency, is what drives the choice of wheels.

questions.stem: A farm pond is used for:
questions.solution:
**Water storage.**

> The source's answer is direct: **water storage.**

**What a farm pond is:**

> **A small excavated or embanked reservoir on a farm, storing runoff or diverted flow for later use.**

> **Its defining purpose is to move water in TIME** — capturing it when it is plentiful and releasing it when the crop needs it.

> **That is the whole answer, and it is why "water storage" rather than any of the control functions is correct.**

**Why the other three options are genuinely tempting:**

> **A farm pond DOES contribute to erosion, flood and runoff control — but each of those is a SIDE EFFECT of storing water, not the reason the pond is built.**

| Option | Relationship to a farm pond |
|---|---|
| **Erosion control** | **Incidental** — intercepting runoff reduces downstream gullying |
| **Flood control** | **Incidental and very small** — a farm pond's volume is trivial against a flood |
| **Runoff control** | **Incidental** — it detains some runoff |
| **WATER STORAGE** | **The PURPOSE** ← |

> **The question asks what the structure is USED FOR, which means its design intent.**

> **A structure built for flood control would be a detention basin or a check dam, and it would be sized on a design flood.** A farm pond is sized on the **crop water requirement and the reliability of supply** — a completely different calculation, and the clearest evidence of what it is for.

**Why farm ponds matter particularly in Nepal:**

> **Roughly 80% of annual rainfall arrives in the four monsoon months**, so the central problem is not a shortage of water but a **shortage of water at the right time.**

> **A farm pond is the smallest and cheapest form of storage that addresses that mismatch**, and it can be built by the farmers themselves without heavy plant, imported materials or a public scheme.

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **No power required** | Gravity or a small pump |
| **Built with local labour and materials** | Often plastic-lined against seepage |
| **Enables a SECOND (winter) crop** | The main economic return |
| **Supports high-value horticulture** | Which needs reliable, not abundant, water |
| Livestock and domestic use | Secondary benefits |

> **Enabling a second crop is the point.** A hill farm dependent on monsoon rain grows one crop a year; with modest stored water it can grow two, which roughly doubles the return from the same land.

**The main design considerations:**

| Consideration | Note |
|---|---|
| **Capacity** | From **crop water requirement × area × reliability** |
| **SEEPAGE** | **The dominant loss — hence plastic or clay lining** |
| **EVAPORATION** | Significant for a shallow pond with a large surface |
| **Silting** | Inlet silt trap; a desilting provision |
| **Spillway** | **Essential — an unlined earth embankment cannot survive overtopping** |
| Safety | Fencing, especially near habitation |

> **Seepage is what determines whether a farm pond works at all.** An unlined pond in permeable soil can lose its entire contents within weeks, which is why **low-cost plastic lining transformed the technique** in hill agriculture.

> **And the spillway is the safety-critical item**: an earth embankment that overtops erodes rapidly from the downstream face and can fail completely. **The surplus must be shed at a protected point, deliberately.**

**The related water-harvesting structures**, since they are easily confused:

| Structure | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **FARM POND** | **STORE water for use** |
| **CHECK DAM** | **Slow the flow in a gully — erosion control and recharge** |
| **Contour bund / trench** | **Reduce runoff velocity — erosion control** |
| **Percolation tank** | **Deliberately recharge groundwater** |
| Detention basin | Attenuate a flood peak |

> **Note that a CHECK DAM and a CONTOUR BUND are the structures genuinely built for erosion control** — which is exactly what option (a) describes. **Each option in this question names the purpose of a different structure**, and that is what makes it a real discrimination rather than a guess.

examTip.trick: **A farm pond moves water in TIME** — stored when plentiful, used when the crop needs it. It is sized on crop water requirement, not on a design flood, which shows what it is for.
examTip.trap: **All three wrong options are real BENEFITS of a farm pond, but side effects rather than purposes.** And each names the purpose of a *different* structure — check dams and contour bunds are the erosion-control works.
examTip.mnemonic: **SEEPAGE decides whether it works at all** — an unlined pond in permeable soil empties in weeks, which is why cheap plastic lining transformed the technique. And the **spillway** is safety-critical.

questions.stem: Which of the following plants uses a reversible turbine that can work at relatively high efficiencies and helps in reducing the cost of such a plant?
questions.solution:
**A pumped storage plant.**

> The source explains: **a reversible turbine has been devised for heads varying between 15 to 90 m that can function both as a turbine as well as a pump. This provision helps considerably in improving the LOAD FACTOR of the power system. They can work at relatively high efficiencies and help in cost reduction.**

**What a pumped storage plant does:**

> **It has two reservoirs at different levels.**

| Period | Operation |
|---|---|
| **OFF-PEAK (night, surplus power)** | **PUMPS water from the lower reservoir to the upper one** |
| **PEAK (evening demand)** | **GENERATES by releasing it back down** |

> **It is a net CONSUMER of energy, not a producer.** Round-trip efficiency is about **70–80%**, so roughly a quarter of the energy is lost.

> **That sounds like a poor deal until the economics are considered: it buys cheap off-peak energy and sells expensive peak energy.** The value of the electricity, not its quantity, is what makes the plant worthwhile.

> **It is the only large-scale, commercially proven means of storing electrical energy**, which is why it remains the dominant form of grid storage worldwide despite the losses.

**Why a REVERSIBLE machine reduces cost — this is the point of the question:**

> **The alternative is to install a separate turbine and a separate pump**, each with its own runner, casing, shaft and generator or motor.

> **A reversible pump-turbine is ONE machine that runs in both directions** — as a turbine one way, as a pump the other, with the electrical machine acting as generator or motor accordingly.

| | **Separate pump + turbine** | **REVERSIBLE pump-turbine** |
|---|---|---|
| Machines | **Two** | **One** |
| Powerhouse size | Larger | **Smaller** |
| Capital cost | **Higher** | **Lower** ← |
| Efficiency in each mode | **Slightly higher (each optimised)** | Slightly lower (a compromise) |

> **The trade-off is explicit: a reversible machine is a compromise design and is marginally less efficient in each mode than a dedicated one would be.** But it halves the machinery and shrinks the powerhouse, and the source's phrase **"relatively high efficiencies"** is exactly that concession — high enough that the saving wins.

**Why it improves the LOAD FACTOR:**

> **Load factor = average load ÷ peak load**, and a high value is desirable because it means generating capacity is well used rather than idle between peaks.

> **A pumped storage plant raises it from both ends simultaneously:**

> **It ADDS demand at night (pumping), lifting the trough. It SUPPLIES the peak (generating), so other plant need not be built for it.**

> **Flattening the load curve from both directions is more valuable than either effect alone**, and it is why the source singles out the load factor rather than the energy balance.

**Why the other plant types are wrong:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **Run-of-river** | **No storage at all** — generates from whatever the river brings |
| **Storage plant** | Has a reservoir, but a **conventional one-way turbine** |
| **Tidal** | **Can use reversible turbines** for ebb and flood generation, but the reversal is of the FLOW direction, not of pump/turbine function |

> **The tidal option is the genuine near-miss**, and worth separating: **a tidal plant may generate on both ebb and flood, so water passes through in both directions — but it is generating in both cases, never pumping.**

> **"Reversible" in this question means switching between generating and pumping, which only pumped storage does.**

**Turbine choice for the head range:**

> **The source's 15–90 m range is the FRANCIS territory**, and Francis machines are indeed the usual basis for reversible pump-turbines. **Their radial inward flow reverses naturally into radial outward pumping.**

> **A PELTON wheel cannot be reversed at all** — it is an impulse machine whose buckets are shaped for a jet in one direction, and it has no enclosed passage to pressurise.

**And Nepal's position:** with **most schemes run-of-river** and roughly **80% of flow arriving in four monsoon months**, the country has a monsoon surplus and a winter deficit. **Pumped storage is one of the options discussed for that mismatch** — though it stores energy over hours, not seasons, so it addresses the daily peak rather than the annual one. **Seasonal storage still requires a reservoir.**

examTip.trick: **One machine instead of two** — a reversible pump-turbine halves the machinery and shrinks the powerhouse. It is marginally less efficient in each mode, which is what "relatively high" concedes.
examTip.trap: **A TIDAL plant can also use reversible turbines**, but the reversal is of FLOW direction — it generates on both ebb and flood, never pumps. Only pumped storage reverses between generating and pumping.
examTip.mnemonic: **It raises the load factor from BOTH ends** — adding night demand and supplying the peak. A net energy consumer (70–80% round trip) that pays by buying cheap and selling dear.

questions.stem: In dense soil, the shear failure that occurs is:
questions.solution:
**General shear failure.**

> The source gives the mapping: **GENERAL shear failure — medium to dense soil and stiff clays. LOCAL shear failure — loose sand and soft clay. PUNCHING shear failure — very plastic soil.**

**The three modes and what distinguishes them:**

| Mode | Occurs in | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **GENERAL shear** | **Dense sand, stiff clay** | **A WELL-DEFINED failure surface reaching the ground surface; HEAVING beside the footing; a clear peak load** |
| **LOCAL shear** | **Medium dense; loose sand, soft clay** | Failure surface only partly developed; **large settlement, no clear peak** |
| **PUNCHING shear** | **Loose sand, very soft or plastic clay** | **The footing punches straight down; NO heaving, NO identifiable failure load** |

**Why a dense soil fails in the general mode — the reason is dilation:**

> **A dense soil must DILATE to shear** — its grains are tightly packed and must ride over one another to move, which requires the soil to expand.

> **That interlocking gives it a PEAK strength well above its ultimate value**, and the strength is mobilised along a continuous surface.

> **Once that surface forms, failure propagates along the whole of it at once, reaching the ground surface and heaving the soil beside the footing.**

> **The load–settlement curve therefore shows a distinct peak and then a drop** — which is what makes the ultimate bearing capacity a genuinely identifiable quantity for dense soil.

> **A loose soil CONTRACTS on shearing instead.** It compresses rather than developing a continuous surface, so the footing settles progressively without any clear failure — **and its ultimate capacity has to be defined arbitrarily**, conventionally at a settlement of 10% of the footing width.

**Why that matters for design:**

> **Terzaghi's bearing capacity equation assumes GENERAL shear failure:**
>
> **q_u = c N_c + γ D N_q + 0.5 γ B N_γ**

> **For soils that fail in local or punching shear, the equation over-predicts capacity** — because it assumes a fully developed failure surface that never forms.

> **The standard remedy is to REDUCE the strength parameters:**
>
> **c′ = ⅔c** and **φ′ = tan⁻¹(⅔ tanφ)**

> **Those reduced values are then used in the same equation** — a pragmatic correction rather than a different theory, and it is why the mode of failure has to be identified before the calculation is done.

**Why option (d) is not one of the three:**

> **"Deep shear failure" is not a standard bearing-capacity mode.** The three modes are general, local and punching.

> **The term does exist in slope stability** — a **BASE failure**, where the failure arc passes below the toe through a soft deep layer. **But that is a slope problem, not a footing one**, so the option belongs to a different topic.

> **Recognising that a plausible-sounding option belongs to a neighbouring subject is often faster than recalling the correct list.**

**The bearing capacity factors, for completeness:**

| Soil | N_c | N_q | N_γ |
|---|---|---|---|
| **φ = 0 (saturated clay)** | **5.7** | **1** | **0** |
| φ = 20° | 17.7 | 7.4 | 5.0 |
| φ = 30° | 37.2 | 22.5 | 19.7 |

> **The φ = 0 row gives the result worth carrying: with N_γ = 0, the bearing capacity of saturated clay is INDEPENDENT of the footing WIDTH.**

> **Widening a footing on saturated clay reduces the pressure by spreading the load, but does not raise the capacity per unit area at all** — which is genuinely counter-intuitive and the opposite of the behaviour on sand.

**And the practical note:** **SETTLEMENT usually governs on sand rather than shear failure**, because sand is strong in shear but compressible. **On soft clay, shear failure is more often the critical check.** So the failure mode identified here also indicates which of the two design criteria is likely to control.

examTip.trick: **Dense soil must DILATE to shear**, so the grains interlock, a continuous failure surface forms, and the soil HEAVES beside the footing with a clear peak load. Loose soil contracts instead.
examTip.trap: **"Deep shear failure" is not a bearing-capacity mode** — the three are general, local and punching. It belongs to slope stability, as a BASE failure below the toe.
examTip.mnemonic: **Terzaghi's equation assumes GENERAL shear**, so for loose soils reduce the parameters: **c′ = ⅔c, φ′ = tan⁻¹(⅔tanφ)**. And on saturated clay (N_γ = 0), capacity is **independent of footing width**.

questions.stem: In the context of Nepal, which of the following power plants is most reliable/suitable?
questions.solution:
**A hydro plant.**

> The source's answer is direct: **hydro plant.**

**Why hydropower suits Nepal, and the reasons are geographic rather than preferential:**

| Factor | Nepal's position |
|---|---|
| **Head** | **Enormous — the Himalayan front drops from 8000 m to 60 m over ~200 km** |
| **Flow** | **Perennial snow- and monsoon-fed rivers** |
| **Theoretical potential** | **≈ 83,000 MW** |
| **Economically feasible** | **≈ 42,000 MW** |
| **Fossil fuel reserves** | **NONE — all fuel is imported** |
| Fuel cost | **Zero for hydro** |

> **The decisive point is the last two together: Nepal has no coal, oil or gas of its own.** Every litre of diesel is imported, paid for in foreign currency, and carried over long mountain roads.

> **A diesel plant is therefore not merely expensive but strategically exposed** — its output depends on an unbroken supply chain through another country, and fuel price shocks pass straight through to the cost of electricity.

> **Hydropower's fuel arrives by gravity and cannot be embargoed.**

**Comparing the options:**

| Plant | Suitability for Nepal |
|---|---|
| **Diesel** | **High running cost; imported fuel; suits only PEAK and STANDBY duty** |
| **Hydro + diesel** | A real hybrid arrangement, but the diesel is a **backup**, not the main plant |
| **HYDRO** | **Abundant resource, zero fuel cost, long life** ← |
| **Wind** | **Limited and poorly mapped resource; difficult mountain access and grid connection** |

> **Option (b) is the closest reasonable alternative and worth taking seriously**: a hydro–diesel combination is genuinely used, with the diesel covering dry-season shortfall.

> **But the question asks which plant is most suitable, and in that pairing the hydro is the plant while the diesel is the insurance.** Naming the hybrid does not identify the primary resource.

**Hydropower's general advantages:**

| Advantage | Note |
|---|---|
| **No fuel** | Running cost is almost entirely operation and maintenance |
| **Long life** | **50 – 100 years**, against 25–30 for thermal |
| **Very fast start-up** | **MINUTES, against hours for thermal** |
| **No combustion emissions** | Renewable |
| High efficiency | 85–90%, well above thermal |

> **The start-up speed is worth emphasising**: it makes hydro uniquely suited to **PEAKING duty and frequency regulation**, so even a plant with modest firm power is valuable to a system for its responsiveness alone.

**And the honest qualifications, which a complete answer should state:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **High CAPITAL cost, long construction** | 5–10 years for a large scheme |
| **SEASONAL variation** | **~80% of flow in four monsoon months** |
| **Run-of-river schemes give little dry-season output** | Exactly when demand peaks |
| **SEDIMENTATION** | Himalayan rivers carry exceptional loads; **quartz abrades runners** |
| Seismic and GLOF risk | Real hazards in this terrain |
| Environmental and social impact | Inundation, displacement, fish migration |

> **The dry-season mismatch is the central problem in Nepal's power system**, not a footnote: most developed schemes are run-of-river, so winter output falls to a fraction of monsoon output precisely when lighting and heating demand is highest.

> **That is the whole argument for STORAGE projects** — a reservoir converts secondary power into **firm power**, which is what a system can actually rely on.

> **And sedimentation is the design problem specific to this geology**: young, rapidly rising mountains with steep unstable slopes deliver very high sediment loads, so **desanding basins are essential** and turbine runner replacement is a recurring operating cost.

**A note on "reliable":** **hydro is the most suitable resource, though a run-of-river plant is not the most reliable form of generation in the dry season.** The two claims are compatible — the resource is right for the country, and the reliability question is answered by adding storage, not by changing the resource.

examTip.trick: **Nepal has no fossil fuel of its own.** Every litre of diesel is imported and carried over mountain roads, so a diesel plant is strategically exposed. Hydro's fuel arrives by gravity.
examTip.trap: **Option (b), hydro + diesel, is a real arrangement** — but there the hydro is the plant and the diesel is the insurance. Naming the hybrid does not identify the primary resource.
examTip.mnemonic: **83,000 MW theoretical, 42,000 MW feasible — but ~80% of flow in four monsoon months.** Hydro is the right resource; the reliability gap is closed by **storage**, not by changing resource.

questions.stem: What is the function of a surge tank?
questions.solution:
**It relieves water hammer.**

> The source explains the phenomenon being relieved: **water hammer is a pressure surge or wave that occurs when a fluid in motion is forced to stop or change direction suddenly. Repeated water hammer may cause significant damage to pumps, valves and instruments, lead to the catastrophic failure of gasketed joints and expansion joints, and affect the integrity of pipe walls and welded joints. Water hammer can damage fittings, joints and connections, resulting in leaks.**

**Note that options (a) and (b) state the OPPOSITE of the function** — the surge tank exists to prevent surge, not to create it. **That leaves (c) and (d) as the real discrimination.**

**The problem the surge tank solves:**

> **When the turbine load is suddenly rejected, the guide vanes close rapidly and the flow in the conduit is stopped almost instantly.**

> **A long column of moving water cannot stop instantly without generating an enormous pressure rise.**

> **Joukowsky: Δp = ρ C ΔV**, with the wave celerity **C = √(K/ρ) ≈ 1440 m/s** in water.

> **Stopping a flow of just 2 m/s instantaneously gives about 2.9 MPa — roughly 300 m of extra head.** In a long tunnel that pressure would burst the lining.

> **Note the irony worth carrying: water hammer exists ONLY BECAUSE water is slightly compressible.** If it were truly incompressible the pressure rise would be infinite. **The property that everyday hydraulics assumes away is the one that makes this problem finite.**

**How the surge tank works, and it works in BOTH directions:**

| Event | Response |
|---|---|
| **Load REJECTION (flow stops)** | **Water surges UP the tank**, converting kinetic energy into potential energy instead of pressure |
| **Load ACCEPTANCE (flow demanded)** | **The tank SUPPLIES water immediately**, before the long tunnel column can accelerate |

> **The load-acceptance role is as important as the pressure relief and is often overlooked.** A long tunnel column has enormous inertia and takes time to accelerate; **without a surge tank the turbine would be starved during that delay and the machine could not follow load.**

**The essential effect on the system:**

> **The surge tank DIVIDES the conveyance into two hydraulically separate parts.**

| Reach | Condition |
|---|---|
| **Tunnel (upstream of the tank)** | **Protected — subject only to slow MASS OSCILLATION** |
| **Penstock (downstream of the tank)** | **Carries the full water hammer — and is designed for it** |

> **The penstock is short, made of steel and designed for high pressure; the tunnel is long, lined and cannot economically be.**

> **Confining the water hammer to the short reach is the entire economic justification for the structure.**

**Why option (d) is the interesting distractor:**

> **"Supplies water at constant pressure" is close to something true but not quite right.**

> **A surge tank does maintain a nearly constant pressure at its base under STEADY conditions** — its water level sits at the hydraulic grade line, which is what makes it a pressure reference point.

> **But that is not its function; it is a by-product.** The tank is provided for the TRANSIENT case, and under steady flow it does nothing at all.

> **A structure is named for the problem it solves, not for its behaviour when there is no problem.**

**Types of surge tank:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Simple** | Plain shaft; **large oscillations, slow damping** |
| **RESTRICTED ORIFICE** | **A throttle at the base damps the surge faster** |
| **DIFFERENTIAL (Johnson)** | **Inner riser plus outer tank — fastest damping, smallest size** |
| Expansion chamber | Extra volume at top and bottom |

> **Damping matters because an undamped oscillation makes the governor unstable** — the machine hunts, chasing a head that is still swinging.

**And the stability condition — the THOMA criterion:**

> **The tank's cross-sectional area must exceed a minimum A_th, or the oscillations GROW instead of decaying.**

> **An undersized surge tank is worse than none at all**, because the resulting instability is progressive rather than merely uncomfortable. **Practice uses 1.5 to 1.8 times the Thoma minimum.**

**Where a surge tank is not needed:** **a short penstock with no pressure tunnel** — the water column is too short to generate a damaging surge, so the expense is not justified. **The alternative protections are slow-closing valves, pressure relief valves and air vessels.**

examTip.trick: **Options (a) and (b) state the opposite of the function**, leaving (c) against (d). The tank splits the conveyance: slow mass oscillation in the tunnel, full water hammer confined to the short steel penstock.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) is nearly true but is a by-product.** A surge tank does hold a steady pressure at its base — but under steady flow it does nothing. A structure is named for the problem it solves.
examTip.mnemonic: **Δp = ρCΔV with C ≈ 1440 m/s** — stopping 2 m/s adds ~300 m of head. And **water hammer exists only because water IS slightly compressible**; otherwise the rise would be infinite.

questions.stem: A surface source of water is:
questions.solution:
**Streams.**

> The source's table divides them, and adds a specific caution: **SURFACE WATER — lakes, ponds, streams, rivers, storage reservoir. GROUND WATER — open wells, tube wells, artesian wells, springs, infiltration. Remember SPRING is NOT a surface water source.**

**The two families:**

| **SURFACE water** | **GROUND water** |
|---|---|
| **Lakes** | **Open wells** |
| **Ponds** | **Tube wells** |
| **STREAMS** ← | **Artesian wells** |
| **Rivers** | **SPRINGS** |
| **Storage reservoirs** | **Infiltration galleries and wells** |

**The test is where the water was IMMEDIATELY BEFORE collection, not where it ends up:**

> **A SPRING is the natural emergence of GROUNDWATER at the surface.** The water has travelled through the aquifer and is merely appearing — it was groundwater a moment earlier.

> **The source flags it explicitly** because it is the classic error: the water is visible at the surface, so it *looks* like a surface source.

> **An INFILTRATION GALLERY is even more clearly groundwater**: it is a perforated conduit laid **below the ground**, usually in the permeable bed beside a river, to collect water that has percolated through the soil.

> **It abstracts water that has been filtered by the ground**, which is precisely why it is used — the soil does the first stage of treatment.

**Why the distinction matters in practice — it decides the treatment train:**

| | **SURFACE water** | **GROUND water** |
|---|---|---|
| **Turbidity** | **HIGH and variable** | **LOW — naturally filtered** |
| **Bacterial contamination** | **HIGH** | **Low** |
| **Colour, organic matter, algae** | **Present** | Usually absent |
| **Hardness** | **Low to moderate** | **Often HIGH** |
| **Dissolved iron and manganese** | Low | **Often high** |
| **Temperature** | Varies seasonally | **Nearly constant** |
| **Typical treatment** | **Screening, coagulation, sedimentation, filtration, disinfection** | **Often disinfection alone; sometimes aeration, iron removal or softening** |

> **Surface water needs full treatment; groundwater often needs only disinfection.** That difference dominates the cost of a water supply scheme and is the single strongest argument for a groundwater source where one is available.

> **But groundwater brings its own problems: hardness, iron and manganese, and — critically in the Terai — ARSENIC**, which requires specific removal and is not addressed by conventional treatment at all.

**Why an infiltration gallery is such a useful compromise:**

> **It draws river water that has already passed through the river bed**, so it gets the reliability of a surface source with much of the quality of a groundwater one.

> **The bed acts as a natural slow sand filter**, removing turbidity and much of the bacterial load before the water reaches the gallery.

> **The limitation is CLOGGING** — the same filtration that cleans the water progressively blocks the bed, so the yield falls over time and the gallery must be cleaned or relocated.

**Selection criteria for any source:**

| Criterion | Note |
|---|---|
| **Quantity** | **Adequate for the DESIGN population over the design period** |
| **Quality** | Determines the treatment required |
| **Reliability** | **Yield in the DRIEST period, not the average** |
| **Elevation** | Gravity supply avoids pumping entirely |
| Distance and cost | Transmission length |
| Legal and competing use | Water rights |

> **Reliability is assessed at the dry-season minimum, not the average**, which for a Nepali stream is a very different number — and it is why a source adequate on paper can fail in March.

> **And elevation is worth more than it appears: a gravity-fed supply has no pumping cost, no power dependence and no mechanical plant to maintain** — which in hill communities is often decisive over a nearer but lower source.

examTip.trick: **Ask where the water was IMMEDIATELY BEFORE collection.** A spring is groundwater merely emerging; an infiltration gallery collects water that has percolated through the ground.
examTip.trap: **A SPRING is the classic error** — the source flags it explicitly. The water is visible at the surface, so it looks like a surface source, but it was groundwater a moment earlier.
examTip.mnemonic: **Surface water needs full treatment; groundwater often only disinfection** — which dominates scheme cost. But groundwater brings hardness, iron and, in the Terai, **arsenic**.

questions.stem: The most reliable mode of transportation is:
questions.solution:
**Air transport**, per the keyed answer.

> The source states it without elaboration: **air transport is the most reliable mode of transport.**

**This item is genuinely contestable, and it is worth being straight about why.**

> **"Reliable" is not defined in the question**, and the four modes rank differently depending on which meaning is taken:

| Meaning of "reliable" | Which mode wins |
|---|---|
| **Independent of terrain and surface condition** | **AIR** — needs no roadbed, bridge or track |
| **Schedule adherence, unaffected by traffic** | **RAIL** — a dedicated right of way, no congestion |
| **Least disrupted by weather** | **RAIL or ROAD** — aircraft are grounded by fog, storm and wind |
| **Availability and door-to-door reach** | **ROAD** |
| Lowest accident rate per passenger-km | **AIR** |

> **The case FOR the keyed answer** is that air transport is unaffected by the intervening terrain: it requires no continuous formation, no bridges, no tunnels, and is not interrupted by a landslide or a washed-out culvert. **In a country like Nepal that is a substantial argument**, and it is why remote districts depend on STOL airstrips.

> **The case AGAINST it** is that many standard textbooks assign "most reliable" to **RAILWAY** transport, on the grounds of schedule adherence and immunity from congestion, and that air services are in practice frequently cancelled for weather — acutely so in Nepal, where mountain airstrips close for days.

> **Both readings are defensible, and the source offers no reasoning to settle it.** The answer is retained as keyed, but the item is flagged rather than presented with false confidence.

**What the four modes are actually good at** — which is the durable material here:

| Mode | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|
| **ROAD** | **Door-to-door; flexible routing; low capital per km** | High cost per tonne-km; congestion; accidents |
| **RAIL** | **Very low cost per tonne-km for bulk over distance; high capacity; energy efficient** | **High capital cost; fixed route; needs terminals** |
| **WATER** | **CHEAPEST for bulk over long distances** | **Slowest; needs navigable water and ports** |
| **AIR** | **FASTEST; reaches inaccessible terrain** | **Most expensive; smallest capacity; weather-dependent** |

> **The economic ordering is clear and not contestable: water is cheapest per tonne-km, then rail, then road, then air.** Speed runs in exactly the reverse order.

> **That inverse relation between speed and cost is the organising fact of transport economics**, and it is why high-value low-bulk goods go by air while coal and ore go by water.

**Nepal's particular position:**

> **Road transport carries the overwhelming majority of both freight and passengers**, because the country is landlocked with no navigable rivers and almost no railway.

| Mode | Nepal |
|---|---|
| **Road** | **Dominant — the national network** |
| **Rail** | **Minimal — a short Janakpur line and the Jayanagar link** |
| **Water** | **None navigable** |
| **Air** | **Essential for remote districts; ~50 airports, mostly STOL** |

> **Air transport's role here is not about reliability in the ordinary sense but about ACCESS** — for districts with no road at all, it is the only mode, which may be what the source intends by the word.

**And the design consequence for roads**, since that is where the syllabus goes next: **the road hierarchy trades MOBILITY against ACCESSIBILITY**, with national highways carrying the highest mobility and lowest access, and local roads the reverse. **The two are inversely related because every access point is a place where vehicles slow, stop and turn.**

verification.notes: The source keys air transport as the most reliable mode but offers no reasoning beyond the bare assertion, and the question does not define "reliable". On a terrain-independence reading air is defensible - it needs no roadbed or bridges, which matters in Nepal. On the more common textbook reading, schedule adherence and freedom from congestion place RAILWAY first, and air services are in practice frequently weather-cancelled, acutely so at Nepali mountain airstrips. The keyed answer is retained, the ambiguity is stated openly in the solution, and the item is flagged for the owner to confirm against the syllabus reference in use.

examTip.trick: **The answer depends on what "reliable" means.** Terrain-independence favours AIR (no roadbed, no bridges); schedule adherence and freedom from congestion favour RAIL. The source gives no definition.
examTip.trap: **Many textbooks assign "most reliable" to RAILWAY**, and Nepali mountain airstrips close for days in bad weather. This item is flagged rather than presented as settled.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cost per tonne-km: water < rail < road < air. Speed runs exactly the reverse.** That inverse relation is the organising fact of transport economics.

questions.stem: The traffic sign used for a school is a:
questions.solution:
**A cautionary sign.**

> The source's figures show "School" among the **triangular cautionary signs**, alongside guarded and unguarded level crossings and pedestrian crossing. It defines the families: **MANDATORY signs — violation can lead to penalties; examples are stop, give way, speed limits, prohibited, no parking and compulsory signs. CAUTIONARY (warning) signs — do's and don'ts for pedestrians, cyclists, bus passengers and motorists; THE CAUTIONARY TRAFFIC SIGN IS OF TRIANGULAR SHAPE. INFORMATION signs — beneficial to passengers and two wheelers; THE INFORMATION TRAFFIC SIGN IS OF RECTANGULAR SHAPE.**

**The three families, and the shape carries the meaning:**

| Family | **Shape** | Purpose | Legal force |
|---|---|---|---|
| **MANDATORY / regulatory** | **CIRCULAR** | **An order** | **Violation is an OFFENCE** |
| **CAUTIONARY / warning** | **TRIANGULAR** | **Alerts to a hazard ahead** | **Advisory** ← |
| **INFORMATORY / guide** | **RECTANGULAR** | Direction, distance, facilities | Advisory |

> **The shapes are deliberate, not conventional: a driver can classify a sign from a distance, before the symbol becomes legible.**

> **CIRCLE = an order. TRIANGLE = a caution. RECTANGLE = information.** That is genuine design, and it is why the shapes are internationally consistent.

**Why a school sign is CAUTIONARY rather than mandatory:**

> **It warns the driver that children may be crossing ahead. It does not itself command anything.**

> **The sign creates no offence.** A driver who passes a school sign at an inappropriate speed has broken no law by ignoring the sign — though they may have broken a speed limit posted separately.

> **A MANDATORY sign would be the circular "30 km/h" plate that often accompanies it**, and that one *is* enforceable.

> **So the two frequently appear together and do different jobs**: the triangle warns of the hazard, the circle imposes the limit. **Confusing them is confusing advice with law.**

**Why option (d) is the tempting one:**

> **"Both informatory and cautionary" sounds accommodating**, and a school sign does in a loose sense inform the driver that a school is there.

> **But the sign classification is EXCLUSIVE — each sign belongs to exactly one family, determined by its shape.** A triangular sign is cautionary; it cannot simultaneously be informatory, because informatory signs are rectangular.

> **The shape settles it, and that is why the shape convention is worth knowing rather than merely the list of examples.**

**The colour convention, which reinforces the shapes:**

| Colour | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **RED** | **Prohibition, danger, stop** |
| **Red border, white ground** | Mandatory or cautionary |
| **BLUE circular** | **A mandatory POSITIVE instruction** (compulsory turn left, ahead only) |
| **GREEN** | Direction on major routes |
| Yellow / amber | Temporary works, caution |

> **A red-bordered circle usually FORBIDS; a blue-filled circle COMMANDS a positive action.** The shape says "this is an order"; the colour says whether the order is *don't* or *do*.

**And the two signs that break the shape rule, deliberately:**

| Sign | Shape | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **STOP** | **OCTAGONAL** | **A unique shape — recognisable from any angle, even reversed, faded or snow-covered** |
| **GIVE WAY** | **Inverted TRIANGLE** | Unique, and distinct from warning triangles |

> **These are the two most safety-critical signs on the road**, so they are given shapes shared with nothing else — a driver can identify them even when the face is unreadable.

**Placement:** a sign must be visible for at least the **stopping sight distance** before the hazard, so the driver has time to read, decide and act. **A sign placed too late is worse than none**, because it invites a sudden reaction — and for a school sign that is precisely the wrong outcome.

examTip.trick: **Shape carries meaning: CIRCLE = order, TRIANGLE = caution, RECTANGLE = information.** Deliberate design, so a driver classifies the sign before the symbol is legible.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) is tempting but the classification is EXCLUSIVE** — each sign belongs to one family, fixed by its shape. A triangle cannot also be informatory, since those are rectangular.
examTip.mnemonic: **The triangle WARNS; the circular 30 km/h plate beside it COMMANDS.** They appear together and do different jobs — confusing them is confusing advice with law.

questions.stem: Which of the following is commonly used as an organic binding material in road construction?
questions.solution:
**Bitumen.**

> The source's answer is direct: **bitumen.**

**Why bitumen is the ORGANIC binder — the word does the work:**

> **ORGANIC means carbon-based, derived from living or fossil organic matter.**

> **Bitumen is the heaviest residue of the FRACTIONAL DISTILLATION OF CRUDE OIL** — a hydrocarbon, and therefore organic.

> **The other three options are all INORGANIC MINERAL materials:**

| Option | Nature | Role in a road |
|---|---|---|
| **Stone dust** | **Inorganic mineral** | **FILLER** — occupies voids in the mix |
| **BITUMEN** | **ORGANIC hydrocarbon** | **BINDER** ← |
| **Limestone** | **Inorganic (calcium carbonate)** | **Aggregate**, or the raw material for cement/lime |
| **Sand** | **Inorganic mineral** | **Fine aggregate** |

> **So the discrimination is not really about roads at all — it is about which of four materials is carbon-based.** One question settles it.

**Binder against filler against aggregate**, since the roles are distinct:

> **The BINDER glues the particles together and waterproofs the mix. The AGGREGATE carries the load. The FILLER occupies the small voids so the mix is dense.**

> **Stone dust is the closest distractor precisely because it is present in a bituminous mix** — as mineral filler passing the 75 micron sieve. **But it binds nothing; it densifies.**

**The two binder families used in roads:**

| | **BITUMINOUS (organic)** | **HYDRAULIC (inorganic)** |
|---|---|---|
| Examples | **Bitumen, tar, cutback, emulsion** | **Cement, lime** |
| Sets by | **Cooling, or solvent/water loss — PHYSICAL** | **HYDRATION — CHEMICAL** |
| Pavement | **FLEXIBLE** | **RIGID** |
| **Behaviour** | **VISCOELASTIC — deforms under sustained load** | **Brittle, elastic** |
| Reversible | **YES — can be reheated and reworked** | **NO — irreversible** |

> **The reversibility is a genuine practical advantage of bitumen**: a bituminous surface can be heated, milled, recycled and relaid, which is why reclaimed asphalt pavement is routinely reused while broken concrete generally is not.

> **And the viscoelasticity is the corresponding drawback: bitumen deforms under sustained load and at high temperature, which is what causes RUTTING in the wheel path** on a hot day under slow heavy traffic.

**Bitumen against TAR — the distinction constantly confused:**

| | **BITUMEN** | **TAR** |
|---|---|---|
| **Source** | **PETROLEUM (crude oil)** | **Destructive distillation of COAL or wood** |
| Temperature susceptibility | Less | **More — hardens and cracks in cold** |
| Durability | Better | Poorer |
| **Health** | — | **CARCINOGENIC — largely banned for road use** |

> **Both are organic, so both would answer this question's wording** — but tar is not "commonly used" any more, having been abandoned on durability and health grounds.

**The bitumen products family:**

| Product | Composition | Use |
|---|---|---|
| **Paving grade** | Straight-run, graded by **penetration** (60/70, 80/100) | **Road pavement** |
| **CUTBACK** | Bitumen + **volatile SOLVENT** | Prime and tack coats; cold weather |
| **EMULSION** | Bitumen droplets **dispersed in WATER** | **Cold application; works on a DAMP surface** |
| Blown (oxidised) | Air blown through hot bitumen | Roofing, waterproofing |

> **EMULSIONS have largely displaced CUTBACKS** on environmental and safety grounds: a cutback releases its solvent to the atmosphere and is a fire risk, while an emulsion releases only water — **and it works on a damp surface, which matters greatly in a monsoon climate.**

**And the specification tests:** **penetration** (hardness), **softening point** (ring and ball), **ductility ≥ 50 cm**, flash and fire point, viscosity, **water content ≤ 0.2%**, and **stripping value (retention > 95%)**.

> **No single test characterises a binder** — one can pass penetration and still be unsuitable — which is why the specification lists them all.

examTip.trick: **ORGANIC means carbon-based.** Bitumen is a hydrocarbon from crude oil; stone dust, limestone and sand are all inorganic minerals. One question settles it.
examTip.trap: **Stone dust IS present in a bituminous mix — as mineral FILLER**, which is what makes it the closest distractor. But it densifies the mix; it binds nothing.
examTip.mnemonic: **Bituminous binders set PHYSICALLY and are reversible; hydraulic ones set CHEMICALLY and are not.** Hence asphalt is milled and recycled, while broken concrete generally is not.

questions.stem: Which one of the following is NOT a fixed facility?
questions.solution:
**A railway locomotive.**

> The source states the distinction: **FIXED FACILITIES are the physical components of the system that are fixed in space. FLOW ENTITIES are the units that traverse the fixed facilities. RAILWAY LOCOMOTIVE IS A FLOW ENTITY.**

**The three components of any transportation system:**

| Component | Definition | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED FACILITIES** | **Physical components FIXED IN SPACE** | **Roadways, railway tracks, airways, terminals, bridges, intersections** |
| **FLOW ENTITIES** | **The units that TRAVERSE the fixed facilities** | **Vehicles, locomotives, aircraft, containers, people** |
| **CONTROL SYSTEM** | **Governs how the entities use the facilities** | **Signals, signs, markings, rules, air traffic control** |

> **The test is simply: does it MOVE?**

> **A locomotive moves; a track does not.** That single question separates the two categories, and it is why the answer is unambiguous once the framework is recalled.

**Why "airway" counts as a fixed facility, which is the subtle part:**

> **An airway has no physical existence in the way a road does — it is a designated corridor in the sky.**

> **But it is FIXED IN SPACE, which is the definition.** It is a defined route between navigational fixes, at specified altitudes, and it does not move.

> **Together with the airports, navigation aids and control facilities, it is the fixed infrastructure of air transport.**

> **So the category is defined by fixity rather than by physical construction** — a point worth grasping, because it is what makes "airway" belong with "roadway" rather than with "aircraft".

**Why the framework matters — it is not merely taxonomy:**

> **The three components fail and are managed in completely different ways, and confusing them leads to the wrong remedy.**

| Problem | Which component to change |
|---|---|
| **Insufficient capacity** | **Fixed facility — widen, add lanes, build a bypass** |
| **Congestion at a given capacity** | **CONTROL SYSTEM — signal timing, one-way, restrictions** |
| **Vehicle emissions or safety** | **Flow entities — vehicle standards, inspection** |
| **Accidents at a junction** | **Usually control, sometimes geometry** |

> **The important practical point is that CONTROL is usually far cheaper than CAPACITY.**

> **Retiming a set of signals, converting a street to one-way, or restricting parking can deliver much of the benefit of a road-widening at a small fraction of the cost** — and without the land acquisition that widening requires.

> **Which is why traffic engineering exists as a discipline distinct from highway construction: it improves the system by managing the control component rather than by building more fixed facility.**

**And the analysis follows the same division:**

| Quantity | Belongs to |
|---|---|
| **Capacity, level of service** | **Fixed facility** |
| **Speed, flow, density** | **Flow entities** |
| **q = k × V_s** | The relation between them |
| **Signal cycle, saturation flow** | **Control system** |

> **The fundamental relation q = k·V_s (flow = density × space mean speed) links the entities to the facility they occupy** — and note it requires the **SPACE** mean speed, not the time mean speed, because flow and density are both defined over a length of road.

**The road hierarchy, which is the fixed-facility side of the syllabus:** **arterial (highest mobility, lowest access) → sub-arterial → collector → local (highest access).** **Mobility and accessibility are inversely related because every access point is where vehicles slow, stop and turn** — so no single facility can maximise both, and the hierarchy exists to let different facilities specialise.

examTip.trick: **Does it MOVE?** A locomotive moves; a track does not. One question separates flow entities from fixed facilities.
examTip.trap: **An AIRWAY is a fixed facility** despite having no physical construction — the category is defined by being **fixed in space**, not by being built. That is why it belongs with roadways.
examTip.mnemonic: **CONTROL is usually far cheaper than CAPACITY** — retiming signals or converting a street to one-way delivers much of a widening's benefit without the land. That is why traffic engineering is a separate discipline.

questions.stem: The distance travelled by a moving vehicle during perception and brake reaction time is known as:
questions.solution:
**Lag distance.**

> The source states it: **during the total reaction time or PIEV time the vehicle may be assumed to proceed forward with a uniform speed at which the vehicle has been moving, and this speed may be taken as the design speed. If V is the design speed in m/s and t the total reaction time of the driver in seconds, then the lag distance will be (V × t) m. If the design speed V is in km/h then lag distance = 0.278 × V × t metres.**

**The two components of stopping sight distance:**

> **SSD = LAG distance + BRAKING distance**
>
> **SSD = 0.278 V t + V²/(254 f)**

| Component | Formula | What happens |
|---|---|---|
| **LAG distance** | **0.278 V t** | **The driver has NOT YET BRAKED — the vehicle travels at full speed while they perceive and react** ← |
| **BRAKING distance** | **V²/(254 f)** | The brakes are applied and the vehicle decelerates |

> **The distinction is that during the lag distance NOTHING IS HAPPENING to slow the vehicle.** The hazard has appeared, but the driver is still processing it — and the car covers ground at undiminished speed.

**PIEV time — the four stages the reaction time comprises:**

| Stage | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **P — Perception** | The driver **sees** the hazard |
| **I — Intellection** | They **understand** what it is |
| **E — Emotion** | The **decision** — brake, swerve, or accelerate |
| **V — Volition** | The **physical act** of moving the foot to the pedal |

> **IRC takes the total reaction time as 2.5 seconds** for design.

> **That is a deliberately generous allowance.** An alert driver reacts in well under a second; the 2.5 s covers a driver who is inattentive, unfamiliar with the road, or elderly. **Design is for the worst reasonable driver, not the average one.**

**The magnitude of the lag distance is what makes it matter:**

> **At 60 km/h: lag = 0.278 × 60 × 2.5 = 41.7 m**

> **Forty-two metres travelled before the brakes are even touched** — and note it is **LINEAR in speed**, while the braking distance is **quadratic.**

| Speed | **Lag (linear)** | **Braking (quadratic, f = 0.35)** | **SSD** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **30 km/h** | **20.9 m** | **10.1 m** | **31 m** |
| **60 km/h** | **41.7 m** | **40.5 m** | **82 m** |
| **100 km/h** | **69.5 m** | **112.5 m** | **182 m** |

> **At low speed the LAG distance dominates; at high speed the BRAKING distance does.** They are about equal near 60 km/h.

> **Which has a real consequence: in a 30 km/h zone, two thirds of the stopping distance is consumed before the driver reacts.** Reducing the limit further helps far less than intuition suggests, because the irreducible reaction component is what is governing.

**Why the other options are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Sight distance** | **The length of road VISIBLE ahead** — a property of the geometry, not of the vehicle's motion |
| **Stopping distance** | **The TOTAL — lag plus braking.** The whole, not the part asked for |
| **Passing distance** | Overtaking sight distance — a different manoeuvre entirely |

> **Option (b) is the closest: "stopping distance" is the sum of which the lag distance is one part.** The question asks specifically for the distance covered during perception and reaction, which is the first term only.

**The three sight distances, for completeness:**

| Distance | Note |
|---|---|
| **STOPPING (SSD)** | **The absolute minimum — provided everywhere** |
| **OVERTAKING (OSD)** | **d₁ + d₂ + d₃; needs a long clear stretch** |
| Intersection sight distance | At uncontrolled junctions |

> **A caution on a common source error: the true relation is ISD ≈ 2 × SSD** — the intersection case needs more, not less. **Some circulating material prints "SSD = 2 ISD", which inverts it.**

> **And on a two-way single carriageway, SSD must be provided for BOTH directions**, so the sight distance available is measured for opposing vehicles as well as for a stationary obstruction.

examTip.trick: **During the lag distance NOTHING slows the vehicle** — the driver is still perceiving and reacting while the car travels at full speed. Lag = 0.278 V t, with t = 2.5 s per IRC.
examTip.trap: **Option (b), stopping distance, is the TOTAL** — lag plus braking. The question asks for the first term only, which is the part before the brakes are touched.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lag is LINEAR in speed, braking is QUADRATIC** — equal near 60 km/h. So at 30 km/h two thirds of the stopping distance is consumed before the driver even reacts.

questions.stem: The minimum qualification of the Registrar of the Nepal Engineering Council is:
questions.solution:
**A Bachelor's degree plus 10 years' experience.**

> The source sets out the Council's composition under the NEC Act 2055 and lists, as item 10: **Member Secretary = 1 (Registrar), Bachelor's degree + 10 years' experience.**

**The Council's composition, as the source gives it — 21 members in total:**

| # | Position | Qualification | Appointed by |
|---|---|---|---|
| **1** | **President** | **Bachelor's + 15 years** | **Nominated by GoN** |
| **2** | **Vice President** | **Bachelor's + 10 years** | **Nominated by GoN** |
| **3** | **7 members** | **Bachelor's + 7 years**, one from each province, **at least three women** | Nominated by GoN |
| **4** | 1 member | President of NEA | Ex officio |
| **5** | **5 members** | — | **ELECTED from NEA** |
| **6** | 1 member | Campus chief of any engineering campus | Nominated by GoN |
| **7** | 1 member | Representative, Institute of Engineering, T.U. | Nominated by GoN |
| **8** | 1 member | Representative of universities teaching engineering | Nominated by GoN |
| **9** | **2 members** | **Bachelor's + 7 years, at least one woman** | **Nominated by the COUNCIL** |
| **10** | **Member Secretary (REGISTRAR)** | **Bachelor's + 10 YEARS** ← | — |

**The experience ladder is the pattern worth carrying:**

> **7 years for ordinary members; 10 years for the Vice President and the REGISTRAR; 15 years for the President.**

> **Three tiers, and the Registrar sits in the middle one alongside the Vice President** — which makes sense, since the Registrar is the Council's chief executive officer rather than its figurehead.

> **That grouping is easier to remember than four separate numbers**, and it also tells you why option (d)'s 7 years is wrong: it is the ordinary-member requirement, not the Registrar's.

**What the Registrar actually does:**

> **The Member Secretary is the Council's permanent executive**, distinct from the President, who presides.

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Maintains the REGISTER** of engineers | The Council's core record |
| **Issues license certificates** | On the Council's authority |
| **Runs the secretariat** | Day-to-day administration |
| **Serves as Member Secretary of the Council** | Both a member and its secretary |
| Implements Council decisions | Executive arm |

> **The 10-year requirement reflects that this is a working professional post requiring judgement about other engineers' qualifications**, not a purely administrative one — which is why an engineering degree is required at all.

**A caution about questions of this kind, and it is worth stating plainly:**

> **Numbers taken from a statute are the most volatile examination material there is.** An amendment changes the answer without changing anything of substance.

> **The NEC Act 2055 has been amended, and the source itself notes elsewhere that penalties under section 30 rose from Rs 3000 to Rs 10,000 and from Rs 2000 to Rs 25,000** — so the figures in circulation are not all current.

> **What is durable is the STRUCTURE**: a 21-member council of nominated, ex-officio, elected and council-nominated members, with a three-tier experience ladder and explicit provision for women's representation.

> **Learn the structure and the reasoning; treat the exact counts as facts to verify against the current Act.**

**The women's representation provisions are worth noticing**, because they appear twice:

> **At least THREE women among the seven provincial members, and at least ONE among the two Council-nominated members.**

> **Both requirements attach to NOMINATED seats rather than elected ones** — deliberately, because nomination is the mechanism available to correct an imbalance that an open election may not produce.

**And what the Council exists to do:** **register engineers and issue licenses, recognise qualifications, conduct the licensing examination, prescribe the CODE OF ETHICS, take disciplinary action including removal from the register, and report to the Government of Nepal.**

> **The power to remove a name from the register is what makes it a regulator rather than an association** — and it is why the reporting obligation to government exists.

examTip.trick: **Three experience tiers: 7 years ordinary members, 10 years Vice President and REGISTRAR, 15 years President.** Grouping them beats memorising four separate numbers.
examTip.trap: **Option (d)'s 7 years is the ORDINARY MEMBER requirement**, not the Registrar's. Every option is a genuine figure from the same Act, at a different level.
examTip.mnemonic: **Statutory numbers are the most volatile exam material there is** — the Act has been amended, and section 30 penalties rose from Rs 3000/2000 to Rs 10,000/25,000. Learn the **structure**, verify the counts.

questions.stem: Which of the following involves continuous betterment in planning and detailing with time?
questions.solution:
**Progressive elaboration.**

**What the term means:**

> **PROGRESSIVE ELABORATION is the practice of developing a project plan in INCREASING DETAIL as more information becomes available.**

> **The plan is not wrong at the start — it is deliberately COARSE, because the information needed to make it fine does not yet exist.**

> **As the project proceeds and uncertainty resolves, the same plan is elaborated: broad phases become activities, activities become tasks, and estimates tighten.**

**Why it is a discipline rather than an excuse:**

> **The alternative — planning everything in full detail at the outset — produces a plan that is precise and wrong.**
