> **The BELL-MOUTHED head is not decoration.** A curved head lets the flow turn gradually into the waterway; a square end would cause severe local eddying and far deeper scour.

**And the scour at the heads is the critical design point:**

> **The guide bank HEAD takes the severest scour of any point in the works — a LOCATION FACTOR of 2.75 on Lacey's normal scour depth**, deeper even than a bridge pier nose at 2.0.

> **Hence the heads carry the heaviest stone pitching and the largest LAUNCHING APRON**, whose width is taken as **1.5 D** for a scour depth D, derived from a launched slope of 2:1.

> **The apron is designed to be destroyed in a controlled way**: as the river scours beside it, the edge stone falls into the hole and armours the newly exposed slope. **It works because the stone is loose — a grouted apron would be undermined and fail as a slab.**

**How many guide banks:** normally **a pair, one on each flank**, though a single guide bank may suffice where one bank is naturally high and non-erodible. **The pair is the default because a river confined on one side only will simply attack the other.**

examTip.trick: **Upstream 1.25 L = 500 m, downstream 0.25 L = 100 m** — the upstream arm is FIVE times the downstream one, because gathering a river requires length while releasing it does not.
examTip.trap: **Options (b) and (d) REVERSE the arms.** Those are conceptual errors, not arithmetic ones — anyone who knows what the arms do cannot pick them.
examTip.mnemonic: **The HEAD takes a scour factor of 2.75 — worse than a bridge pier's 2.0.** Hence the bell-mouthed shape, the heaviest pitching, and a launching apron 1.5 D wide.

questions.stem: A 4 m diameter tunnel has been constructed through an earth dam with a bell mouth entry. The water levels on the upstream and downstream sides of the dam are at RL 226 m and 210 m respectively. What will be the discharge through this outlet?
questions.solution:
**178.12 m³/s.**

> The source works it: **Q = C_d · A · (2gH)^{1/2}, where H = 226 − 210 = 16 m. Q = 0.8 × (π/4 × 16) × (2 × 9.81 × 16)^{1/2} = 178.12 cumecs.**

**Working:**

> **Head H = 226 − 210 = 16 m** (the difference in water levels)
>
> **Area A = πd²/4 = π × 4²/4 = 4π = 12.566 m²**
>
> **Velocity √(2gH) = √(2 × 9.81 × 16) = √313.9 = 17.72 m/s**
>
> **Q = 0.8 × 12.566 × 17.72 = 178.1 m³/s** ✓

**The head is the difference in WATER LEVELS, not a depth:**

> **This is a submerged outlet — the tunnel discharges below the downstream water surface.**

> **So the driving head is the difference between the two reservoir levels**, and the tunnel's own elevation does not enter the calculation at all.

> **That is why no invert level is given, and its absence is a clue rather than an omission.**

> **For a free-discharging outlet the head would instead be measured from the upstream level to the outlet centreline** — a different calculation, and the reason the submerged condition must be recognised.

**Why C_d = 0.8 — the BELL MOUTH is doing the work:**

> **The stem specifies a bell mouth entry, and that is what justifies the high coefficient.**

| Entry | **C_d** | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Sharp-edged / square** | **≈ 0.6** | **Flow separates, forming a vena contracta** |
| **Slightly rounded** | ≈ 0.7 | Partial guidance |
| **BELL-MOUTHED** | **≈ 0.8 – 0.98** | **Streamlines guided smoothly in; little or no separation** |

> **A sharp-edged entry loses a great deal because the flow cannot turn the corner: it separates, contracts to a vena contracta, and then re-expands with turbulent loss.**

> **A bell mouth guides the streamlines and eliminates the separation**, which is why intakes, penstock entries and outlet works are shaped rather than cut square.

> **The gain is out of all proportion to the forming work involved** — raising C_d from 0.6 to 0.8 increases the discharge by a third for the same head and diameter.

**A useful check on the answer's size:**

> **The theoretical (frictionless) discharge would be A√(2gH) = 12.566 × 17.72 = 222.7 m³/s.**

> **The keyed answer of 178 m³/s is exactly 0.8 of that** ✓ — so the coefficient has been applied once and correctly.

> **Option (c), 165 m³/s, corresponds to roughly C_d = 0.74; option (b), 104 m³/s, to about 0.47.** Neither follows from a stated coefficient.

**What the outlet is for, since this is a dam:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Supply irrigation or water supply demand** | The everyday duty |
| **Generate power** | Where the outlet feeds a turbine |
| **DRAW DOWN the reservoir** | **For inspection, repair or in an emergency** |
| Pass compensation flow | Downstream environmental release |
| **Divert the river during construction** | Often the tunnel's original purpose |

> **The drawdown function is the safety-critical one.** A dam that cannot be emptied cannot be inspected internally or relieved if a problem develops — and **the outlet capacity therefore sets how fast the reservoir can be lowered.**

> **But rapid drawdown is itself a design case for the upstream slope**: lowering the water quickly removes the external support while pore pressures inside the embankment have not yet dissipated, so the effective stress falls and the slope can fail. **Earth dam upstream slopes are checked specifically for it.**

> **So the outlet must be large enough to empty the reservoir but must not be used faster than the embankment allows** — two requirements that pull against each other.

**And a note on the tunnel through an earth dam:**

> **A conduit passing through an embankment is a classic seepage path.** Water can travel along the interface between the concrete and the compacted fill, and **PIPING along that contact has caused dam failures.**

> **The remedies are ANTI-SEEP COLLARS or a filter diaphragm around the conduit**, and careful compaction against the structure — which is difficult precisely where it matters most.

examTip.trick: **H is the DIFFERENCE in water levels (226 − 210 = 16 m)** because the outlet is submerged — the tunnel's own elevation never enters, which is why no invert level is given.
examTip.trap: **Check the coefficient once**: theoretical Q = A√(2gH) = 222.7, and 0.8 × 222.7 = 178.1 ✓. The other options correspond to no stated C_d.
examTip.mnemonic: **The BELL MOUTH is what justifies C_d = 0.8** against 0.6 for a square entry — a third more discharge for the same head, which is why intakes are shaped rather than cut.

questions.stem: Which of the following is correct? (i) A diesel engine works as base load. (ii) Storage hydropower is used for peak time.
questions.solution:
**Statement (ii) only.**

> The source's reasoning is one line: **diesel engine: PEAK AND STAND-BY plants. So option (a) is wrong.**

**Why statement (i) is false:**

> **A diesel plant is a PEAK and STANDBY plant, not a base load plant.**

> **Base load duty demands the opposite economics from what diesel offers:**

| Requirement of base load | Diesel |
|---|---|
| **Runs continuously — thousands of hours a year** | **Fuel cost accumulates ruinously** |
| **LOW running cost per unit** | **HIGHEST running cost of any plant** |
| Large unit capacity | Small units |
| High capital cost acceptable | **Low capital cost — its one advantage** |

> **Base load plant is chosen for LOW RUNNING COST because it runs almost all the time. Peaking plant is chosen for LOW CAPITAL COST and FAST START because it runs rarely.**

> **Diesel has exactly the wrong profile for base load: cheap to build, expensive to run.** Running it continuously would maximise the cost that matters least to justify and minimise the advantage it has.

> **In Nepal the objection is sharper still — all diesel is imported**, so continuous base load operation would mean a permanent foreign currency drain and exposure to fuel price shocks.

**Why statement (ii) is true:**

> **STORAGE hydropower is ideally suited to peaking**, and for two independent reasons.

> **1. It can START AND REACH FULL LOAD IN MINUTES**, against hours for a thermal plant. Nothing else on a grid responds so quickly.

> **2. Its reservoir lets it choose WHEN to generate.** Water stored during off-peak hours can be released during the evening peak, so the plant's output is scheduled rather than dictated by the river.

> **That second point is the essential difference from a RUN-OF-RIVER plant, which must generate whatever the river brings at that moment and therefore serves BASE load, not peak.**

> **So the distinction inside hydropower matters as much as the distinction between fuels**, and the statement is specifically about *storage* hydro for that reason.

**The plant types and their duties:**

| Plant | Duty | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Run-of-river hydro** | **BASE** | **Output follows the river; cannot be scheduled** |
| **Nuclear, large thermal** | **BASE** | Low running cost; slow to start and stop |
| **STORAGE hydro** | **PEAK** | **Fast start; output can be scheduled** |
| **Pumped storage** | **PEAK** | Fast; also absorbs off-peak surplus |
| **DIESEL, gas turbine** | **PEAK and STANDBY** | **Fast start, low capital, high running cost** |

> **Note that both storage hydro and diesel serve the peak, but for different reasons: hydro because it is cheap to run and quick, diesel because it is cheap to build and quick.**

**The load curve is what the whole classification serves:**

> **Demand varies through the day, and different plant is used to meet different parts of it.**

| Part of the curve | Met by |
|---|---|
| **Base — the constant minimum** | **Run-of-river hydro, nuclear, large thermal** |
| **Intermediate** | Thermal on part load |
| **PEAK — the evening spike** | **Storage hydro, pumped storage, gas turbine, diesel** |

> **The economic logic is that a plant should run for as many hours as its running cost justifies**, and that is what sorts the fleet.

> **LOAD FACTOR (average ÷ peak load) measures how flat the curve is**, and a high value is desirable because generating capacity is then well used rather than idle.

> **Which is why tariff structures — off-peak rates, time-of-day metering, demand charges — exist: flattening the load curve is cheaper than building capacity that will sit idle.**

**And a diesel plant's real value in Nepal:**

> **Not base load, and not really peaking either, but STANDBY.**

> **Its low capital cost and fast start make it the right choice for emergency backup** — hospitals, telecoms, industry during load shedding — where the cost per unit is irrelevant because the hours are few and the alternative is no supply at all.

> **A plant chosen for reliability rather than economy is being used correctly**, and that is the honest place for diesel in this system.

examTip.trick: **Base load wants LOW RUNNING cost; peaking wants LOW CAPITAL cost and fast start.** Diesel is cheap to build and expensive to run — exactly the wrong profile for base load.
examTip.trap: **RUN-OF-RIVER hydro serves BASE load, not peak** — it must generate whatever the river brings. Statement (ii) specifies *storage* hydro for precisely that reason.
examTip.mnemonic: **Storage hydro and diesel both serve the peak, for opposite reasons** — hydro because it is cheap to run and quick, diesel because it is cheap to build and quick. Diesel's honest role here is **standby**.

questions.stem: Benkelman beam deflection studies were carried out on a highway pavement at a temperature of 40 °C. The rebound deflection was found to be 1.41 mm. What would be the corrected rebound deflection?
questions.solution:
**1.36 mm.**

> The source works it: **the correction for temperature is to be applied, as in the question the test temperature is 40 °C but the standard is 35 °C. So the correction to be applied is NEGATIVE and it is taken as 0.01 per degree. Corrected D_c = D_c + (standard temperature − field temperature) × 0.01 = 1.41 + (35 − 40) × 0.01 = 1.36 mm.**

**Working:**

> **Standard temperature = 35 °C; field temperature = 40 °C**
>
> **Correction = (35 − 40) × 0.01 = −0.05 mm**
>
> **Corrected deflection = 1.41 − 0.05 = 1.36 mm** ✓

**Why the correction is NEGATIVE here — and the sign is the whole question:**

> **Bitumen is VISCOELASTIC: it softens as it warms.**

> **A pavement tested at 40 °C is warmer and therefore softer than the 35 °C standard, so it deflects MORE than it would at the standard temperature.**

> **The measured 1.41 mm therefore OVERSTATES the pavement's deflection at standard conditions**, and the correction must reduce it.

> **Test warmer than standard → deflection overstated → subtract. Test cooler than standard → deflection understated → add.**

> **That reasoning gives the sign without needing to remember the formula's arrangement**, which is worth having because the formula is easy to write backwards.

**Note that option (c), 1.40 mm, would be a correction of only −0.01** — the right direction with the per-degree rate applied once instead of over the full 5 °C difference. **And options (a) and (b) subtract too much.**

**What the Benkelman beam does:**

> **It measures the REBOUND DEFLECTION of a flexible pavement under a standard wheel load.**

| Test condition | Value |
|---|---|
| **Standard axle load** | **8170 kg (80 kN) on dual wheels** |
| **Tyre pressure** | **5.6 kg/cm²** |
| **Standard temperature** | **35 °C** |
| Measurement points | At intervals along the wheel path |

> **The probe is placed between the dual tyres, the truck moves off, and the pavement rebounds as the load is removed.** The beam measures that rebound.

> **Deflection is used as a measure of the pavement's STRUCTURAL ADEQUACY** — a large deflection means a weak pavement, and the deflection value determines the thickness of strengthening overlay required.

**The other corrections applied to a Benkelman result:**

| Correction | For |
|---|---|
| **TEMPERATURE** | **Standardise to 35 °C — this question** |
| **Seasonal / moisture** | **Pavements are weakest when the subgrade is wet** |
| Leaf spring correction | Truck suspension movement |

> **The SEASONAL correction is the more consequential of the two in practice**, and it points the same way as the CBR test's four-day soak: **a pavement must be adequate in its WORST condition, not its average one.**

> **Testing in the dry season and applying no seasonal correction would flatter the pavement**, and the overlay designed on that basis would be too thin.

**Why the characteristic deflection is a statistical value, not a mean:**

> **D_char = D_mean + 2σ** for major roads (or **D_mean + σ** for others)

> **The design takes a value that most of the pavement is better than, not the average** — because a pavement fails at its weakest points, and an overlay sized on the mean would leave half the length under-strengthened.

**And how the result is used:**

> **The corrected characteristic deflection is entered into IRC 81's design chart against the traffic in cumulative standard axles, and the chart gives the required overlay thickness in equivalent bituminous material.**

> **So the whole test exists to answer one practical question: how thick an overlay does this road need?**

**A note on what has superseded it:** **the Falling Weight Deflectometer (FWD)** applies a dynamic impulse load and measures a whole deflection basin rather than a single point, allowing the layer moduli to be back-calculated. **It gives far more information, but the Benkelman beam remains in use because it is simple, cheap and needs no specialist vehicle** — which matters where equipment must be maintained locally.

examTip.trick: **Test WARMER than standard → bitumen softer → deflection overstated → SUBTRACT.** 1.41 + (35 − 40) × 0.01 = **1.36 mm**. The reasoning gives the sign without recalling the formula's arrangement.
examTip.trap: **Option (c), 1.40 mm, applies the 0.01 rate once instead of over the full 5 °C difference.** Right direction, wrong multiplier.
examTip.mnemonic: **Standard conditions: 80 kN axle, 5.6 kg/cm² tyre pressure, 35 °C.** And use **D_mean + 2σ**, not the mean — a pavement fails at its weakest points, not its average ones.

questions.stem: A hexagonal pyramid rests on its base on the horizontal plane with its axis vertical. Its top view is:
options: A rectangle with a vertical centre line
A hexagon showing the six sloping faces converging at the apex
questions.solution:
**A hexagon showing the six sloping faces converging at the apex.**

> The source's figure gives the answer as the hexagon divided by radial lines into six triangles.

**Why that is the top view — reason it out rather than picture it:**

> **A top view (plan) is what you see looking vertically DOWNWARD.**

> **The pyramid's BASE is a hexagon lying on the horizontal plane, so its outline in plan is a HEXAGON** — the base is seen at its true shape and size, because it is parallel to the plane of projection.

> **The APEX is directly above the centre of the base (the axis is vertical), so in plan it projects onto the CENTRE POINT.**

> **The six sloping edges run from the six base corners up to the apex. Seen from above, each projects as a straight line from a corner to the centre.**

> **The result is a hexagon with six radial lines — that is, divided into six triangles.** ✓

**A general rule worth extracting:**

> **In the view along the axis, a pyramid or cone shows its BASE at true shape, with the apex at the centre and the sloping edges as radial lines.**

> **In a view perpendicular to the axis, the same solid shows as a TRIANGLE** (for a cone or a pyramid seen across the flats).

> **So the two principal views of a pyramid are a polygon-with-radials and a triangle** — and knowing which is which requires only knowing the direction of view.

**Checking the distractors against that rule:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **(a) A single triangle** | **The FRONT VIEW (elevation)** — the view perpendicular to the axis |
| **(b) A rectangle with a centre line** | The front view of a **PRISM**, not a pyramid |
| **(c) Hexagon with radial lines** | **The top view** ✓ |
| **(d) A circle with radial lines** | The top view of a **CONE**, not a hexagonal pyramid |

> **Option (a) is the trap, because a triangle is genuinely one of the pyramid's views — just the wrong one.**

> **And option (d) is the same correct reasoning applied to a cone**, which shows a circle rather than a hexagon in plan. **Both distractors are right answers to adjacent questions.**

**The three principal orthographic views:**

| View | Direction of sight | Projected onto |
|---|---|---|
| **Front view (elevation)** | Horizontal, from the front | **Vertical plane (VP)** |
| **TOP view (plan)** | **Vertically DOWNWARD** | **Horizontal plane (HP)** ← |
| **Side view** | Horizontal, from the side | Profile plane |

> **A surface parallel to a plane of projection appears at TRUE SHAPE in that view**, which is exactly why the hexagonal base is seen as a true hexagon in plan.

> **A surface perpendicular to a plane appears as a LINE, and an inclined surface appears FORESHORTENED** — the three cases that govern every orthographic projection.

**And the convention that determines the layout:**

> **First angle projection (India, Nepal, Europe): the TOP VIEW is placed BELOW the front view.**
>
> **Third angle projection (USA, Japan): the top view is placed ABOVE it.**

> **The views appear on the OPPOSITE side in first angle and the SAME side in third angle** — one sentence that covers every layout difference between the two.

> **A drawing read in the wrong convention is MIRRORED**, and parts have been manufactured backwards for exactly that reason — which is why every drawing carries the projection symbol in its title block, and why checking it is the first thing to do on an unfamiliar drawing.

verification.notes: The source presents this item as "Identify top view" with four unlabelled figures, which the scan reproduces but which cannot be carried into a text question. The intended answer is recoverable unambiguously from the source's own answer page, which redraws the correct option as a hexagon divided into six triangles by radial lines. The stem has been rewritten to state the solid explicitly (a hexagonal pyramid on its base, axis vertical) and the options as descriptions, so the item tests the same projection reasoning without depending on figures. The keyed letter (d) in the source corresponds to that hexagonal figure; here it is option (c).

examTip.trick: **Along the axis, a pyramid shows its BASE at true shape with the apex at the centre and the sloping edges as radial lines.** Perpendicular to the axis it shows as a triangle.
examTip.trap: **Option (a), a triangle, is genuinely one of the pyramid's views — the FRONT view.** And option (d) is the correct plan of a CONE. Both distractors answer adjacent questions correctly.
examTip.mnemonic: **A surface PARALLEL to a projection plane appears at TRUE SHAPE; perpendicular appears as a LINE; inclined appears FORESHORTENED.** Those three cases govern every orthographic view.

questions.stem: As per the NEC Act (Amended 2079), section 30(c), the punishment on violation of rules is:
questions.solution:
**Rs 25,000.**

> The source sets out the whole section: **NEC section 30 describes punishments for offences. Section 30(1) says no one should do engineering jobs without a license. Section 30(2) says the punishment for violating 30(a) is up to Rs 10,000 or up to 3 months in prison or both (it is the punishment for a person WITHOUT a license) — it used to be Rs 3000 instead of Rs 10,000 in the initial Act. Section 30(3) says punishment for offenders WITH a license is up to Rs 25,000; it is the punishment for every offence not included in 30(b) — it used to be Rs 2000 instead of Rs 25,000 in the initial Act.**

**The structure of section 30, which is what makes the answer identifiable:**

| Sub-section | Offence | **Penalty (amended 2079)** | **Original Act** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **30(1)/(a)** | **Practising engineering WITHOUT a license** | — (the prohibition itself) | — |
| **30(2)/(b)** | **Violation of that prohibition — an UNLICENSED person** | **Up to Rs 10,000, or up to 3 months' imprisonment, or both** | **Rs 3000** |
| **30(3)/(c)** | **Any other offence — by a LICENSED engineer** | **Up to Rs 25,000** ← | **Rs 2000** |

> **The key distinction is WHO commits the offence:**

> **30(b) punishes an UNLICENSED person for practising at all.**
>
> **30(c) punishes a LICENSED engineer for every other breach of the Act or rules.**

> **And notice that the penalty for the licensed engineer is HIGHER — Rs 25,000 against Rs 10,000.**

> **That ordering is deliberate and worth understanding rather than memorising: a registered professional is held to a higher standard than an unqualified outsider.** The license carries obligations as well as privileges, and breaching them from a position of professional trust is treated more seriously.

> **Though note the unlicensed offence also carries the possibility of IMPRISONMENT, which 30(c) does not** — so the two are not simply ranked on the fine alone.

**Why all four options are in the set:**

> **Every one is a genuine figure from this same section — two current and two superseded.**

| Option | What it is |
|---|---|
| **Rs 2000** | **The ORIGINAL 30(c) penalty, before amendment** |
| **Rs 3000** | **The ORIGINAL 30(b) penalty** |
| Rs 20,000 | Not a stated figure — the only invented option |
| **Rs 25,000** | **The CURRENT 30(c) penalty** ✓ |

> **So the question is testing whether the candidate knows the AMENDED figures rather than the original ones**, and the stem says "Amended 2079" precisely to signal that.

> **Reading that qualifier is the step being tested** — a candidate working from an older text would answer Rs 2000 and be marked wrong on a technically correct reading of a superseded Act.

**And this is exactly why statutory numbers are the most volatile examination material there is:**

> **The same section carried Rs 2000 and Rs 3000 before amendment and Rs 25,000 and Rs 10,000 after.** An amendment changes the answer without changing anything of substance.

> **What is DURABLE is the structure**: section 30 penalises practising without a license more severely in kind (imprisonment available) and other breaches more severely in amount (a higher fine), with the distinction resting on whether the offender holds a license.

> **Learn the structure and the reasoning; verify the amounts against the current Act.**

**Why the offence exists at all:**

> **Section 30(1)'s prohibition — that no one may practise engineering without a license — is the provision that gives the whole Act its force.**

> **Without it, registration would be voluntary and the Council's disciplinary powers meaningless**, since a struck-off engineer could simply continue practising.

> **The penalty is what makes the register more than a list**, and it is why the licensing requirement and the punishment clause always appear together.

**The Council's other enforcement powers**, which run alongside the fines: **suspension of registration, and removal of a name from the register.** **Those are often the more serious sanction** — Rs 25,000 is recoverable, whereas losing the right to practise ends a career.

examTip.trick: **30(b) punishes the UNLICENSED (Rs 10,000 + possible imprisonment); 30(c) punishes the LICENSED for other breaches (Rs 25,000).** The licensed engineer's fine is higher — a professional is held to a higher standard.
examTip.trap: **Rs 2000 and Rs 3000 are the ORIGINAL figures for the same two sub-sections.** The stem says "Amended 2079" for a reason — a candidate working from an older text answers Rs 2000.
examTip.mnemonic: **Removal from the register is the sanction that bites** — Rs 25,000 is recoverable; losing the right to practise ends a career. And section 30(1) is what makes the register more than a list.

questions.stem: While representing the diameter in dimensioning, it is represented as:
questions.solution:
**Ø.**

> The source states it: **while representing the diameter in dimensioning it is represented as Ø.**

**The standard dimensioning symbols:**

| Symbol | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Ø** | **DIAMETER** ← |
| **R** | **Radius** |
| **SØ** | Spherical diameter |
| **SR** | Spherical radius |
| **□** | Square |
| **×** | "By", in a size such as 50 × 25 |
| **t** | Thickness |

> **The symbol PRECEDES the value: Ø40 means a 40 mm diameter, and R20 a 20 mm radius.**

**Why a SYMBOL rather than an abbreviation — and the reason is the point of the question:**

> **A symbol is LANGUAGE-INDEPENDENT.**

> **"Dia" is an English abbreviation and means nothing to a fabricator who does not read English.** **Ø is understood on a drawing anywhere in the world.**

> **Engineering drawing is deliberately constructed as a language of symbols and conventions precisely so that a drawing produced in one country can be built in another** — which is why ISO and IS standards specify symbols rather than words wherever possible.

> **That is also why option (c), "Dia", is the instructive distractor: it is what people write informally, and it is exactly what the standard exists to replace.**

**Why options (a) and (d) are wrong:**

> **D and d are ALGEBRAIC symbols used in formulae and calculations, not dimensioning symbols on a drawing.**

> **In text one writes "a pipe of diameter D"; on a drawing one writes Ø40.** The two conventions serve different purposes and are not interchangeable.

> **And note that D and d appearing as separate options is itself a hint**: a well-formed convention would not distinguish upper and lower case for the same quantity, so neither is likely to be the standard symbol.

**The general dimensioning rules that accompany it:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Units** | **Millimetres, and the unit is NOT repeated on every dimension** |
| **Dimension lines** | Thin continuous, with arrowheads at both ends |
| **Extension lines** | Thin, with a small gap from the outline |
| **Placement** | **Outside the view where possible; never inside if avoidable** |
| **Readability** | Aligned with the dimension line, readable from the bottom or the right |
| **Repetition** | **Each dimension given ONCE only — never duplicated** |

> **The no-duplication rule matters more than it appears.** A dimension given twice can be revised in one place and missed in the other, so the drawing then contradicts itself — and the fabricator must guess which is current.

> **That is the same reasoning behind generating documents from a single source rather than maintaining copies**, and it applies to drawings as much as to anything else.

**And the related conventions for diameters specifically:**

| Situation | Convention |
|---|---|
| **Circle, dimensioned across** | **Ø with the dimension line through the centre** |
| **Arc less than a semicircle** | **R, with the dimension from the centre** |
| **Small hole** | Ø on a leader line pointing at the circle |
| **Repeated holes** | **"4 × Ø10" — four holes of 10 mm diameter** |

> **The choice between Ø and R is not stylistic: an ARC is dimensioned by radius and a full CIRCLE by diameter**, because that is what each is defined by and what the workshop needs in order to set out or machine it.

**Drawing sheet context, since it belongs to the same subject:** **A0 is 1 m² with a 1:√2 aspect ratio, each size down halving the area**, and the standard scales run **1, 2, 5 within each decade** — which is why 1:3 and 1:400 are not standard scales.

**A note on two of the distractors:**

> **The printed paper offered a plain capital D and a plain lower-case d as separate options**, differing only in case.

> **They are wrong for the same reason, so the distinction between them carries no marks:** a plain letter is an algebraic variable, not a dimensioning symbol. **On a drawing, D or d would be read as a labelled dimension whose value is given elsewhere** -- in a table of sizes, say -- and not as a statement that the feature is circular.

> **That is the substantive difference: the symbol tells the fabricator the feature IS a diameter; a letter merely names a quantity.**

verification.notes: Option text disambiguated. The printed paper offered a plain capital D and a plain lower-case d as two separate options, distinguishable only by letter case -- which no candidate can rely on across print runs, and which is a defect in the options rather than in the key. Each is now labelled explicitly. The keyed answer is unchanged: the diameter symbol is the slashed circle, not either plain letter.

examTip.trick: **A symbol is LANGUAGE-INDEPENDENT.** Ø is read on a drawing anywhere; "Dia" means nothing to a fabricator who does not read English. That is why standards specify symbols over words.
examTip.trap: **"Dia" is what people write informally — and exactly what the standard exists to replace.** D and d are algebraic symbols for formulae, not drawing symbols.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ø for a full CIRCLE, R for an ARC** — each is dimensioned by what defines it and by what the workshop needs to set it out. And give every dimension **once only**.

questions.stem: In the standard consistency test on cement, the Vicat plunger should penetrate to a point 5 to 7 mm from the bottom of the mould. The water content at which this occurs is expressed as a percentage of:
options: The weight of the wet paste
The weight of cement plus water
questions.solution:
**The weight of dry cement.**

**What the test determines:**

> **STANDARD (or normal) CONSISTENCY is the water content at which the cement paste has a defined stiffness**, measured by the penetration of the **Vicat plunger of 10 mm diameter.**

| Test detail | Value |
|---|---|
| **Plunger diameter** | **10 mm** |
| **Penetration required** | **5 to 7 mm from the bottom** of the mould |
| **Expressed as** | **% of the weight of DRY CEMENT** |
| **Typical result** | **26 to 33%** |

> **Every water content in cement and concrete work is expressed against the weight of CEMENT**, never against the paste or the total.

**Why that convention, and it is not arbitrary:**

> **Because the WATER–CEMENT RATIO is the quantity that governs strength**, by Abrams' law.

> **w/c is water weight ÷ cement weight**, so expressing water as a percentage of cement makes the consistency result **directly comparable with the w/c ratio** used everywhere else.

> **If consistency were reported against the weight of the paste, it could not be compared with anything** — every mix design, every strength relation and every durability limit in IS 456 is written on the cement basis.

> **Consistency of 30% simply means w/c = 0.30**, and that equivalence is the whole reason for the convention.

**Why the test matters — it is a PREREQUISITE, not an end in itself:**

> **The consistency result is used to set the water content for the OTHER cement tests**, so that all of them are performed on paste of comparable stiffness:

| Test | Water content used |
|---|---|
| **Setting time (initial and final)** | **0.85 × standard consistency** |
| **SOUNDNESS (Le Chatelier)** | **0.78 × standard consistency** |
| Compressive strength (mortar cubes) | **(P/4 + 3.0)%**, where P is the consistency |

> **Without a standard consistency, setting times could not be compared between cements at all** — a wetter paste sets later, so the result would measure the water rather than the cement.

> **That is why consistency is always the first test performed**, and why an examination question about it is really a question about the basis of comparison.

**The setting time limits it feeds (IS 269):**

| Setting time | Requirement |
|---|---|
| **Initial set** | **NOT LESS than 30 minutes** |
| **Final set** | **NOT MORE than 600 minutes (10 hours)** |

> **Note the directions differ deliberately**: the initial set has a **minimum** (time to transport, place and compact) and the final set a **maximum** (so formwork can be struck and work proceed). **Reversing them is a common slip.**

**And the apparatus distinction worth carrying:**

> **The VICAT apparatus is used for all three of consistency, initial set and final set** — only the attachment changes:

| Attachment | Test |
|---|---|
| **10 mm PLUNGER** | **Standard consistency** |
| **1 mm² square NEEDLE** | **Initial setting time** |
| **Needle with an annular collar** | **Final setting time** |

> **One instrument, three attachments, three tests** — which is a tidy piece of laboratory design and an easy source of examination questions.

examTip.trick: **All water contents in cement work are expressed against the weight of CEMENT**, because that makes the result directly comparable with the **w/c ratio** — consistency of 30% means w/c = 0.30.
examTip.trap: **Consistency is a PREREQUISITE, not an end in itself** — setting time uses 0.85 × it and soundness 0.78 × it, so that all tests run on comparably stiff paste.
examTip.mnemonic: **One Vicat apparatus, three attachments**: 10 mm plunger for consistency, 1 mm² needle for initial set, needle with collar for final set. Initial ≥ 30 min, final ≤ 600 min.

questions.stem: A damp proof course (DPC) in a building is provided primarily to:
options: Increase the load-bearing capacity of the wall
Provide a level bed for the superstructure
Improve the thermal insulation of the wall
Prevent the upward movement of moisture into the wall
questions.solution:
**To prevent the upward movement of moisture into the wall.**

**The problem it solves:**

> **Masonry is porous, and the pores form a network of fine capillaries.**

> **Ground moisture is drawn up through them by CAPILLARY ACTION, exactly as water rises in a fine tube.**

> **h = 4σcosθ/(γd), so h ∝ 1/d** — and because the pores in brick and mortar are very fine, the potential rise is substantial. **Damp can climb a metre or more up an unprotected wall.**

> **That is RISING DAMP, and a DPC is the barrier that interrupts the capillary path.**

**Why rising damp matters:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **EFFLORESCENCE** | **Salts carried up in solution crystallise as the water evaporates, spalling the surface** |
| **Plaster and paint failure** | Finishes blister and detach |
| **Timber decay** | Skirtings, joists and door frames rot |
| **Reduced insulation** | **Wet masonry conducts heat far better than dry** |
| Unhealthy interior | Mould growth |

> **EFFLORESCENCE is the mechanism that does the structural damage**, and it is worth understanding: the water is merely the carrier. **Dissolved sulphates and chlorides travel up with it, and when the water evaporates at the surface the salts crystallise, expanding as they do so and breaking the surface off.**

> **So the damage continues as long as the moisture cycle continues**, and it is progressive rather than a one-off.

**Where a DPC is placed:**

| Location | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **HORIZONTAL, at plinth level** | **The principal DPC — blocks rise from the foundation** |
| **Under the ground floor slab** | Blocks rise through the floor |
| **VERTICAL, on basement walls** | Blocks lateral penetration |
| Over openings, at parapets, sills | Blocks other paths |

> **The horizontal course at plinth level is the one meant by "DPC" without qualification**, and it must be **continuous** — a gap anywhere defeats it, because water will find the one path left open.

**Materials used:**

| Material | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bitumen felt / mastic asphalt** | **Flexible, the traditional choice** |
| **Cement concrete, rich mix (1:1.5:3)** | **Common in Nepal; often with a waterproofing admixture** |
| Metal sheets — lead, copper | Durable, expensive |
| Polythene / PVC sheet | Cheap and effective |
| Engineering bricks in cement mortar | Low absorption |

> **A concrete DPC is rigid, so it must not be relied upon where differential settlement is expected** — a crack through it reopens the capillary path. **Flexible materials tolerate movement, which is their advantage over the cheaper rigid options.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Comment |
|---|---|
| **Load capacity** | **A DPC does not strengthen the wall — and a bitumen felt layer can even act as a SLIP PLANE, reducing shear resistance** |
| **Level bed** | **That is the plinth or a levelling course**, a construction convenience |
| **Thermal insulation** | **A by-product at best** — keeping masonry dry does improve its insulation, but that is a consequence, not the purpose |

> **Option (a) is worth noticing because it is not merely wrong but backwards**: a flexible DPC introduces a horizontal plane of low friction, which is a genuine consideration in seismic design where the wall must transfer shear.

> **Option (c) is the most defensible of the three**, since dry masonry does insulate better — but the DPC is provided to exclude water, and the thermal gain follows from that rather than motivating it.

**And the related provisions:** **CAVITY WALLS** resist lateral rain penetration by an air gap; **plinth protection and surface drainage** keep water away from the wall base in the first place; and **weep holes** relieve water pressure behind retaining walls.

> **The best defence against damp is drainage rather than a barrier** — a DPC stops what reaches it, but keeping water away from the plinth is cheaper and more reliable than intercepting it.

examTip.trick: **Masonry pores are fine capillaries, and h ∝ 1/d** — so damp can climb a metre or more. A DPC interrupts that capillary path; it does nothing else.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is backwards** — a flexible bitumen DPC can act as a **SLIP PLANE**, reducing the wall's shear resistance. That matters in seismic design.
examTip.mnemonic: **EFFLORESCENCE does the damage, not the water** — dissolved salts crystallise at the surface and expand, spalling it. The cycle continues as long as moisture does, so the damage is progressive.

questions.stem: In earthwork calculation by the trapezoidal rule, the volume between two cross-sections of areas A₁ and A₂ spaced at distance d is:
questions.solution:
**d(A₁ + A₂)/2** — the average of the two end areas, times the distance between them.

**The reasoning:**

> **The trapezoidal (or average end area) rule assumes the cross-sectional area varies LINEARLY between the two sections.**

> **The mean area over the length is then simply (A₁ + A₂)/2**, and the volume is that mean area times the distance:
>
> **V = d × (A₁ + A₂)/2** ✓

> **It is the volumetric equivalent of the area of a trapezium**, which is where the name comes from.

**For a series of sections at constant spacing d:**

> **V = d[(A₁ + Aₙ)/2 + A₂ + A₃ + … + Aₙ₋₁]**

> **The end areas are HALVED and the intermediate ones counted in full** — the same structure as the trapezoidal rule for areas, and worth recognising as the same formula.

**The alternative — the PRISMOIDAL rule:**

> **V = (d/6)(A₁ + 4A_m + A₂)**, where **A_m is the area at the MID-SECTION**

> **Note that A_m is the area of the section measured at the midpoint, NOT the average of A₁ and A₂** — that is the single commonest error in applying it.

| | **TRAPEZOIDAL** | **PRISMOIDAL** |
|---|---|---|
| Assumes | **LINEAR variation** | **PARABOLIC (second-degree) variation** |
| Needs | **Two end areas** | **Two end areas AND the mid-area** |
| Accuracy | **Approximate** | **More accurate — exact for a prismoid** |
| **Bias** | **OVER-estimates volume** | Correct |
| Simplicity | **Simpler; used for routine work** | More work |

> **Option (c) in this question, d(A₁ + 4A₂)/6, is a corrupted prismoidal formula** — it has the 4 and the 6 but applies the weighting to an end area rather than the mid-area, and omits one term. **It is there for anyone who half-remembers the prismoidal rule.**

**Why the trapezoidal rule over-estimates:**

> **Because the real variation of area along a cut or embankment is usually CONVEX** — the section changes faster near the ends than a straight line implies.

> **A linear interpolation therefore sits above the true curve, and the volume comes out high.**

> **The difference is the PRISMOIDAL CORRECTION, always SUBTRACTED from the trapezoidal result:**
>
> **C_p = (d/6)(A₁ + A₂ − 2A_m)** for the simple case, or **(d/12)(h₁ − h₂)(w₁ − w₂)** for a level-section cutting.

> **The correction is small when the sections are similar and significant when they differ greatly** — which tells you when it matters: **at the ends of a cut, at transitions between cut and fill, and wherever the ground changes rapidly.**

**Why the over-estimate matters commercially:**

> **Earthwork is paid by volume, so the choice of rule is a payment question, not merely a technical one.**

> **A contract must state which rule applies**, and disputes have arisen from its omission. **Using the trapezoidal rule where the contract specifies prismoidal over-pays the contractor on every section.**

> **For a long road project the cumulative difference is real money**, which is why the method of measurement is part of the contract documents rather than left to the engineer's preference.

**And the related earthwork tools:**

| Tool | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **MASS HAUL DIAGRAM** | **Cumulative volume against chainage — plans the movement of earth** |
| Balancing line | Where cut equals fill, so haul is minimised |
| **Free haul / overhaul** | The distance within which haul is unpaid, and beyond which it is paid extra |
| Borrow and spoil | Where material is imported or dumped |

> **The mass haul diagram is what converts volumes into a HAUL PLAN**, and its whole purpose is to answer where each cubic metre of cut should go — because moving earth twice, or further than necessary, is the largest avoidable cost in road construction.

examTip.trick: **Mean area × distance.** Linear variation gives a mean of (A₁ + A₂)/2, so V = d(A₁ + A₂)/2 — the volumetric form of a trapezium's area.
examTip.trap: **Option (c) is a corrupted PRISMOIDAL formula** — it carries the 4 and the 6 but weights an end area instead of the MID-area, and drops a term. A_m is measured at the midpoint, not averaged.
examTip.mnemonic: **Trapezoidal always OVER-estimates**, because real sections vary convexly. Subtract the prismoidal correction — and note the choice of rule is a **payment** question, so the contract must state it.

questions.stem: For a simply supported beam of span L carrying a point load W at mid-span, the maximum bending moment and maximum shear force are respectively:
questions.solution:
**WL/4 and W/2.**

**Working:**

> **By symmetry each reaction carries half the load: R_A = R_B = W/2**
>
> **Maximum shear force = the reaction = W/2**, constant from each support to the load
>
> **Maximum bending moment, at mid-span = R_A × L/2 = (W/2)(L/2) = WL/4** ✓

**The two standard cases must be kept apart, and this is where the confusion arises:**

| Loading | **Maximum BM** | **Maximum SF** | **Maximum deflection** |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Point load W at mid-span** | **WL/4** | **W/2** | **WL³/(48EI)** |
| **UDL w over the whole span** | **wL²/8** | **wL/2** | **5wL⁴/(384EI)** |

> **WL/4 belongs to the POINT LOAD; wL²/8 belongs to the UDL.**

> **Option (a) and option (c) both offer WL/8, which is not the maximum moment for either case** — it is a conflation of the point-load and UDL formulae, taking the /8 from one and the W from the other.

> **That conflation is the single commonest error in the topic**, and it is why both wrong options carry it.

**A useful cross-check between the two cases:**

> **A UDL of total weight W = wL gives a maximum moment of wL²/8 = WL/8.**

> **So for the SAME total load, a point load at mid-span produces TWICE the moment of a uniformly distributed one** — WL/4 against WL/8.

> **That factor of two is worth carrying**, because it explains why concentrating a load is so much more onerous than spreading it, and it gives an instant sanity check on which formula is which.

**The diagram shapes:**

| Diagram | Point load at mid-span |
|---|---|
| **SFD** | **Constant +W/2, then a JUMP of W at the load, then constant −W/2** |
| **BMD** | **Two straight lines forming a TRIANGLE, peak WL/4 at mid-span** |

> **The moment diagram is TRIANGULAR, not parabolic** — a parabola requires a distributed load.

> **From V = dM/dx: with the shear constant on each side, the moment must be linear there**, which gives the straight lines. **The kink at mid-span corresponds to the jump in shear.**

**Why the shear jumps rather than passing through zero:**

> **At a concentrated load the shear force changes discontinuously, by the magnitude of the load.**

> **So the maximum moment occurs at a point where the shear NEVER EQUALS ZERO as a value** — it jumps from +W/2 straight to −W/2.

> **The usual rule "maximum moment where shear crosses zero" still holds in the sense that the shear changes sign there**, but the derivative dM/dx is undefined at that section. **It is the one common case where the rule must be read as a sign change rather than a zero value.**

**The governing relations:**

> **w = −dV/dx** and **V = dM/dx**

| Applied | SFD | BMD |
|---|---|---|
| **Point load W** | **JUMPS by W** | **KINK** |
| **COUPLE M** | **NO change** | **JUMPS by M** |
| **UDL w** | **LINEAR** | **PARABOLIC** |
| **No load** | **Constant** | **LINEAR** |

> **The last row explains this beam entirely**: with no load between support and mid-span, the shear is constant and the moment linear.

**And the deflection comparison is worth noting:**

> **WL³/48EI for the point load against 5WL⁴/384EI for a UDL of the same total weight** — working the second out, **5(W/L)L⁴/384EI = 5WL³/384EI = WL³/76.8EI.**

> **So the point load deflects the beam about 1.6 times as much as the same total weight spread uniformly** — a smaller ratio than the moment's factor of two, because deflection integrates the curvature over the whole span rather than taking its peak.

examTip.trick: **R = W/2 gives the shear directly, and M = (W/2)(L/2) = WL/4.** Two lines, no formula needed.
examTip.trap: **WL/8 appears in TWO options and is the maximum moment for neither case** — it conflates the point-load W with the UDL's /8. That mix-up is the commonest error in the topic.
examTip.mnemonic: **For the same TOTAL load, a point load at mid-span gives TWICE the moment of a UDL** (WL/4 vs WL/8) — an instant check on which formula is which.

questions.stem: A steel bar 2 m long and of cross-sectional area 500 mm² carries an axial tensile load of 50 kN. Taking E = 200 GPa, the elongation of the bar is:
questions.solution:
**1.0 mm.**

**Working:**

> **δ = PL/(AE)**
>
> **P = 50 kN = 50,000 N; L = 2 m = 2000 mm; A = 500 mm²; E = 200 GPa = 200,000 N/mm²**
>
> **δ = (50,000 × 2000)/(500 × 200,000) = 100,000,000/100,000,000 = 1.0 mm** ✓

> **The numbers are chosen so the numerator and denominator are identical — both 10⁸ — which is worth noticing, because it means the arithmetic can be done by inspection.**

**The consistent-units point, which is where this calculation usually goes wrong:**

> **Work throughout in NEWTONS and MILLIMETRES.**

| Quantity | In N-mm |
|---|---|
| **50 kN** | **50,000 N** |
| **2 m** | **2000 mm** |
| **200 GPa** | **200,000 N/mm²** |
| **Result** | **mm** |

> **1 GPa = 1000 MPa = 1000 N/mm²**, so **200 GPa = 200,000 N/mm²** — and that is the conversion most often fumbled.

> **Mixing metres with millimetres, or MPa with GPa, gives answers wrong by factors of 1000**, which is why the options here are spaced at factors of 2 rather than 10: the question is testing the formula, not the unit conversion.

**Deriving the formula rather than recalling it:**

> **Stress σ = P/A = 50,000/500 = 100 N/mm²**
>
> **Strain ε = σ/E = 100/200,000 = 0.0005**
>
> **Elongation δ = εL = 0.0005 × 2000 = 1.0 mm** ✓

> **Three short steps, each meaningful, and they give a stress value worth having: 100 N/mm² is comfortably below mild steel's yield of about 250 N/mm²**, so the bar is elastic and Hooke's law applies — which the formula assumes.

> **Checking that the stress is within the elastic range is not a formality**: δ = PL/AE is valid only up to the proportional limit, and applying it beyond yield would give a badly wrong answer.

**A strain of 0.0005 is 0.05%**, which is a useful sense of scale:

| Material state | Strain |
|---|---|
| **This bar, at 100 N/mm²** | **0.0005 (0.05%)** |
| **Mild steel at yield (250 N/mm²)** | **0.00125 (0.125%)** |
| **Mild steel at failure** | **0.20 – 0.25 (20–25%)** |
| **Concrete at crushing** | **0.0035 (0.35%)** |

> **Note how small elastic strains are, and how large the plastic ones become.** Steel yields at about an eighth of one per cent and fails at twenty per cent — a factor of nearly 200 between the two, and that ratio is what DUCTILITY means quantitatively.

**Extensions of the formula worth knowing:**

| Case | Elongation |
|---|---|
| **Uniform bar** | **PL/(AE)** |
| **Stepped bar** | **Σ P_iL_i/(A_iE_i)** — sum the segments |
| **Tapered circular bar** | **4PL/(πE d₁d₂)** |
| **Under self-weight only** | **γL²/(2E)** |
| **Composite bar (equal strain)** | Load shares in proportion to **AE** |

> **The self-weight case is worth noting because the LENGTH is squared** — which is why a very long hanging member (a mine shaft rope, a deep pile being lifted) can be governed by its own weight rather than by the load it carries.

> **And in a COMPOSITE bar the two materials share the load in proportion to their AE products, because they must strain equally** — which is the whole basis of reinforced concrete, where steel and concrete are forced to deform together.

examTip.trick: **δ = PL/AE = (50,000 × 2000)/(500 × 200,000)** — numerator and denominator are both 10⁸, so the answer is 1.0 mm by inspection.
examTip.trap: **200 GPa = 200,000 N/mm², not 200.** Work throughout in newtons and millimetres; mixing GPa with MPa or metres with millimetres gives errors of a factor of 1000.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check the stress is elastic first**: 100 N/mm² against a 250 N/mm² yield, so Hooke's law holds. δ = PL/AE is valid only to the proportional limit.

questions.stem: In the limit state design of a singly reinforced beam, the depth of the rectangular stress block is taken as:
questions.solution:
**0.80 x_u.**

**The IS 456 stress block, and where each number sits:**

> **The design stress block for concrete in flexure is PARABOLIC for the top portion and RECTANGULAR below it:**

| Part | Extent | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **Parabolic portion** | **From the neutral axis up to 0.43 x_u** | Strain below 0.002 |
| **RECTANGULAR portion** | **The remaining 0.57 x_u, of depth ≈ 0.80 x_u from the top... ** | — |

> **More precisely: the rectangular part extends over the top 3/7 of x_u and the parabolic part over the lower 4/7** — and taken together the equivalent rectangular block used in design has a depth of **0.80 x_u** with a uniform stress of **0.446 f_ck.**

> **The three coefficients that come out of integrating that block are the ones actually used, and they must be kept apart:**

| Coefficient | What it is |
|---|---|
| **0.36** | **The COMPRESSIVE FORCE coefficient: C = 0.36 f_ck b x_u** |
| **0.42** | **The CENTROID of the block, at 0.42 x_u from the top** |
| **0.80** | **The DEPTH of the equivalent rectangular block** ← |
| **0.87** | **f_y/1.15 — the steel's design strength, nothing to do with the block** |

> **Every option in this question is a genuine number from singly reinforced beam design, attached to a different quantity** — which is what makes it a real discrimination rather than a recall test.

**How 0.36 and 0.42 arise from the block:**

> **Integrating the parabolic-rectangular stress distribution over its depth gives a total force of 0.36 f_ck b x_u** — so 0.36 already contains both the 0.446 stress and the shape of the block.

> **Taking moments of that distribution about the top gives its centroid at 0.42 x_u.**

> **So 0.36 and 0.42 are DERIVED from the block, while 0.80 describes it.** Confusing the description with its consequences is the trap here.

**Where they are all used together:**

> **Moment of resistance: M_u = 0.36 f_ck b x_u (d − 0.42 x_u)**
>
> **Equilibrium: 0.36 f_ck b x_u = 0.87 f_y A_st**

> **That second equation is how x_u is found in the first place** — force equilibrium between the concrete compression and the steel tension.

> **Rearranged: x_u = 0.87 f_y A_st/(0.36 f_ck b)**

**And the limiting depths that x_u is then checked against:**

| Steel grade | **x_u,max/d** |
|---|---|
| **Fe 250** | **0.53** |
| **Fe 415** | **0.48** |
| **Fe 500** | **0.46** |

> **From x_u,max/d = 700/(1100 + 0.87 f_y)** — and higher-grade steel gives a **smaller** limit, because a stronger steel reaches its design strain at a higher stress.

> **If x_u exceeds x_u,max the section is OVER-REINFORCED and IS 456 does not permit it** — not because it is weaker, but because the concrete would crush before the steel yields, giving a **sudden brittle failure with no warning.**

> **The limit is a DUCTILITY requirement**, and it is why the answer to "the section needs more moment capacity" is a deeper section or compression steel, never simply more tension steel.

**The strain assumptions underlying all of it:**

> **Concrete ultimate strain = 0.0035** (a fixed value, independent of grade)
>
> **Steel design strain for Fe 415 = 0.87 f_y/E_s + 0.002 = 0.0038**

> **The additional 0.002 is the code's allowance for the non-linear portion of a cold-worked bar's stress–strain curve**, which has no sharp yield point. **For mild steel, which does have one, that allowance is absent.**

**And the limiting moment, for completeness:** **M_u,lim = 0.138 f_ck b d² for Fe 415**, 0.148 for Fe 250 and 0.133 for Fe 500 — obtained by substituting x_u,max into the moment equation above.

examTip.trick: **0.80 DESCRIBES the block's depth; 0.36 and 0.42 are DERIVED from it** — the compressive force coefficient and the centroid respectively. Confusing description with consequence is the trap.
examTip.trap: **All four options are genuine numbers from this same topic**: 0.36 (force), 0.42 (centroid), 0.87 (f_y/1.15 — the steel, not the block), 0.80 (block depth).
examTip.mnemonic: **0.36 f_ck b x_u = 0.87 f_y A_st** finds x_u; then **M_u = 0.36 f_ck b x_u(d − 0.42x_u)**. Check x_u ≤ 0.48d for Fe 415 — a **DUCTILITY** limit, not a strength one.

questions.stem: A two-way slab simply supported on all four edges is one in which the ratio of the longer to the shorter span is:
questions.solution:
**Less than 2.**

**The classification:**

| Ratio l_y/l_x | Slab type | Spans |
|---|---|---|
| **< 2** | **TWO-WAY** | **Both directions** ← |
| **≥ 2** | **ONE-WAY** | **Predominantly the SHORTER direction** |

> **where l_y is the longer span and l_x the shorter.**

**Why 2 is the dividing line — the reason is in how load is shared:**

> **A slab supported on all four edges tries to span both ways, and the two directions share the load in proportion to their STIFFNESS.**

> **Stiffness varies as 1/L³ for a given thickness**, so the shorter span is far stiffer and takes far more of the load.

> **At a ratio of 2 the shorter direction is 2³ = 8 times stiffer, so it carries roughly 8/9 — about 89% — of the load.**

> **The longer direction is then contributing so little that ignoring it is a reasonable and conservative simplification**, and the slab is designed as spanning one way only.

> **That is where the number 2 comes from: it is the ratio at which the second direction stops being worth calculating.** It is not an arbitrary code threshold.

**The load sharing at various ratios:**

| Ratio | Share taken by the SHORT span |
|---|---|
| **1.0 (square)** | **50%** |
| 1.5 | ≈ 77% |
| **2.0** | **≈ 89%** |
| 3.0 | ≈ 96% |

> **A square slab shares equally, which is why option (d) is wrong** — a ratio of exactly 1 is a *special case* of a two-way slab, the most efficient one, not the definition of the class.

> **Option (d) is the trap for anyone who reasons that "two-way" means "equal in both directions".** It does not; it means both directions are significant.

**Why the distinction matters in design:**

| | **ONE-WAY** | **TWO-WAY** |
|---|---|---|
| **Main steel** | **Along the SHORTER span only** | **BOTH directions** |
| **Steel in the other direction** | **Distribution steel — minimum only (0.12% for Fe 415)** | **Designed, not nominal** |
| Moment coefficients | Simple beam analysis | **IS 456 Table 26/27, by ratio and edge condition** |
| **CORNER reinforcement** | Not required | **REQUIRED at corners held down** |
| Economy | Thicker for the same span | **Thinner — load shared** |

> **The corner reinforcement is the provision most often omitted, and it matters.** In a two-way slab with corners prevented from lifting, **the corners try to rise and develop TORSION**, which cracks them diagonally on both faces.

> **IS 456 requires torsion reinforcement in the corners — mesh in both faces over a fifth of the shorter span** — and a slab detailed without it cracks at the corners regardless of how well the spans were calculated.

**And the economy point is the reason two-way action is exploited wherever possible:**

> **Sharing the load between two directions reduces the moment in each, so a two-way slab can be appreciably thinner than a one-way slab of the same shorter span.**

> **Which is why column grids in buildings are laid out as near square as the architecture allows** — a 6 × 6 m panel is materially cheaper than a 4 × 9 m panel of the same area.

**Deflection control, which usually governs slab thickness:**

> **Span/effective depth ratios (IS 456): 20 for simply supported, 26 for continuous, 7 for cantilever** — modified by the tension steel percentage.

> **Slabs are almost always governed by DEFLECTION rather than by strength**, so the thickness is set by these ratios and the reinforcement then follows. **That is the reverse of beam design, where strength usually governs.**

**A note on the boundary case:** at exactly **l_y/l_x = 2** the codes permit either treatment, and designing as one-way is the conservative choice — it puts all the load in the short span, which is where nearly all of it goes anyway.

examTip.trick: **Stiffness varies as 1/L³, so at a ratio of 2 the short span is 8× stiffer and takes ~89% of the load.** The second direction stops being worth calculating — that is where the number 2 comes from.
examTip.trap: **Option (d), exactly 1, is a SPECIAL CASE of a two-way slab, not its definition.** "Two-way" means both directions are significant, not that they are equal.
examTip.mnemonic: **CORNER torsion reinforcement is the provision most often omitted** — corners held down try to lift and crack diagonally. And slab thickness is governed by **deflection** (span/d = 20, 26, 7), not strength.

questions.stem: In a bolted connection, the pitch of bolts is the:
options: Distance from the bolt centre to the edge of the plate
Distance between two adjacent bolt lines measured perpendicular to the direction of force
Centre-to-centre distance between adjacent bolts measured along the direction of force
questions.solution:
**The centre-to-centre distance between adjacent bolts, measured ALONG the direction of the force.**

**The four spacing terms, which must be kept apart:**

| Term | Definition |
|---|---|
| **PITCH** | **Centre-to-centre spacing ALONG the line of force** ← |
| **GAUGE** | **Centre-to-centre spacing PERPENDICULAR to the force** — between bolt lines |
| **EDGE distance** | **From the bolt centre to the plate EDGE, perpendicular to the force** |
| **END distance** | **From the bolt centre to the plate END, along the force** |

> **Each option in this question is a genuine term from the same topic**: option (b) defines the GAUGE and option (a) the EDGE distance. **Only the direction of measurement distinguishes them.**

> **Pitch is along the force; gauge is across it.** That single sentence separates the two most easily confused.

**The IS 800 limits, and each has a distinct reason:**

| Limit | Value | **Why** |
|---|---|---|
| **Minimum pitch** | **2.5 d** | **Room to tighten; avoids splitting between holes** |
| **Maximum pitch** | **16t or 200 mm, whichever is less** | **Prevents BUCKLING of the plate between bolts, and keeps the joint tight against moisture** |
| **Minimum edge distance** | **1.5 d (or 1.7 d for a sheared edge)** | **Prevents the bolt TEARING OUT through the edge** |
| **Maximum edge distance** | **12tε** | Prevents corrosion between plates |

> **where d is the bolt diameter and t the thinner plate thickness.**

**The minimum and maximum exist for opposite reasons, which is the point worth grasping:**

> **The MINIMUM protects the PLATE from being torn apart between closely spaced holes** — too little material remains to carry the force between them.

> **The MAXIMUM protects against BUCKLING and CORROSION** — widely spaced bolts leave unstiffened plate that can buckle in compression, and a gap through which moisture enters and rusts the interface.

> **So a designer is squeezed from both ends, and neither limit can be treated as merely nominal.**

**Why edge distance matters more than it appears:**

> **Insufficient edge distance causes a BEARING or TEAR-OUT failure**, where the bolt simply ploughs through the remaining material to the edge rather than the plate failing in tension.

> **That is a brittle, sudden failure mode**, and it is one of the commonest defects in poorly detailed connections — especially where a member has been trimmed on site to fit.

**The failure modes a bolted connection must be checked against:**

| Mode | Check |
|---|---|
| **Bolt SHEAR** | **V_dsb = (A_nb f_ub)/(√3 γ_mb)** |
| **Bolt BEARING on the plate** | Depends on pitch, edge distance and plate thickness |
| **Plate TENSION (net section)** | Gross area less the bolt holes |
| **BLOCK SHEAR** | **A tear-out of a whole block of plate** |
| Bolt tension | Where the connection carries tension |

> **The connection's capacity is the LEAST of these, not the bolt shear alone** — which is the mistake in treating a connection as "so many bolts × the bolt value".

> **BLOCK SHEAR is the mode most often overlooked**: instead of individual bolts failing, a rectangular block of plate containing all of them tears out, failing in tension across one face and shear along the other. **It governs particularly in short, deep connections with small edge distances.**

**And the net section point:**

> **Bolt holes reduce the plate's tension capacity, and the hole is taken as the bolt diameter plus a clearance (typically 1.5–2 mm).**

> **Staggering the bolts increases the net area** by lengthening the failure path, which is why a **zigzag arrangement** is used where the net section governs — the tear must travel diagonally rather than straight across.

**Why bolts rather than welds on site:** **γ_mb for bolts is 1.25, and weld γ_mw is 1.25 in the shop but 1.5 on SITE** — because field welding conditions cannot be controlled. **Which is why the standard practice is to weld in the shop and bolt on site.**

examTip.trick: **Pitch is ALONG the force; gauge is ACROSS it.** One sentence separates the two most confused terms — and options (a) and (b) are the genuine definitions of edge distance and gauge.
examTip.trap: **A connection's capacity is the LEAST of bolt shear, bearing, net-section tension and BLOCK SHEAR** — not the bolt shear alone. Block shear is the mode most often overlooked.
examTip.mnemonic: **Minimum pitch 2.5d protects the PLATE from splitting; maximum 16t prevents BUCKLING and corrosion.** Opposite reasons squeezing from both ends — neither limit is nominal.

questions.stem: The primary function of a service reservoir in a water distribution system is to:
options: Balance the variation between a steady supply and a fluctuating demand
Provide the head required to treat the water
Allow suspended solids to settle before distribution
Store the annual water requirement of the town
questions.solution:
**To balance the variation between a steady supply and a fluctuating demand.**

**Why that is the primary function:**

> **A treatment works runs most economically at a STEADY rate. Consumer demand is anything but steady** — it peaks in the morning and evening and falls almost to nothing overnight.

> **The service reservoir sits between them and absorbs the difference.** It is filled at a constant rate over the day and drawn down at the varying rate.

> **The consequence is the important part: the works upstream of the reservoir need only be sized for the MAXIMUM DAILY demand, while the mains downstream must meet the MAXIMUM HOURLY demand.**

> **Without a service reservoir the treatment works would have to be sized for the peak hour**, making it roughly twice as large and correspondingly more expensive.

> **That is the reservoir's real justification — not storage against interruption, but flattening the demand the plant has to meet.**

**Its functions, in order of importance:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **BALANCING storage** | **Absorbs the hourly variation — the primary purpose** ← |
| **Maintains PRESSURE** | Its water level sets the head in the network |
| **BREAKDOWN reserve** | Typically a few hours' supply |
| **FIRE reserve** | A defined volume kept available |
| Reduces pumping cost | Pumps run at off-peak tariff |

> **The pressure function is worth noting alongside**: the reservoir's water level fixes the hydraulic grade line for the whole distribution zone, which is why it is sited on high ground or elevated on a tower.

> **A distribution system without one has to be pumped continuously against the varying demand**, and the pressure then fluctuates with the flow — which is precisely what a service reservoir prevents.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Comment |
|---|---|
| **Provide treatment head** | **Treatment happens BEFORE the service reservoir.** A service reservoir holds treated water; it is not part of the treatment process |
| **Allow solids to settle** | **That is a SEDIMENTATION tank**, upstream in the works. Settling in a service reservoir would be a fault, not a function |
| **Store the annual requirement** | **A scale error of enormous size** — that is what an impounding RESERVOIR does, not a service reservoir |

> **Option (c) is worth dismissing carefully: any significant settlement in a service reservoir indicates the treatment has failed.** The water entering it should already be clarified, and accumulated sludge in a service reservoir is a water-quality problem requiring cleaning.

> **And option (d) is out by three orders of magnitude.** A service reservoir holds hours of supply, not a year's:

| Storage | Typical capacity |
|---|---|
| **SERVICE reservoir** | **⅓ to ½ of the maximum DAILY demand — i.e. 8 to 12 hours** |
| **Impounding (storage) reservoir** | **A season or a year of supply** |

> **The distinction between a SERVICE reservoir and an IMPOUNDING reservoir is one of purpose and of scale**, and confusing them is the substantive error in this question.

**How the balancing volume is determined:**

> **From a MASS CURVE: cumulative demand plotted against cumulative supply over 24 hours.**

> **The required storage is the sum of the maximum surplus and the maximum deficit** — the greatest vertical departures of the demand curve above and below the supply line.

> **That is the same mass-curve technique used to size an impounding reservoir from annual inflow and demand**, applied over a day rather than a year. **One method, two time scales.**

**Types and siting:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Ground-level (surface) reservoir** | Where high ground exists — cheapest |
| **ELEVATED tank / tower** | **Where the ground gives insufficient head** |
| Underground | Where appearance or space demands |

> **A ground-level reservoir on high ground is always preferred to an elevated tank**, because the head is free and the structure far cheaper. **An elevated tank is what you build when the topography does not oblige.**

> **In Nepal's hill towns that is rarely a problem — gravity supply from a high-level reservoir is the norm**, and it brings the further advantage of needing no power and no mechanical plant.

**And the pressure requirement it must satisfy:** **a minimum residual head of about 7 m (for two storeys) up to 17 m or more in larger towns**, measured at the consumer's connection during the peak hour — which is what fixes the reservoir's minimum water level relative to the district it serves.

examTip.trick: **It decouples a steady works from a fluctuating demand** — so the plant is sized for the maximum DAILY rate while the mains meet the maximum HOURLY rate. Without it the works would be twice as large.
examTip.trap: **Option (d) confuses a SERVICE reservoir with an IMPOUNDING one** — hours of supply against a year's. And settlement in a service reservoir (option c) would be a fault, not a function.
examTip.mnemonic: **Capacity ⅓ to ½ of the maximum daily demand (8–12 hours)**, found from a **MASS CURVE** — the same technique that sizes an impounding reservoir, applied over a day instead of a year.

questions.stem: In a rapid sand filter, backwashing is carried out when:
options: The filtered water turbidity falls below 1 NTU
The head loss through the bed reaches the permitted maximum
The filter has run continuously for 24 hours
The chlorine residual in the filtered water is exhausted
questions.solution:
**When the head loss through the bed reaches the permitted maximum.**

**Why head loss is the trigger:**

> **As a filter runs, the retained solids progressively block the pores of the sand bed.**

> **The bed's resistance rises, so the head required to drive the same flow through it increases.** That rising head loss is a direct, continuously measurable index of how clogged the bed has become.

| Filter condition | Head loss |
|---|---|
| **Clean bed (start of run)** | **0.3 m** |
| **Terminal (backwash due)** | **2.5 to 3.0 m** |

> **When the available head is used up, the filter can no longer pass its design flow** — and continuing beyond that point causes the second, more serious problem below.

> **So the trigger is a hydraulic measurement, not a clock and not a quality test.**

**The second trigger, which matters as much:**

> **TURBIDITY BREAKTHROUGH.** If a filter is run too long, the accumulated solids begin to be pushed through and the filtered water quality deteriorates.

> **A filter is therefore backwashed at whichever comes first — terminal head loss or turbidity breakthrough** — and a well-designed filter reaches both at about the same time.

> **A filter that breaks through well before reaching terminal head loss is under-designed for its duty**, which is a genuine diagnostic.

**Why option (a) is exactly backwards:**

> **Filtered turbidity BELOW 1 NTU means the filter is performing WELL.** That is the target, not a reason to interrupt the run.

> **Backwashing a filter that is producing good water wastes both water and time** — and each backwash consumes **2 to 5% of the filtered output.**

> **The option is the trap for anyone who reads "turbidity" and reacts to the word rather than the direction.**

**Why options (c) and (d) are wrong:**

> **A fixed 24-hour interval ignores the actual loading.** Run length depends on the raw water quality and the filtration rate, and it varies from a few hours in a turbid monsoon flow to several days on clear water. **A clock cannot capture that.**

> **Chlorine residual is a DISINFECTION matter, applied after filtration.** It has nothing to do with the state of the sand bed, and no filter is operated on it.

**How backwashing works:**

> **Clean water is forced UPWARD through the bed at a high rate, expanding it by 20 to 50% so the grains are held in suspension and rub against one another, releasing the trapped solids.**

| Parameter | Value |
|---|---|
| **Backwash rate** | **0.3 – 0.6 m³/m²/min** |
| **Duration** | **10 – 15 minutes** |
| **Bed expansion** | **20 – 50%** |
| **Water used** | **2 – 5% of filtered output** |
| Air scour | Often used first, to break up the mat |

> **The bed must FLUIDISE but not be carried away** — too low a rate leaves the mat intact, too high a rate washes the finer sand out over the troughs and permanently degrades the bed.

**And the reason the bed remains graded afterwards:**

> **When the backwash stops, the grains settle by size — coarse first, fine last — so the bed re-forms with the FINEST sand at the TOP.**

> **That is hydraulic sorting, and it is why a rapid sand filter is inherently a surface filter**: most straining happens in the top few centimetres, where the sand is finest.

> **It is also why DUAL-MEDIA filters (coarse anthracite over fine sand) were developed** — the lighter anthracite stays on top despite being coarser, giving genuine depth filtration and much longer runs.

**Rapid against slow sand filters:**

| | **RAPID sand** | **SLOW sand** |
|---|---|---|
| **Rate** | **100 – 150 m³/m²/day** | **2 – 5 m³/m²/day** |
| **Cleaning** | **BACKWASHING, every 1–3 days** | **SCRAPING the top layer, every 1–3 months** |
| Pre-treatment | **Coagulation essential** | Not required |
| **Bacterial removal** | 80 – 90% | **98 – 99% — better** |
| Land | Small | **Large** |
| Skill required | Higher | **Low — suits small communities** |

> **The slow sand filter removes bacteria far better because of the SCHMUTZDECKE** — the biological mat on its surface, which is a living treatment layer rather than a mechanical strainer.

> **Which is why a slow sand filter must never be backwashed**: doing so would destroy the very layer that does the work.

examTip.trick: **Rising head loss is a direct measure of clogging** — 0.3 m clean, 2.5–3.0 m terminal. It is a hydraulic trigger, not a clock and not a quality test.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is backwards — turbidity BELOW 1 NTU means the filter is working well.** Backwashing then wastes 2–5% of output for nothing. React to the direction, not the word.
examTip.mnemonic: **Backwash at terminal head loss OR turbidity breakthrough, whichever comes first** — a good design reaches both together. And a **slow** sand filter is never backwashed: it would destroy the schmutzdecke.

questions.stem: The capacity factor of a hydropower plant is defined as the ratio of:
options: Average load to the installed capacity
Average load to the peak load
Peak load to the installed capacity
Sum of individual peaks to the system peak
questions.solution:
**Average load to the installed capacity.**

**The four factors, which are constantly confused:**

| Factor | **Definition** | Note |
|---|---|---|
| **CAPACITY (plant) factor** | **Average load ÷ INSTALLED CAPACITY** | ≤ load factor ← |
| **LOAD factor** | **Average load ÷ PEAK load** | ≤ 1 always |
| **Utilisation factor** | **PEAK load ÷ installed capacity** | How fully the plant is used at peak |
| **Diversity factor** | **Sum of individual peaks ÷ system peak** | **> 1 always** |

> **Every option here is a genuine factor from this topic, so the question is purely about which definition goes with which name.**

**The relationship that keeps them straight:**

> **Capacity factor = Load factor × Utilisation factor**

> **Check: (Avg/Peak) × (Peak/Installed) = Avg/Installed** ✓

> **So capacity factor ≤ load factor**, because the utilisation factor cannot exceed 1 (a plant cannot be loaded beyond its installed capacity).

> **Note also that LOAD and CAPACITY factors share the same numerator — the average load — and differ only in the denominator.** That is the fastest way to tell them apart: **peak load for one, installed capacity for the other.**

**Why the DIVERSITY factor is the odd one out:**

> **It is the only one greater than 1**, which alone identifies it.

> **Consumers do not all peak at the same instant, so the sum of their individual maximum demands exceeds the system's actual maximum.**

> **A system serving 1000 households each with a 2 kW individual peak does not need 2000 kW** — it might need 700 kW, giving a diversity factor of about 2.9.

> **That statistical fact is what makes an interconnected grid fundamentally cheaper than isolated supply**, and it is the same effect as the peak factor in water supply, where small populations peak harder because nothing averages out.

**What a capacity factor tells you about a plant's role:**

| Plant | Capacity factor | Why |
|---|---|---|
| **Run-of-river hydro** | **HIGH (0.5 – 0.7)** | **Runs continuously; serves BASE load** |
| **Nuclear, large thermal** | **HIGH** | Base load, low running cost |
| **PEAKING plant (storage hydro, gas turbine)** | **LOW (0.1 – 0.3)** | **Runs only during the peak — BY DESIGN** |
| **Diesel standby** | **VERY LOW** | Emergencies only |

> **A LOW capacity factor is not necessarily a fault, and that is the point most worth taking from this question.**

> **A peaking plant is DESIGNED to run few hours a year.** Judging it by its capacity factor is a category error — it is doing exactly what it was built for.

> **What matters instead is whether it is available when the peak arrives**, and hydropower's ability to reach full load in **minutes** rather than hours is what makes it valuable for that duty regardless of how few hours it runs.

**And in Nepal the capacity factor carries a further complication:**

> **Roughly 80% of river flow arrives in the four monsoon months**, so a run-of-river plant's output is high in the wet season and a fraction of that in the dry.

> **Its annual capacity factor therefore understates its monsoon performance and overstates its dry-season one** — a single average figure conceals exactly the variation that matters most to the power system.
