> **Which is why FIRM POWER — the output guaranteed even in the driest period, taken from the Q₉₅ or Q₉₀ point of the flow duration curve — is the more meaningful measure here**, and why storage projects are argued for on that basis rather than on capacity factor.

**The related planning quantities:** **firm (primary) power**, guaranteed at all times, against **secondary power**, available only when flows exceed the minimum. **A reservoir converts the second into the first**, which is the whole economic case for storage.

examTip.trick: **Load and capacity factors share the numerator (average load)** and differ only in the denominator — peak load versus installed capacity. And **Capacity = Load × Utilisation** links all three.
examTip.trap: **Every option is a genuine factor from this topic.** Diversity factor is the odd one out because it is **always > 1** — the sum of individual peaks exceeds the system peak.
examTip.mnemonic: **A LOW capacity factor is not a fault** — a peaking plant is designed to run few hours. In Nepal, **firm power from the Q₉₅ point** is the meaningful measure, since 80% of flow arrives in four months.

questions.stem: In a run-of-river hydropower scheme, the forebay is located:
options: At the intake, immediately behind the diversion weir
At the powerhouse, downstream of the turbines
At the end of the headrace, immediately before the penstock
questions.solution:
**At the end of the headrace, immediately before the penstock.**

**The layout of a run-of-river scheme, in order:**

> **Intake → gravel trap → settling basin → headrace canal or tunnel → FOREBAY → penstock → powerhouse → tailrace**

| Component | Position | Function |
|---|---|---|
| **Intake / diversion weir** | At the river | Divert the flow |
| **Gravel trap** | Just after the intake | Catch the **coarse** bed load |
| **Settling basin** | Before the headrace | Remove **suspended** sediment |
| **Headrace** | The long conveyance | Carry water at minimum head loss |
| **FOREBAY** | **End of the headrace, before the penstock** | **Buffer for load changes; final check** ← |
| **Penstock** | Down the slope | Deliver water under pressure |
| Powerhouse, tailrace | At the bottom | Generate; return the water |

**What the forebay does:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **Provides water for LOAD CHANGES** | **A small volume the turbine can draw on instantly** |
| **Final sediment and trash check** | Catches what the settling basin missed |
| **Air release** | Prevents air entering the penstock |
| **Spillway for surplus** | Sheds water when the turbine shuts down |
| Transition to the penstock | Smooth entry, avoiding vortex formation |

> **The load-change function is the primary one, and it is the same problem a surge tank solves.**

> **A long headrace has considerable inertia and cannot accelerate instantly.** When the turbine demands more water, the forebay supplies it immediately while the headrace flow builds up.

> **And when the turbine shuts down, the water still arriving down the headrace has to go somewhere — hence the forebay spillway.** Without it the headrace would overtop.

**Forebay against surge tank — the distinction worth fixing:**

| | **FOREBAY** | **SURGE TANK** |
|---|---|---|
| **Used with** | **An OPEN headrace CANAL** | **A pressure TUNNEL** |
| **Open to atmosphere** | **Yes — it is an open basin** | Yes, but a shaft |
| Primary purpose | **Load balancing; final sediment check** | **Relieving WATER HAMMER** |
| Position | End of the headrace | On the tunnel, before the penstock |

> **They occupy the same position in the layout and serve the same load-change purpose**, but a forebay belongs to a low-pressure open-canal scheme and a surge tank to a pressurised tunnel scheme. **Which one a scheme has tells you how its water was conveyed.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

> **Option (a) confuses it with the INTAKE.** A forebay at the intake would serve no purpose — there is no long conveyance yet to buffer against.

> **Option (b) confuses it with the settling basin.** The two are distinct structures at opposite ends of the headrace, and their sediment roles differ accordingly: **the settling basin protects the headrace, the forebay only catches the remainder.**

> **Option (c) is downstream of the turbines, which is the TAILRACE** — the wrong end of the plant entirely.

**And the sediment point is worth drawing out, because it explains why both structures exist:**

> **Sediment removed at the FOREBAY has already travelled the whole length of the headrace**, abrading the lining on the way.

> **That is why the settling basin is placed at the START, not the end** — its job is to protect the conveyance, not merely the turbines.

> **The forebay's sediment function is a final safeguard against what escaped**, and in Himalayan rivers, where the load is high and largely quartz, that safeguard matters: **quartz is harder than turbine steel, and erosion rises roughly as the cube of jet velocity**, so a high-head scheme is especially vulnerable.

**Why run-of-river dominates in Nepal:** **it needs no large reservoir, so it avoids inundation, displacement and the cost of a dam** — but it has **little or no storage, so dry-season output falls to a fraction of monsoon output** exactly when demand peaks. **A few hours of pondage at the forebay gives a PEAKING run-of-river scheme**, which converts a flat output into a peak-hour one at a small fraction of a reservoir's cost.

examTip.trick: **The forebay buffers load changes for a long headrace**, so it must sit at the END of it, just before the penstock. At the intake it would have nothing to buffer against.
examTip.trap: **A FOREBAY belongs to an open canal scheme; a SURGE TANK to a pressure tunnel.** Same position, same load-change role — which one a scheme has tells you how the water was conveyed.
examTip.mnemonic: **The settling basin is at the START to protect the headrace itself** — sediment caught at the forebay has already abraded the whole conveyance. The forebay is only the final safeguard.

questions.stem: Cavitation in a reaction turbine is most likely to occur at the:
options: Outlet of the runner and the entry to the draft tube
Guide vane inlet, where the velocity is highest
questions.solution:
**At the outlet of the runner and the entry to the draft tube.**

**Why there — it is where the pressure is lowest:**

> **CAVITATION occurs where the local pressure falls to the VAPOUR PRESSURE of water**, so that vapour bubbles form.

> **In a reaction turbine the pressure drops continuously through the runner as the water gives up its energy** — that is the definition of reaction: pressure energy is converted within the runner.

> **So the MINIMUM pressure in the whole machine is at the runner EXIT**, just before the draft tube.

> **And the draft tube's own action makes it worse: by decelerating the flow and recovering kinetic energy, it creates SUCTION at the runner outlet** — which is exactly the point of a draft tube, and exactly why cavitation appears there.

> **The very feature that improves efficiency creates the cavitation risk.** That tension is the heart of reaction turbine setting.

**What cavitation does:**

| Effect | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **PITTING of the runner blades** | **Bubbles collapse on reaching higher pressure, and the implosion produces enormous local pressures** |
| **Loss of efficiency** | Vapour disrupts the flow pattern |
| **Noise and VIBRATION** | Characteristic crackling |
| Reduced output | — |

> **The damage is caused by the COLLAPSE, not the formation.** A bubble carried into a higher-pressure region implodes, and if it does so against the blade surface the local pressure is high enough to remove metal.

> **Repeated over millions of cycles that produces the spongy pitted surface characteristic of cavitation damage**, and it is progressive.

**How it is prevented:**

> **By controlling the turbine's SETTING — its height above the tailwater level.**

> **The governing parameter is the CAVITATION COEFFICIENT (Thoma's sigma):**
>
> **σ = (H_atm − H_vapour − H_s)/H**

> **where H_s is the suction head — the height of the runner above the tailwater — and H the net head.**

> **The design must keep σ above a critical value σ_c that depends on the specific speed.**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Lower the turbine setting** | **The most direct remedy — reduces H_s** |
| **Set the runner BELOW tailwater** | Gives a negative H_s; common for Kaplan turbines |
| Cavitation-resistant materials | Stainless steel runners, or stainless overlay |
| Avoid part-load operation | Off-design flow worsens it |
| Smooth blade profiles | Avoid local low-pressure zones |

> **The most consequential design implication is that a reaction turbine cannot be set arbitrarily high above the tailwater** — and since σ_c rises with specific speed, **a high-specific-speed Kaplan must be set lower than a Francis, often below the tailwater surface.**

> **That is why Kaplan powerhouses are dug in while Pelton powerhouses sit above the river.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | Comment |
|---|---|
| **Spiral casing inlet** | **The HIGHEST pressure point in the machine** — the opposite end of the range |
| **Guide vane inlet** | Velocity is high but pressure is still well above vapour pressure |
| **Headrace canal surface** | **At atmospheric pressure — cavitation is impossible** |

> **Option (c) is the instructive one: high velocity alone does not cause cavitation.** By Bernoulli, high velocity means low pressure — but at the guide vanes the absolute pressure remains far above the vapour pressure, so nothing boils.

> **It is the ABSOLUTE pressure relative to the vapour pressure that matters, not the velocity.**

**And the parallel with pumps is worth noting:**

> **In a PUMP, cavitation occurs at the SUCTION side — the impeller inlet — for the same reason: it is the lowest-pressure point.**

> **Which is why a pump's suction lift is limited to about 7 m in practice** against a theoretical 10.3 m: the remainder is consumed by friction, velocity head and the **NPSH** required to keep the impeller inlet above vapour pressure.

> **Turbine outlet, pump inlet — in both cases the lowest-pressure point in the machine**, and in both the remedy is to reduce the elevation difference.

**Note also that an IMPULSE turbine does not cavitate**: a Pelton runner operates at **atmospheric pressure throughout**, spinning in air, so there is no low-pressure region for vapour to form in. **Cavitation is a reaction-turbine problem specifically.**

examTip.trick: **Pressure falls continuously through a reaction runner, so the minimum is at its EXIT** — and the draft tube's suction, which is what makes it efficient, drives the pressure lower still.
examTip.trap: **High velocity alone does not cause cavitation** (option c). What matters is the ABSOLUTE pressure relative to the vapour pressure — at the guide vanes it is still far above it.
examTip.mnemonic: **Turbine OUTLET, pump INLET — the lowest-pressure point in each machine.** And an **impulse turbine cannot cavitate**: a Pelton runner is at atmospheric pressure throughout.

questions.stem: A transition curve is provided between a straight and a circular curve principally to:
options: Reduce the length of the circular curve required
Increase the sight distance around the bend
Allow the superelevation to be drained away
Introduce the centrifugal force and the superelevation gradually
questions.solution:
**To introduce the centrifugal force and the superelevation gradually.**

**The problem a transition solves:**

> **On a straight the radius is INFINITE, so the centrifugal force is zero. On a circular curve of radius R it is mV²/R.**

> **Joining them directly would require the full centrifugal force to appear INSTANTANEOUSLY at the point of tangency** — a step change from zero to its maximum value.

> **A vehicle cannot do that.** The driver would have to apply a sudden steering input, and the vehicle would swing wide or the occupants be thrown sideways.

> **A TRANSITION CURVE has a radius that decreases gradually from infinity at the straight to R at the circular curve**, so the centrifugal force builds up progressively.

**The four purposes, in order:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **Gradual introduction of centrifugal force** | **The primary reason** ← |
| **Gradual application of SUPERELEVATION and extra widening** | The cross-fall is rotated over the transition length |
| **Comfort and safety** | No sudden lateral jerk |
| **Improved appearance** | Avoids a visual kink in the alignment |

> **The superelevation point is the practical one: the cross-fall has to change from the normal camber to the full banked value somewhere, and the transition provides the length over which to do it.**

> **Without a transition there is nowhere to rotate the pavement**, and the superelevation would have to be introduced on the straight — which would be uncomfortable and would drain water toward the inside of the road.

**The curve used:**

> **A SPIRAL (clothoid) is the ideal transition, because its radius varies inversely with its length: R ∝ 1/L.**

> **That gives a constant RATE of change of centrifugal force, which is exactly what comfort requires.**

> **Cubic parabolas and lemniscates are used as approximations**, but the spiral is the theoretically correct form and is what IRC specifies.

**The transition LENGTH is the GREATEST of three criteria, and each covers a different concern:**

| Criterion | Formula | Concerns |
|---|---|---|
| **1. Rate of change of centrifugal acceleration** | **L = 0.0215 V³/(C R)**, with C = 80/(75 + V) | **Comfort** |
| **2. Rate of introduction of superelevation** | **L = e N (W + W_e)** — N being 150 for plain, 100 for hilly | **Drainage and appearance** |
| **3. IRC empirical formula** | **L = 2.7 V²/R** (plain and rolling), **L = V²/R** (hilly) | Practice |

> **Taking the GREATEST is the point** — each criterion protects against a different failure, so satisfying only one leaves the others unmet.

> **Criterion 1 is about comfort, criterion 2 about how fast the pavement can be twisted without ponding water or looking distorted, and criterion 3 is a practical minimum.**

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

> **Option (a) is backwards.** A transition ADDS length to the alignment; it does not reduce the circular curve required. **Half the transition length is inserted before and half after, and the circular curve is shortened only in the sense that the total curve is longer.**

> **Option (b) confuses it with SET-BACK DISTANCE.** Sight distance around a bend is provided by clearing the obstruction on the inside of the curve, not by a transition.

> **Option (c) inverts the drainage relationship.** The transition is where superelevation is INTRODUCED, not drained away — and the rate at which it is introduced is itself limited partly so that water does not pond on the pavement during the rotation.

**And the shift, which is what makes a transition geometrically possible:**

> **Inserting a transition requires the circular curve to be SHIFTED inward by S = L²/(24R).**

> **The circular arc is moved toward the centre so that the spiral can begin on the tangent and end tangentially to the arc** — without that shift the three elements cannot be made to fit.

**The full set of curve provisions**, all needed together on a sharp bend: **superelevation e = V²/(225R) capped at e_max; minimum radius R = V²/(127(e + f)); extra widening nl²/2R + V/(9.5√R); transition length as above; grade compensation (30 + R)/R %; and set-back for sight distance.**

> **Omitting any one produces a curve that is uncomfortable, unsafe, or unusable by long vehicles.**

examTip.trick: **Radius goes from INFINITE on the straight to R on the curve.** Joining them directly would make the full centrifugal force appear instantaneously — a spiral (R ∝ 1/L) introduces it at a constant rate.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) is backwards — a transition ADDS length.** And option (b) confuses it with **set-back distance**, which is how sight distance around a bend is actually provided.
examTip.mnemonic: **Transition length is the GREATEST of three criteria** — comfort, rate of superelevation, and the IRC empirical formula — because each guards a different failure. And the curve must be **shifted by L²/24R**.

questions.stem: The aggregate impact value test measures the resistance of aggregate to:
questions.solution:
**Sudden shock or impact.**

**The four aggregate strength tests, each defined by HOW the load is applied:**

| Test | **Loading** | Method |
|---|---|---|
| **IMPACT value** | **SUDDEN shock** | **15 blows of a 13.5–14 kg hammer falling 380 mm** ← |
| **CRUSHING value** | **GRADUAL compression** | **40 tonnes applied over 10 minutes** |
| **LOS ANGELES ABRASION** | **Prolonged rubbing** | **Rotating drum with steel balls, 500–1000 revolutions** |
| **SOUNDNESS** | **Chemical weathering** | Alternate immersion in sodium or magnesium sulphate |

> **Naming the loading identifies the test**, which makes the set recoverable without memorising four procedures — and it is why each option here describes a different mode of attack.

**Why impact and crushing are separate tests:**

> **They measure genuinely different properties, and a material can perform well in one and poorly in the other.**

> **A gradually applied load allows the aggregate to redistribute stress internally.** A sudden blow does not — the energy arrives faster than the material can accommodate it, and brittle fracture results.

> **So the impact test detects BRITTLENESS**, which the crushing test can miss. **An aggregate with adequate crushing strength may still shatter under the hammer blow of traffic passing over an uneven surface.**

> **That is a real distinction in service, not a laboratory nicety**: a wheel striking a pothole edge or a joint delivers an impact, not a gradual compression.

**Why the impact test is the more commonly used of the two:**

> **It is faster, needs no compression machine, and its result correlates well with the crushing value** — so it is often used as a convenient substitute.

> **The apparatus is portable, which matters for site testing.**

**IRC limits:**

| Layer | **Impact value (max)** | Crushing value (max) |
|---|---|---|
| **Bituminous SURFACE course** | **24%** | **30%** |
| Bituminous base / binder | 27 – 30% | 30 – 45% |
| **WBM base course** | **30 – 35%** | 45% |
| Sub-base | — | — |
| **Concrete (wearing surfaces)** | **30%** | **30%** |

> **The limits TIGHTEN toward the surface**, and the reason is direct: **the surface course receives the traffic's impact and abrasion directly**, while lower layers are protected by the material above them.

> **That graded requirement is the same economic logic as the layered pavement itself** — good material where the stress is, cheaper material below.

**And in every one of these tests a LOWER value is better:**

> **The result is the percentage of material broken down to pass a 2.36 mm sieve** (for impact and crushing).

> **So the number measures DAMAGE, not strength** — 24% means a quarter of the sample was pulverised.

> **A candidate who reads the limit as a minimum has the direction of every one of these tests backwards**, which is why the point is worth stating explicitly.

**The other aggregate properties tested:**

| Test | Measures | Limit |
|---|---|---|
| **FLAKINESS and elongation index** | **Particle SHAPE** | **≤ 15% for surface courses** |
| **STRIPPING value** | **Resistance to bitumen being displaced by water** | **Retention > 95%** |
| **Water absorption** | Porosity | Usually ≤ 2% |
| **Polished stone value** | Resistance to polishing | For high-speed surfaces |
| Specific gravity | For mix design | — |

> **FLAKY particles are excluded because they BREAK under compaction and traffic**, and they pack poorly, leaving voids.

> **STRIPPING is the failure that drainage problems produce**: water displaces the bitumen film from the aggregate, the binder loses its grip, and the mix ravels. **It is a common cause of premature failure in Nepal's monsoon conditions**, countered with anti-stripping agents or by choosing aggregate with better affinity for bitumen.

> **And the POLISHED STONE VALUE is specified separately for surfacing on high-speed roads and at junctions**, because an aggregate can be perfectly sound structurally and still polish smooth under traffic — giving a surface that is **dangerously slippery when wet** and whose failure is invisible until it causes accidents.

examTip.trick: **Each test names its own loading**: sudden shock (impact), gradual compression (crushing), prolonged rubbing (abrasion), chemical attack (soundness). Naming the loading identifies the test.
examTip.trap: **In all these tests a LOWER value is better** — the number is the percentage pulverised, so it measures DAMAGE, not strength. Reading the limit as a minimum inverts every one of them.
examTip.mnemonic: **Impact detects BRITTLENESS that the crushing test misses** — a sudden blow gives no time for stress to redistribute. Which matters, since a wheel striking a pothole edge delivers impact, not compression.

questions.stem: In a timber beam, a shear failure along the grain near the supports is called:
questions.solution:
**Horizontal shear failure.**

**Why timber fails this way — the reason is anisotropy:**

> **Timber is highly ANISOTROPIC: it is far stronger ALONG the grain than ACROSS it, often by a factor of ten to twenty.**

> **Shear parallel to the grain is one of its weakest modes**, because the fibres are simply bundles held together by comparatively weak lateral bonds — the wood splits between them rather than the fibres themselves shearing.

> **And in a beam the maximum shear stress occurs AT THE NEUTRAL AXIS, near the SUPPORTS**, where the shear force is greatest.

> **Those two facts together locate the failure: a horizontal split along the grain, at mid-depth, near the support.** It is a characteristic and easily recognised timber failure.

**Timber's shear strengths compared:**

| Direction | Relative strength |
|---|---|
| **Parallel to the grain (horizontal shear in a beam)** | **WEAKEST — the governing case** |
| Perpendicular to the grain | Higher |
| Compression parallel to grain | High |
| **Tension perpendicular to grain** | **Very weak — avoided entirely in design** |

> **Cross-grain TENSION is so weak that good detailing avoids it altogether** — which is why notches, bolt holes near the ends, and connections that pull across the grain are all treated with care.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

| Option | What it actually is |
|---|---|
| **Buckling** | **A COMPRESSION member instability** — applies to a column or the compression flange of a deep beam, not a shear failure |
| **Crushing** | **Compression failure**, typically where a load bears on the top fibres |
| **BEARING failure** | **Local crushing PERPENDICULAR to the grain at the support** — a genuine and related timber failure, but a different one |

> **Option (c) is the closest distractor and worth separating carefully**, because it occurs at the same location.

> **BEARING failure is local crushing across the grain where the beam sits on its support** — the fibres are compressed perpendicular to their length and the timber dents.

> **HORIZONTAL SHEAR is a split along the grain at mid-depth.**

> **Both happen near the supports, but one is a crushing of the end grain area and the other a longitudinal split.** They are checked separately in design, and the remedies differ.

**The design checks for a timber beam, in the order they usually govern:**

| Check | Note |
|---|---|
| **BENDING** | σ = M/Z — usually governs a long span |
| **DEFLECTION** | **Often governs, because timber's E is low** |
| **HORIZONTAL SHEAR** | **τ = 1.5V/(bd) — governs SHORT, DEEP beams** ← |
| **BEARING at supports** | Compression perpendicular to grain |
| Lateral stability | Deep narrow beams need restraint |

> **Note that shear governs SHORT beams while bending governs long ones**, for the same reason as in any material: **the moment grows as L² while the shear grows only as L.**

> **So a heavily loaded short timber beam — a lintel over a wide opening, say — is a shear problem rather than a bending one**, and checking only the bending stress would miss it.

**The remedy when shear governs:**

> **Increase the WIDTH rather than the depth**, since τ_max = 1.5V/(bd) is inversely proportional to both — but increasing depth also increases the bending capacity, which was not the problem.

> **Or reduce the span, or introduce an intermediate support.**

> **Notches near supports must be avoided**: a notch at the end of a beam removes material exactly where the shear stress is highest and creates a stress concentration that initiates the split. **A notched beam end is one of the classic timber failures.**

**And the moisture caution, since it affects all of these:**

> **Timber strength falls markedly as moisture content rises**, and there is no shrinkage or strength change until the **FIBRE SATURATION POINT (25–30%)** is passed.

> **Structural timber must therefore be seasoned to 12–18%**, and to roughly the moisture content it will live at — or it will move after installation, opening joints and losing the strength the design assumed.

examTip.trick: **Shear parallel to the grain is one of timber's weakest modes**, and beam shear peaks at the NEUTRAL AXIS near the SUPPORTS — so the failure is a horizontal split at mid-depth near the end.
examTip.trap: **BEARING failure happens at the same location** but is local crushing ACROSS the grain, not a split along it. Both are checked, and the remedies differ.
examTip.mnemonic: **Shear governs SHORT deep beams, bending governs long ones** (M ∝ L², V ∝ L). And **never notch a beam end** — it removes material exactly where shear is highest.

questions.stem: A canal escape is provided to:
options: Raise the water level for an offtake to draw
Measure the discharge passing down the canal
Discharge surplus water out of the canal
Lower the canal bed where the ground falls steeply
questions.solution:
**To discharge surplus water out of the canal.**

**Why an escape is necessary:**

> **A canal's banks are EARTHEN and cannot survive overtopping.** Once water flows over an earth bank, it erodes the downstream face rapidly and a **BREACH** follows — which empties the canal, floods the land beside it, and takes weeks to repair.

> **So any surplus must be shed deliberately, at a protected point of the engineer's choosing, rather than accidentally wherever the bank happens to be lowest.**

> **That is the whole logic of an escape: it is a controlled failure point.**

**When surplus arises:**

| Cause | Note |
|---|---|
| **Sudden closure of downstream outlets** | **Rain in the command area — farmers stop taking water** |
| **Rainfall entering the canal directly** | Adds to the supply |
| **Mis-regulation at the head** | More let in than needed |
| **Emergency — a breach or repair downstream** | The canal must be emptied |
| Canal closure for maintenance | Dewatering |

> **The first is the commonest and the most instructive: heavy rain in the command means the crops no longer need irrigating, so every outlet closes at once — and the water already in the canal has nowhere to go.**

> **The escape is what saves the banks in exactly that situation**, and it is why escapes are provided at intervals along a main canal rather than only at its tail.

**The types of escape:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **Weir or surplus escape** | **A weir in the bank, set at FSL — spills automatically when the level rises** |
| **Sluice or scouring escape** | **Gated, at bed level — can empty the canal completely and also flush silt** |
| Tail escape | At the canal's end, maintaining the tail level |

> **The weir type is automatic and needs no operator, which is its great advantage** — it acts on the level itself, and a rising level is precisely the danger.

> **The sluice type is operated deliberately and can DEWATER the canal for inspection or repair**, which a weir set at FSL cannot do. **It also scours accumulated silt from the bed**, so it does double duty.

> **Where an escape discharges into a natural drainage line, that channel must be able to take the flow** — otherwise the problem is merely moved.

**Why each distractor names a different structure — and this is the discrimination:**

| Option | The structure that does it |
|---|---|
| **Raise the water level for an offtake** | **CROSS REGULATOR** — placed across the parent canal downstream of the offtake |
| **Measure discharge** | **A METER FALL, flume or notch** |
| **Discharge surplus** | **ESCAPE** ✓ |
| **Lower the canal bed** | **A FALL or drop** |

> **All four are genuine canal structures**, and each option is the correct purpose of one of them — which makes this a clean four-way match rather than a guess.

> **Option (a) is the closest, because a cross regulator also controls levels** — but it does so by **holding water back to raise the level upstream**, the opposite of shedding it.

**The regulating structures on a canal system, for completeness:**

| Structure | Function |
|---|---|
| **HEAD regulator** | **Controls the DISCHARGE entering an offtake** |
| **CROSS regulator** | **Controls the LEVEL in the parent canal** |
| **ESCAPE** | **Sheds SURPLUS out of the canal** ← |
| **FALL / drop** | **Lowers the bed where the ground falls faster than the canal may** |
| **Outlet / module** | Delivers water to a watercourse |
| Cross-drainage work | Carries the canal past a natural drain |

> **Head and cross regulators are built as a PAIR at every offtake**: the head regulator meters the flow into the branch, and the cross regulator guarantees there is enough head for it to be metered at all.

> **Confusing those two is the commonest error in the topic**, and the distinction is positional: **the CROSS regulator is across the PARENT canal, the HEAD regulator at the HEAD of the OFFTAKE.**

**And the safety point worth stating:** **a canal breach is among the more damaging failures in irrigation engineering** — it destroys the embankment, floods and scours the adjacent fields, and interrupts supply to the whole command downstream. **The escape is cheap insurance against it, and its omission is a false economy.**

examTip.trick: **An earthen bank cannot survive overtopping**, so surplus must be shed deliberately at a protected point. An escape is a controlled failure point — that is its whole logic.
examTip.trap: **All four options are the correct purpose of a DIFFERENT canal structure** — cross regulator, meter fall, escape, fall. A clean four-way match, not a guess.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rain in the command closes every outlet at once**, and the water already in the canal has nowhere to go. The **weir-type escape acts on the level itself**, automatically — which is why no operator is needed.

questions.stem: In a Water Bound Macadam (WBM) road, the function of the screening and binding material is to:
options: Provide the main load-bearing strength of the layer
Fill the voids in the coarse aggregate and lock the stones together
Increase the flexibility of the pavement
questions.solution:
**To fill the voids in the coarse aggregate and lock the stones together.**

**How a WBM layer works:**

> **The layer is built from three materials in sequence:**

| Material | Role |
|---|---|
| **COARSE AGGREGATE** | **Carries the load by GRAIN-TO-GRAIN interlock — the structural element** |
| **SCREENINGS** | **Smaller stone chips that fill the voids between the coarse aggregate** |
| **BINDING MATERIAL** | **Fine material (usually good earth or stone dust) that fills the remaining small voids** |

> **The coarse aggregate provides the strength; the screenings and binder provide the INTERLOCK.**

> **Without them the coarse stones would shift and rock under load** — each one moving independently instead of the layer acting as a unit.

> **The screenings wedge between the larger stones, and water is then applied and the layer rolled, which washes the fines into the remaining voids.** That is where "water bound" comes from: **the water is a construction aid, carrying the fines into place, not a permanent part of the layer.**

**Why option (a) is wrong, and it is the key discrimination:**

> **The COARSE AGGREGATE carries the load, not the screenings.**

> **The load path is grain-to-grain contact between the large stones**, spreading the wheel load downward in a widening cone at roughly 45°.

> **The screenings do not carry load in their own right — they prevent the load-carrying stones from moving relative to one another.**

> **That is a supporting role, and confusing it with the primary one inverts how the layer works.**

**Why options (c) and (d) are wrong:**

> **WBM is NOT waterproof.** It is a granular layer with interconnected voids, and water passes into it readily — which is precisely its weakness.

> **A WBM layer must be protected by a bituminous surfacing or a surface dressing**, and that is what provides the waterproofing.

> **And flexibility is a property of the whole layered pavement, not something the binding material confers.**

**The construction sequence, which explains the material roles:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Prepare the subgrade or lower course** | Camber and level |
| **2. Provide LATERAL CONFINEMENT** | **Shoulders or kerbs built first — essential** |
| **3. Spread the coarse aggregate** | To the specified loose thickness |
| **4. Dry roll** | Establishes the interlock |
| **5. Apply SCREENINGS in stages, rolling between** | Fills the larger voids |
| **6. Sprinkle water and roll (wet rolling)** | **Washes fines into the voids — the "water bound" step** |
| **7. Apply binding material, water, and roll to a dense surface** | Completes the lock |
| 8. Allow to set, then surface | — |

> **Step 2 is the one most often underestimated: LATERAL CONFINEMENT must be in place BEFORE the aggregate is spread.**

> **A granular layer derives its strength from confinement.** Without shoulders to restrain it, the edges spread sideways under the roller and under traffic, and the interlock is never achieved at the edges — which is why WBM roads characteristically fail from the edge inward.

**Where WBM stands today:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Cost** | **Low — uses local stone and labour** |
| **Equipment** | **Minimal — a roller and water** |
| **Suits** | **Low-volume rural roads; base course under a bituminous surface** |
| **Weakness** | **Not waterproof; needs surfacing; poor under heavy traffic** |
| **Modern alternative** | **WMM (Wet Mix Macadam) — aggregate and water mixed in a plant, laid mechanically** |

> **WMM has largely replaced WBM on major works** because it is faster to lay and gives more consistent quality — but **WBM remains appropriate where plant is unavailable and labour is not**, which describes much of rural Nepal.

> **That is a genuine engineering judgement rather than a compromise: a technique buildable and repairable with local resources may outperform a better technique that cannot be maintained.**

**And the drainage point applies here as much as anywhere:** **water is the principal enemy of any granular layer.** It weakens the subgrade, and under repeated loading it **pumps the fines out of the WBM**, destroying the very interlock the binding material was placed to create.

examTip.trick: **Coarse aggregate carries the load; screenings and binder provide the INTERLOCK.** Without them the large stones rock independently instead of acting as a layer.
examTip.trap: **Option (a) inverts the roles.** The screenings do not carry load — they stop the load-carrying stones moving relative to one another. A supporting role, not the primary one.
examTip.mnemonic: **LATERAL CONFINEMENT must be built BEFORE the aggregate is spread** — a granular layer gets its strength from confinement, which is why WBM roads fail from the edge inward.

questions.stem: A project has a benefit–cost ratio of 0.85 at a discount rate of 12%. The project is:
options: Economically acceptable, since the ratio is positive
Economically acceptable, since the ratio exceeds 0.5
Not economically acceptable at that discount rate
questions.solution:
**Not economically acceptable at that discount rate.**

**The decision rule:**

> **B/C ratio = (present value of benefits) ÷ (present value of costs)**

| B/C | Decision |
|---|---|
| **> 1** | **ACCEPT — benefits exceed costs** |
| **= 1** | Marginal — exactly breaks even |
| **< 1** | **REJECT — costs exceed benefits** ← 0.85 |

> **A ratio of 0.85 means the project returns 85 paisa of discounted benefit for every rupee of discounted cost.** It destroys value rather than creating it.

> **The threshold is 1, not 0 and not 0.5** — and options (a) and (b) invent thresholds that have no basis. **A positive ratio is inevitable for any project with any benefits at all**, so "positive" carries no information.

**Why the DISCOUNT RATE qualification matters, and it is the substance of the question:**

> **The stem says "at a discount rate of 12%", and that phrase is doing real work.**

> **B/C is not a property of the project alone — it depends on the rate at which future flows are discounted.**

> **A project rejected at 12% may be accepted at 8%**, because a lower rate values distant benefits more highly.

| Discount rate | Value of a benefit 50 years away |
|---|---|
| **4%** | **14% of face value** |
| **8%** | **2.1%** |
| **12%** | **0.3%** |

> **At 12% a benefit fifty years out is worth almost nothing**, which is why **a high discount rate systematically penalises long-lived infrastructure** — a dam delivering benefits for a century is judged almost entirely on its first two decades.

> **So the correct statement is that the project fails AT THAT RATE**, not that it fails absolutely. Option (d) says exactly that, and its qualifier is what makes it right rather than merely negative.

**Why the choice of discount rate is genuinely contested:**

> **It often determines the answer more than any engineering input does**, which is why **SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS on the discount rate is essential** rather than optional.

> **A responsible appraisal reports the B/C at several rates**, and identifies the **switching value** — the rate at which the project becomes marginal.

> **For a project at 0.85, the question worth answering is: at what rate would it reach 1.0?** If that rate is 9%, the project is arguably viable under a lower social discount rate; if it is 2%, it is not viable on any defensible basis.

**The three appraisal measures and how they relate:**

| Measure | Definition | Accept when |
|---|---|---|
| **NPV** | **Σ(benefits − costs) discounted** | **NPV > 0** |
| **B/C ratio** | **PV benefits ÷ PV costs** | **B/C > 1** |
| **IRR** | **The discount rate at which NPV = 0** | **IRR > the cost of capital** |

> **NPV > 0, B/C > 1 and IRR > discount rate are mathematically EQUIVALENT tests** — a project passing one passes all three.

> **So B/C = 0.85 necessarily means NPV < 0 and IRR < 12%.** The three cannot disagree, which is a useful consistency check on any appraisal.

**Where they differ is in RANKING projects rather than accepting them:**

> **NPV measures the ABSOLUTE value created; B/C measures value per rupee spent.**

> **Under a budget constraint, B/C is the better ranking measure** — it identifies which projects give most for the limited money.

> **Without a constraint, NPV is better** — a large project with a modest B/C may create more total value than a small one with a high B/C.

> **Ranking by the wrong measure is a real error in programme planning**, and it is why both are normally reported.

**And a caution on what belongs in the numerator:**

> **Benefits and costs must be counted consistently and once only.** The commonest abuses are **double-counting benefits** (time saving *and* the vehicle operating cost saving that arises from the same journey), **omitting externalities** (environmental damage, resettlement), and **ignoring the residual value** of long-lived assets.

> **A B/C ratio is only as sound as its numerator**, and a ratio of 0.85 computed honestly may be preferable to a ratio of 1.3 computed optimistically.

examTip.trick: **The threshold is 1, not 0.** A ratio of 0.85 returns 85 paisa per rupee spent — it destroys value. Options (a) and (b) invent thresholds with no basis.
examTip.trap: **The phrase "at 12%" is doing real work** — B/C depends on the discount rate, so the project fails *at that rate*, not absolutely. That qualifier is what makes option (d) right.
examTip.mnemonic: **NPV > 0, B/C > 1 and IRR > discount rate are EQUIVALENT tests** — they cannot disagree. But rank by **B/C under a budget constraint** and by **NPV without one**.

questions.stem: In construction quality management, the difference between quality assurance and quality control is that quality assurance is:
options: Process-oriented and preventive, while quality control is product-oriented and detective
Carried out only by the client, while quality control is carried out by the contractor
Applied after completion, while quality control is applied during construction
Concerned with cost, while quality control is concerned with time
questions.solution:
**Quality assurance is process-oriented and PREVENTIVE; quality control is product-oriented and DETECTIVE.**

**The distinction:**

| | **QUALITY ASSURANCE (QA)** | **QUALITY CONTROL (QC)** |
|---|---|---|
| **Focus** | **The PROCESS** | **The PRODUCT** |
| **Purpose** | **PREVENT defects** | **DETECT defects** |
| **Question asked** | **"Are we working the right way?"** | **"Is this item acceptable?"** |
| **Timing** | **Before and throughout** | **During and after each activity** |
| **Activities** | Procedures, method statements, training, audits, document control | **Testing, inspection, measurement, sampling** |
| Nature | **Proactive** | **Reactive** |

> **QA sets up the system so that defects are unlikely; QC checks whether any got through anyway.**

> **Both are needed** — QA without QC is an untested assumption, and QC without QA means finding the same defects repeatedly without ever removing their cause.

**Concrete examples on a site:**

| Activity | QA or QC |
|---|---|
| **Writing the concreting method statement** | **QA** |
| **Approving the mix design before work starts** | **QA** |
| **Training the gang in compaction technique** | **QA** |
| **Calibrating the batching plant** | **QA** |
| **Taking cube samples and crushing them at 28 days** | **QC** |
| **Slump testing each load** | **QC** |
| **Measuring cover with a cover meter** | **QC** |
| **Rejecting a load that fails its slump test** | **QC** |

> **The cube test is the clearest QC example** — it examines the product after the fact and can only tell you whether what was already placed is acceptable.

> **Calibrating the batching plant is the corresponding QA action**: it reduces the chance of a bad batch ever being made.

**Why the distractors are wrong:**

> **Option (b) misattributes them to parties.** Both the contractor and the client operate QA and QC. **The contractor has primary responsibility for the quality of the work and runs its own QC; the client's representative carries out independent QA audits and QC checks.**

> **Quality is not a client function that the contractor merely submits to** — a contractor without its own quality system cannot deliver.

> **Option (c) inverts the timing.** QA comes **first**, before work begins, because prevention must precede the activity. Applying QA after completion would be pointless — there is nothing left to prevent.

> **Option (d) confuses the quality dimension with the cost and time dimensions**, which are the other two corners of the project management triangle. **Quality, cost and time are the three constraints, and QA/QC both belong to the quality corner.**

**Where they sit in the wider framework:**

| Level | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **QC — quality control** | **Inspection and testing of the output** |
| **QA — quality assurance** | **The system that makes the output right** |
| **TQM — total quality management** | **An organisation-wide culture of CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT** |

> **The progression is from checking the product, to managing the process, to changing the organisation** — each level containing the one before it.

> **TQM is where CONTINUOUS IMPROVEMENT (kaizen, the Deming PDCA cycle) belongs**, and it is worth distinguishing from **progressive elaboration**, which is about adding detail to a plan rather than improving a process.

**And the economic argument for QA over QC:**

> **The cost of correcting a defect rises steeply the later it is found.**

| Found at | Relative cost to fix |
|---|---|
| **Design stage** | **Lowest** |
| During construction | Moderate |
| **After completion** | **High — rework, delay, disruption** |
| **In service** | **Highest — plus liability and reputational cost** |

> **QC finds defects late by its nature, because it inspects finished work.** QA is what moves the discovery earlier, or prevents it entirely.

> **Which is why a well-run project invests in method statements, mix approvals, trials and training before pouring anything** — and why the documents that look like paperwork are in fact the cheapest quality measure available.

**The contract link:** **SPECIFICATIONS define the required quality**, and the distinction between **prescriptive** specifications (which state the method, so the employer bears the risk of the result) and **performance** specifications (which state the result, leaving method and risk with the contractor) determines **whose QA system governs.**

examTip.trick: **QA asks "are we working the right way?"; QC asks "is this item acceptable?"** Process versus product, prevention versus detection. Calibrating the batching plant is QA; crushing the cube is QC.
examTip.trap: **Option (b) misattributes them to parties** — both client and contractor run QA and QC. And option (c) inverts the timing: QA must come FIRST, since prevention precedes the activity.
examTip.mnemonic: **The cost of fixing a defect rises steeply the later it is found** — design, construction, completion, service. QC inspects finished work and so finds defects late; QA is what moves discovery earlier.
